And they come to visits armed with all sorts of info that they have gotten from there. And they really are saying much more loudly what they want for treatment versus a decade ago. Back then, they weren’t showing up with anything and the conversation was very one-sided in terms of the pediatrician saying, okay, we’re going to try this, this, and this. And now it’s very much moved into shared decision-making space. I think that’s ultimately a good thing. But we need to learn a lot more, a lot more. Pareeta Kotecha A graduate student at the University of Florida’s College of Pharmacy. Kotecha was the lead author of a systemic review published last year that examined the effectiveness and safety of GLP-1s in children and teens. What we know about GLP-1 medications for the treatment of obesity in children and adolescents is encouraging but still incomplete. Our team recently conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis of 18 randomized clinical trials involving more than 1,400 children and adolescents between 6 and 17 years of age. Importantly, these trials did not all study GLP-1 medications for obesity: 11 were conducted in young people with obesity, six in those with type 2 diabetes, and one in those with prediabetes. Overall, GLP-1 receptor agonists improved both weight-related and metabolic outcomes. Weight and BMI improvements were particularly evident in trials focused on obesity, while improvements in glycemic control were especially relevant in trials involving young people with type 2 diabetes. We also found improvement in systolic blood pressure. It is also important to recognize that pediatric GLP-1 use does not represent a single indication or age group. In the United States, certain GLP-1 medications are FDA-approved for the treatment of obesity in adolescents starting at age 12, while some GLP-1 receptor agonists are approved for type 2 diabetes starting at age 10. These populations can overlap, since obesity commonly coexists with type 2 diabetes in young people. This makes it important, particularly when interpreting real-world prescribing trends, to understand why the medication was prescribed rather than assuming that every GLP-1 prescription in a young person represents treatment specifically for obesity. The safety picture also requires nuance. Gastrointestinal side effects were more common with GLP-1 medications, which is consistent with what we see in adults. Reassuringly, in the randomized trials we analyzed, we did not find significant differences between GLP-1 medications and placebo in treatment discontinuation, depression, or suicidal thoughts or behaviors. At the same time, absence of a statistically significant safety signal does not mean that every potential risk has been definitively ruled out. The duration and size of existing randomized trials may not be sufficient to characterize uncommon adverse events or outcomes that could emerge with longer-term treatment. There are also important outcomes for which evidence remains limited. For example, eating disorders were not reported as an outcome in the trials included in our analysis, so we cannot draw conclusions from these trials about how GLP-1 treatment may affect disordered eating or eating-disorder risk in young people. This is an area that warrants further investigation. That is why I think the conversation should move beyond whether these drugs are simply “good” or “bad” for children. Obesity itself is a chronic disease with consequences that can accumulate over a lifetime, and effective treatment earlier in life could potentially reduce future metabolic and cardiovascular complications. At the same time, children and adolescents are still growing and developing, and we need better long-term evidence about outcomes such as growth, nutrition, mental health, eating disorders, weight trajectories after treatment discontinuation, and uncommon or delayed adverse effects. This need for evidence is becoming increasingly important as GLP-1 use among young people rises rapidly. Continued real-world evidence will therefore be critical for understanding long-term safety, treatment patterns, and outcomes in children and adolescents who receive these medications. Tahniat Syed A clinical associate professor of pediatrics at the University of Pittsburgh School of Medicine and clinical director for the Center for Adolescent and Young Adult Health at the UPMC Children’s Hospital of Pittsburgh. I think we know a lot at this point. First of all, the diagnosis of being overweight or having obesity is something that has been well defined. In pediatrics we use growth percentiles to track weight. And those who track above the 95th percentile are considered to be in the obesity range, as opposed to adults, where we use a body mass index and typically over 30. Children are growing and developing. They’re going through puberty. Their height is changing. So many aspects of their lives are changing pretty rapidly. So you want to make sure that you have the correct diagnosis of obesity and that you’re treating the correct thing. And there are a variety of anti-obesity medications, including GLP-1s. A GLP-1 drug, its full name is a GLP-1 receptor agonist. We have receptors all throughout your body, including receptors for GLP-1 in particular. So when you’re stimulating this receptor by providing an agonist, what that’s going to do is that it’s going to help your body to actually secrete more insulin to help you digest food. It will slow down the gastric emptying. That helps you feel more full and also acts at the brain level to help with satisfying your hunger. And then it also does some other things that we’re still learning about. So it helps how your metabolism works and potentially increases that a little bit, and it helps with some impulse control. A lot of times what my patients tell me is that what these drugs really, really help with is, quote unquote, food noise. Without being asked, they’ll comment that it’s quieted their food noise. And we know from the studies that have been conducted since 2021 that these GLP-1 receptor agonists are effective at decreasing weight. We’re seeing meaningful weight loss. Meaningful in the sense that it will help with metabolic conditions if they already have that. And that, in turn, helps in so many other ways. It’s important to remember that GLP-1 medications for adolescence are indicated for obesity. So it’s not indicated for a patient as treatment for an eating disorder. But does someone with obesity have disordered eating? Typically, they do, because that’s what this food noise is. There are different forms of eating disorders. A lot of times when people are referring to, quote, unquote, eating disorders, they’re referring to anorexia nervosa, which is when someone has a severe intentional restriction of calories such that they become very underweight, very undernourished. And that’s actually a thought disorder where they believe that they are bigger than what they are, so they restrict calories further to become smaller. But another eating disorder is called binge eating disorder, and that’s where there may be some overlap of what you find when you’re questioning someone who has obesity. There’s also hyperphagia, which refers to having this internal feeling of like needing to eat more and more. There’s sort of this fine line between hyperphagia and binge eating, and then you can also have obesity. I actually just saw a patient just before I came on the phone with you who came to me for weight management, and she has a binge eating disorder. So I’m treating her binge eating disorder and also uncovered that she has anxiety. Those are the things I’m treating while we get to the point of stabilizing her weight and actually helping her weight to come down a little bit. Alaina Vidmar Medical director of obesity medicine and bariatric surgery at Children’s Hospital Los Angeles. I think first and foremost, it’s important just to acknowledge that pediatric obesity is a complex chronic disease. So we know that it’s not the fault of the young person or their parents; it’s really a sort of difference in their biology, in how their brain controls when they’re hungry and when they’re full and how their body uses their calories for energy. But now we have a growing toolkit of ways to help young people living in larger bodies to achieve greater health over time. It’s really not about the number on the scale or the size of one’s body, but we want to help kids to hopefully prevent things like diabetes, high blood pressure, and high cholesterol from developing over time. That toolkit has expanded over the last several years to include oral medications and injectable medications, and it’s continuing to expand over time. So we can really take a shared decision-making model to connect with the patient family and understand what is the best tool for us to use for the patient in front of us, while acknowledging that every medication has a different efficacy and a different side effect profile. We can target and really find the best treatment for the kid we’re taking care of. Certainly we’ve been getting a lot of data quickly over the last few years, which is excellent. But I think the biggest thing we want to understand is: How do we best use the medications for various ages? There are lots of different groups who are studying them in younger kids, teenagers, and just spanning the pediatric lifespan. I also think we want to understand who they work the best for. So are there certain patients who respond better to certain medications, and is there any way to predict which medications are going to have which side effects in which kids? Or the flip of that, can we predict which patients are going to have the best effect from a certain medication? There’s a precision approach that we’re hoping to achieve. We do have to acknowledge that just like pediatric obesity is a really complex chronic disease, disordered eating is also another complex chronic disease, and kids can be living with both of them simultaneously. So we need to be thoughtful stewards of both how we screen and uncover multiple chronic diseases that a young person could be living with, and then also how our treatments could be either a part of treating both of them or uncovering another disease that needs to be taken care of. I think that comes from really thoughtful histories that we take where we learn about patients—what is their own history, their family history? And then we also have to thoughtfully monitor treatment over time, just like you would with any kind of response to a medication. We want to understand how this medication changes your eating behaviors or your relationship with food. That’s something we can gather so we can help make sure our patients have what they need to be successful. Lastly, it would be great to understand how we use these medications long-term. I think a lot of us, when we think about obesity as a complex chronic disease, we understand that there’s going to be a cohort of these young people that might need these medications long-term into adulthood. So what does it look like for them? And then what does it look like to take them into a maintenance period? Maybe you need a treatment dose for several years, and then you decrease to a lower dose or [taper off]. And so I think understanding what those algorithms look like and how best to help support patients and families as they’re traversing that would be very helpful. Giz Asks is a recurring Gizmodo series in which experts answer big questions in their own words, offering a range of perspectives on the ideas, discoveries, and debates that affect our lives and shape our understanding of the world.

item.title: LG Denies Its TVs Are Spying on You (Unless You Opted In)
item.description:
Source: Gizmodo Score: 5.19
LG is pushing back against claims that its TVs eavesdrop on owners constantly after a joint report by Gamers Nexus and Level1Techs discovered unsettling details about how much data it phones home—including when the devices are offline or in standby mode. The report used packet capture and firmware analysis to conclude that a range of LG retail OLED TVs scan local area networks to identify devices like phones and smartwatches, as well as the location data of nearby Wi-Fi networks, for LG Ad Solutions. Gamers Nexus and Level1Techs also said they’d found evidence LG TVs also record audio via their microphones, even when on standby or disconnected, and take samples of audio and video data to identify content for advertisers (Automatic Content Recognition or ACR, which is ubiquitous). In a statement on Saturday, LG wrote that “LG smart TVs do not continuously record or transmit users’ conversations.” Instead, the company argued, LG TVs only record voices when users state a wake word or hit a corresponding voice/AI button on a remote control. (“Continuously” is a bit of a weasel word, as the original report contained a clip of an LG TV transcribing ambient conversation long after the authors had stopped addressing it.) “Audio used for wake-word detection is processed locally on the TV and, if no wake word is detected, audio is not converted to text, stored, or transmitted,” LG wrote. That process may generate “voice-recognition results and related technical logs,” and TVs may use speech-recognition results “to support voice-related features” but don’t later upload that data if it’s recorded while the TV is offline or disconnected. Finally, LG stated that “Automatic Content Recognition (ACR), voice recognition, and interest-based advertising are optional” and opt-in on their TVs. It stated its ACR features record audio samples via a TV’s internal audio processor, not a speaker, and “does not collect screenshots, screen recordings, video recordings, voice recordings, or other audio recordings” from a device. As Pocket Lint noted in its guide to turn off data collection on LG TVs—requiring five separate steps—LG’s “opt-in” process slips itself into the middle of a bunch of user agreements during initial setup. The Next Web argued that European regulators may want to look into whether LG’s consent processes comply with the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) and ePrivacy rules, though Americans are probably out of luck. “People often consent to things they don’t fully understand during a speedy setup—they just want to get the thing done and up and working,” Newcastle University Professor of Law, Innovation, and Society Lillian Edwards told TechRadar. Consumer Reports has a rundown on how to disable ACR across most major TV manufacturers, though you could also do what I do: Plug in an Xbox and never connect the TV itself to the internet in the first place.

item.title: Massive Footprints Found in North Dakota Reveal How T. Rex Walked
item.description:
Source: Gizmodo Score: 4.82
Few dinosaurs are as instantly recognizable as Tyrannosaurus rex, and its fossil remains have been found across western North America. While the bones and teeth of this iconic predator are relatively well known, evidence of how it actually moved across the ancient landscape is far rarer. Now, the discovery of a series of giant footprints offers scientists a rare glimpse into the movement of one of the most famous dinosaurs ever to walk the Earth. A team of paleontologists have uncovered four three-toed footprints left behind by an adult T. rex in the Hell Creek Formation of southwestern North Dakota. While isolated footprints from the apex predator have been found before, the recent discovery marks the first known trackway of a fully grown T. rex. The findings, published in the Journal of Vertebrate Paleontology, provide new insight into the behavior of the famous dinosaur as it moseyed its way across an ancient path millions of years ago. 1, 2 step The trackway was first discovered in 2025 on federal land near the town of Marmath, North Dakota. A team of scientists from the Denver Museum of Nature & Science and Liverpool John Moores University in England identified the footprints as belonging to T. rex due to their massive size and narrow shape of the toes. “Bones tell us an enormous amount about these animals, but footprints capture a moment of behavior,” Tyler Lyson, senior curator of vertebrate paleontology at the Denver Museum of Nature & Science and co-author of the new study, said in a statement. “With a trackway, we can actually follow an animal as it moved across the landscape. That is incredibly rare for T. rex.” The researchers imaged each footprint using a high-resolution 3D surface scanner, allowing them to examine the tracks in detail. The entire trackway measures 23-feet long (7 meters), and includes two left and two right footprints. Each of the footprints is about 3 feet (0.91 meters) long, with a stride of about 13 feet (3.96 meters). The trackway dates back to about 66.5 million years ago, according to the study. Casual stroll Based on its path, this particular dinosaur was not in a hurry. The researchers estimate that the T. rex was walking at a pace of approximately 3.5 to 4.5 miles per hour (5.6 to 7.2 kilometers per hour). That’s comparable to a brisk walking speed for a human. The team of paleontologists is planning to excavate three of the four footprints later this year and transport them to the Denver Museum of Nature & Science by helicopter. “As a teacher, I’m always telling my students that science starts with curiosity, passion and careful observation,” Kent M. Hups, a teacher at Northglenn High School who discovered the site and co-author of the paper, said. ”I never imagined that could lead me to a discovery like this.”

item.title: Scientists Thought Ancient Water Carved Martian Gullies. New Analysis Says Otherwise
item.description:
Source: Gizmodo Score: 4.62
Ever since spotting gullies on Mars, scientists really hoped that they meant our neighboring planet once harbored liquid water. Then, in 2014, NASA put a damper on that theory; the gullies were a lot younger than we thought. Instead of water, seasonal freezing of carbon dioxide—dry ice—was responsible for these familiar terrains. But now, the mystery shifted: How exactly did frozen carbon dioxide form these gullies? In a new paper, a French team of astrophysicists explores this question in great detail based on decades’ worth of observational data from Mars Express and the Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter. For its analysis, the team specifically studied Sisyphi Cave, a region near the Martian south pole with a criss-cross of gullies. The researchers found two things. First, it really is very unlikely that liquid water had a hand in creating the gullies. Second—and the more surprising result—CO₂ geysers, a popular alternative, also don’t seem to be responsible for the gullies. “Instead, the data favor CO₂-ice-driven fluidization or avalanche processes that can operate during the late stages of seasonal ice sublimation,” the team wrote in the paper, which has yet to be peer-reviewed and is currently available as a preprint on arXiv. The shocking upheaval Gullies, by definition, are trenches typically carved out of the earth by running water. Emphasis on “water.” Needless to say, when NASA’s Mars Global Surveyor sent back images of multiple gullies on Mars, scientists and space enthusiasts were thrilled. This must point to the presence of water—the alleged smoking gun of extraterrestrial life—on our neighboring planet. Cue many, many papers explaining liquid water on Mars. But not all astronomers were on board with this idea. For instance, Australian geologist Nick Hoffman proposed in 2002 that the gullies were formed by frozen carbon dioxide. For that blasphemy, Hoffman was reportedly met with a lot of skepticism from colleagues—but of course, as of 2026, we now know that he wasn’t necessarily on the wrong side of science history. The universe is very funny that way. Pushing beyond Once dry ice escaped “fringe theory” territory, astronomers proposed a number of alternatives, such as CO₂ geysers, aquifers, and snowpacks of ice and dust. But first, for the new work, the team made sure to check that the latest data also reliably ruled out water from the equation. The researchers could not find any spectral signals associated with water during Martian spring, when the gullies form, according to the paper. Then, the team compared the timing of gully formation with the occurrence of CO₂ geysers. However, there was a “clear temporal mismatch” between the two; the dark spots formed via geyser activity appeared much earlier than gullies. It’s possible that there is some connection between geysers and gullies, but the timing and physical constraints make the correlation rather faint, the team explained in the study. Martian equifinality While the researchers didn’t go into too much detail about alternatives, they did mention that one possible explanation is CO₂ ice-driven sublimation. In this scenario, turbulent carbon dioxide gas bubbles serve as a lubricant that allows dry ice and dust to levitate, kind of like how an air hockey puck is suspended midair thanks to a thin cushion of air beneath it. Then, this amalgam of Martian ice and regolith flows down the surface, carving out a gully. The resulting terrain is just like a gully we see on Earth, but formed through different means. The team added that gullies at lower altitudes may or may not share this process, and, again, it’s too early to completely disregard geysers. Importantly, the gullies are far from being the only thing scientists are counting on to find water on Mars.

item.title: iOS 27 and Siri AI Are Officially Available to Download
item.description:
Source: Gizmodo Score: 4.57
Did you want to check out what all the hubbub was about with Siri AI? Starting today, Sept. 14, you can finally download iOS 27 to your compatible iPhone. Just as promised, iOS 27 brings us Siri AI, with the age-old assistant now capable of understanding personal context based on your texts, emails, calendar events, and more. The update grants Siri the ability to take actions on your behalf, like taking some appointment details from your texts and adding them to your calendar. Apple still calls Siri AI a “beta,” essentially admitting that the chatbot is still fully capable of screwing something up. As is always the case with AI, it’s a buyer beware situation. Users who update will find a dedicated Siri app that’s built to either handle new chatbot prompts or change Siri settings. If you have an iPhone 17, an M3 MacBook Air or M3 MacBook Pro, or an M4 iPad or later, you can also change Siri’s pitch, speed, and accent. Here’s something else you need to know: Siri AI is rolling out in English first. You’ll have to wait until October for French, Japanese, Korean, Portuguese, and Spanish. As always, if you don’t see the update on your iPhone, just give it a few hours and you should find it propagate in your device settings. iOS 27 introduces a few more Apple Intelligence features, including more refined photo editing tools with capabilities for “spatial reframing.” That essentially allows you to mess with the perspective of a photo after it’s already been taken, though it relies on AI image generation to input the missing pixels. There are several more additions to iOS 27 that have nothing to do with AI, including several changes to the ever-controversial Liquid Glass aesthetic. You now have access to a Liquid Glass opacity slider, which lets you decrease the amount of transparency for your app icons and UI elements. For parents out there, Apple has also created new child safety features that let you restrict your children’s ability to visit certain websites or limit their screentime across specific apps. Apple is also bringing the new macOS 27, iPadOS 27, watchOS 27, and visionOS 27 to all recent devices. For instance, a Vision Pro will now let you set your own panorama as a “spatial scene” you can reside within the headset. macOS Golden Gate in particular has a few unique features alongside Siri AI, including the ability to use a chatbot interface to create new Shortcuts automatications for your laptop or desktop. Recent Apple Watches receive a “Workout Buddy” feature, though if you want to talk to Apple’s AI through your wrist, you’ll need to own an Apple Watch Series 9, Apple Watch SE 3, or Apple Watch Ultra 2 or later to get all the new capabilities. Let us know what you think of the updates. Gizmodo will be sure to let you know how they interact with the upcoming iPhone 18 Pros, Apple Watch Series 12, and M6 Mac mini as they roll out over the next few weeks.

item.title: A Boy Spent 8 Hours a Day With a Laptop on His Body. He Ended Up With ‘Toasted Skin’
item.description:
Source: Gizmodo Score: 4.56
The harms of screen time can even extend to your skin, a new case report shows—at least if you’re keeping a warm screen hugged to your body for too long. Doctors in the UK recently detailed the case of a boy with a peculiar skin condition. He developed a bruise-like rash from spending hours of his day with a laptop resting on his abdomen. Thankfully, the heat-triggered condition is usually benign and reversible, and once the boy stopped using himself as a laptop dock, his skin cleared up. “Early recognition is important to prevent misdiagnosis and avoidable radiation exposure,” the authors wrote in their paper, published this month in BMJ Case Reports. ‘Toasted skin syndrome’ The skin condition is formally called erythema ab igne, or EAI. It’s also more colorfully known as “toasted skin syndrome.” It’s caused by repeated and prolonged exposure to low levels of heat and/or infrared radiation. Though this exposure doesn’t lead to immediate burns, it can still damage the skin and its underlying blood vessels and elastic fibers given enough time. The doctors provide no specific age for this boy in this case, calling him “mid-childhood.” According to the report, he visited the emergency room with reddish-brown lesions in a net-like pattern on his lower abdomen originally described by a nurse as “spontaneous bruising.” His skin had started changing a week earlier, but he only told his parents after it failed to improve and grew darker. Neither him nor his parents could think of any likely cause, and early tests failed to uncover a glaring culprit. Though doctors initially suspected a possible liver injury, the boy felt and seemed normal otherwise, making that unlikely. While having his blood drawn, the boy stated he and his sibling had been playfighting a week earlier, and that he had gotten pushed into a chair at some point (the boy didn’t mention the incident at first for fear of getting his sibling in trouble). Doctors then thought he might have had a mild traumatic injury, but imaging scans failed to support that idea either. With little else to go on, the boy was discharged with an antibiotic prescription and advice to keep an eye on his condition. Weeks later, the boy returned with a larger and worsening rash, along with increased tenderness. The lesions now had pink-hued patches, indicating a breakdown of the skin and its underlying tissues. This led the doctors to completely throw out the bruising theory. The boy and family initially said no when asked about common heat sources, but upon further questioning this time, the doctors learned the boy was homeschooled and that he routinely used a laptop during the day. The boy then revealed that he frequently rested the laptop on his abdomen for up to eight hours a day, often while charging it. With that key detail and a lack of other plausible explanations, the doctors diagnosed the boy with EAI. Toasty but temporary Toasted skin syndrome usually isn’t too serious and is treated by simply removing the source of exposure. If the condition goes untreated for too long, though, it can cause permanent discoloration of the skin. The condition might also raise the risk of certain skin cancers, though this seems to be a rare occurrence that can take years, even decades, of prolonged exposure to manifest. In this case, the doctors applied a wound dressing to the boy’s affected skin and told him to keep his abdomen laptop-free from now on. Several months later, the boy’s father told the doctors over the phone that his skin gradually improved and was now rash-free. Though toasted skin syndrome is a condition that’s been documented for centuries, historically among bakers and other professions working with hot objects, laptops and other electronic devices have become a more frequent source of exposure in the modern day. The authors say the condition is typically well-recognized when it happens in adults, but might be more likely to go unnoticed in children. The covid-19 pandemic may have also had an indirect effect on cases lately via the rise of remote learning and prolonged screen time, they add. “This case highlights the importance of considering EAI in children presenting with reticulated rashes, particularly in the context of increasing electronic device use,” the doctors concluded. Personally, I just hope having a cat on your lap or chest isn’t hot enough to cause toasted skin, because otherwise I could be in trouble down the line.

item.title: Apple May Pivot the Beats Brand Into a Way of Marketing Less Polished Products, Starting With Gamer Gear
item.description:
Source: Gizmodo Score: 4.12
Did you ever drive a Scion? Status-obsessed people may have scoffed at your budget-friendly car, but you probably knew at the time it was just a Toyota with a different nameplate on it. According to a new report from Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman, Apple may be looking to turn the Beats brand into a similar repository for lower-priced goods. A couple weeks ago, hidden code was found, seemingly exposing a secret Apple project aimed at developing gaming controllers—perhaps not unlike some of the cool and fun-to-use third-party accessories that already exist. And Gurman now says his anonymous inside sources have told him Apple “has indeed been working on gaming controllers for the iPhone for a bit over a year.” However, Gurman claims, the controllers Apple has in mind may never carry Apple branding. The controller idea is being developed under the aegis of Beats, Gurman writes. At the same time, he says, Apple has begun to use Beats as a potential spigot for experimental, un-Apple-like product possibilities. You may recall that Beats began as a headphones brand at one time owned by music executive Jimmy Iovine and AI-loving rapper and music producer Dr. Dre., and Apple bought it in 2014 for $3 billion, (in a transaction that was not without its share of drama). Beats does indeed make a ton of good headphones that don’t get quite as much press as AirPods. But Gurman says Apple increasingly sees Beats as a way to “capitalize on the third-party accessories market” more broadly, without impacting the Apple brand. Did you know, for instance, that Beats, and therefore Apple, makes an $18.99 woven USB-C cable? Marketing a gaming controller is tricky if you’re Apple, Gurman says, because in order to sell well, it can’t exactly require the consumer to be at, let’s say, the Vision Pro income level. That means Apple may steer clear of premium materials and high-status finishes that make an Apple product read as an Apple product the second you see it. “The culture and lifestyle around gaming controllers also could fit naturally under the Beats umbrella,” Gurman claims.

item.title: Universal Studios Japan Celebrates Halloween With First R-Rated Attraction
item.description:
Source: Gizmodo Score: 3.75
Theme parks tend to do a little something extra for Halloween, and this year, Universal Studios Japan is doing even more extra for the occasion. With this year being the park’s 25th anniversary, Japanese attendees will get to experience two big horror-focused attractions. First is Zanzō (or Lights Out: Nightmare Isolation), where guests enter a facility that’s researching nightmares. As they’re tasked with getting out of private rooms housing “unescapable situations” with others or on their own, attendees will be “slowly consumed by a fear [with] no end.” As the translated press preview notes, this is the USJ’s first R-18 attraction, and will require a signed waiver before going in. If that doesn’t sound like your thing, Universal Studios Japan also has an attraction based around Capcom’s Resident Evil Requiem. Known as The Dive, parkgoers will explore recreations of the Wrenwood Hotel and Rhodes Hill Chronic Center, two of that game’s major locations. Expect “creatures attacking from every action,” including The Girl and the Kitchen Chef. Resident Evil has been at many a Halloween Horror Night at Universal Studios Japan. The inclusion here isn’t just because the franchise (known locally as Biohazard) turns 30 this year, it’s also to help celebrate the annual event. HHN celebrates two anniversaries this year—the 25th for its Orlando launch in 1991, and its 15th for Singapore’s in 2011. Japan wouldn’t get this until 2012, but the timing’s apparently too good to not celebrate its local 15th a little ahead of schedule. For anyone traveling as the year winds down and headed for Universal Studios Japan, Zanzō will be around until November 8, and Resident Evil Requiem: The Dive until December 27. The former will cost extra to get in, while The Dive is included with admission. Want more io9 news? item.title: Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei Calls for Pause in AI Development, Sort Of
item.description:
Source: Gizmodo Score: 3.72
After yet another whirlwind week of AI developers making wild claims about how it could kill the entire human race, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei has a pitch: Let’s slow this whole thing down a little. Amodei wrote in a Saturday blog post that while he remains optimistic AI will be the “latest in a long line of technological miracles that have uplifted and ennobled humanity,” researchers must “pace the frontier” due to risks like rogue AI, use for crime and terrorism, and economic disruption. “Over the last few months, I have become convinced that fully addressing the risks requires even more prudence—not just investing in risk prevention, but pacing the rate of capabilities advancement so that risk prevention has time to keep up,” Amodei wrote. “We must slow the pace at which we improve the capabilities of AI models,” he added. “Progress will still seem fast, and we must make wise use of the time we gain.” Amodei’s proposed plan has three steps, none of which would constitute much of a slowdown on their own. He asks for AI firms to allow embedded third-party evaluators, to coordinate between each other and governments on safety standards, and for the U.S. government to seek global coordination on AI safety (including with “authoritarian governments,” i.e. China and Russia). Those steps on their own wouldn’t slow down the pace of AI development, so Amodei suggested various possible agreements “in order of increasing difficulty.” Those include a narrow agreement prohibiting the most obviously malicious uses of AI like bioweapons, a broader international agreement to test models before release for “acute risks,” a “speed limit” on recursive self-improvement, and a “full pacing, or even ‘pause,'” on AI development between governments. While Amodei wrote he supported the final option, but suggested it was quite unlikely to happen. Rather convenient for him, no? The Anthropic CEO cited an incident this summer in which a swarm of OpenAI bots attacked competitor Hugging Face as particular reason for caution. Anthropic itself said it would allow third-party evaluators after releasing a report this week admitting its models had hacked other companies or exploited vulnerabilities on at least four occasions. Amodei’s letter follows the resignation of an Anthropic researcher, Jacob Coxon, who claimed in a social media post that AI firms are “racing straight to self-improving superintelligence.” He added that industry leaders “earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade.” That helped AI doomerism achieve a sort of crescendo this week, with loud opining from developers, scientists and politicians alike. This is the point where we note that AI doomerism is also a shameless marketing device deployed to convince everyone that these firms are all-powerful, their products inescapable, and their victory inevitable. While it’s obvious AI can be dangerous, there is ample room to be skeptical about what is essentially wild speculation. By exaggerating the risk of apocalyptic consequences, AI firms attempt to steer conversation away from their many other questionable business practices. “Being able to comprehend and reliably navigate novel problems in the messy, open systems of the physical world is an obvious prerequisite for AI systems posing a threat on the scale that the doomers propose,” Duke University tech policy researcher Casey Mock told Nature earlier this year. Current-day AI is nowhere near that point. “The burden of proof should really be on those making the claim that we are on a runaway train toward developing a super intelligence that will exterminate humanity,” Mock added. Nature noted that when University College London researchers polled around 4,000 AI researchers for a March preprint study, just 3% responded that “existential risk” was their top worry (far behind malicious use, job impacts, and hype, to name a few). The New York Times noted that OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and SpaceX/Tesla CEO Elon Musk both immediately agreed with the plan on social media, which should make you deeply suspicious about whatever’s going on.

item.title: The Himalayas Are Melting Faster Than Ever. Scientists Worry Nepal’s Floods Are Just the Beginning
item.description:
Source: Gizmodo Score: 3.35
Over 5,130 people are still missing and at least 1,386 more are confirmed dead in Nepal since a collapsing glacier high atop Langtang Lirung in the Himalayas cascaded into devastating flash floods on August 26, 2026—washing away entire towns and flooding hydroelectric power plants. With hundreds more missing and dozens dead across the border in China and relief crews scrambling to locate an estimated 900 utility workers trapped in Nepal’s wrecked hydroelectric tunnels, a new report warns that the Himalayas’ icy peaks are just beginning their deadly thaw. The roughly 1439 cubic miles (6,000 cubic kilometers) of glacial ice capping Asia’s towering mountain range is now melting 65% faster than it was a decade ago, according to a private industry report conducted with technical assistance from the Indian government. Sustainable development consultancy Systemiq collaborated with India’s Govind Ballabh Pant National Institute of Himalayan Environment and other groups focused on the mountains to produce its assessment. The report warns that the entire region is facing a tipping point of “peak water” by mid-century, a phase of increasingly cataclysmic floods before nearly dry Himalayan peaks cut off fresh water to rivers, reservoirs, and agriculture across large swaths of south Asia. “The Himalayas are the Third Pole,” as economist Nicholas Stern, chair of the London School of Economics’ Grantham Research Institute on Climate Change and the Environment and a member of the UK House of Lords, explained to the BBC. “Unlike the Arctic or Antarctic, this pole has hundreds of millions of people living beneath it.” Slippery slopes If anything, Stern’s analysis vastly undersells the scope of the potential consequences. For one thing, Systemiq’s new report notes that rivers sustained by the Himalayas’ historic hydrological cycle of seasonal glacial growth and melt are ultimately responsible for the food and water security of about 2 billion people. “On current trajectories, the Hindu Kush Himalaya could lose up to 80% of its present glacier volume by 2100,” according to the report, echoing increasingly more dire estimates from the International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development. (Like the Indian government, ICIMOD contributed technical information for Systemiq’s report.) Perhaps the most alarming aspect of these findings, however, is the room for mass-casualty surprises. Only about 21 of the estimated 40,000 glaciers across the Himalayas—and the Karakoram mountain range to its northwest bordering Pakistan, China and India—are monitored by scientists in any sort of detail. Similar concerns plague China’s neighboring Tien Shan mountain range. An unknown tally of unstable glacial lakes are quietly swelling, in other words, with no early warning systems in place for their almost inevitable breach, some on the border between two regional nuclear powers who don’t especially get along. But even with these large unknown variables, what’s known about the meltwater pooling into these makeshift natural dams of loose rock is concerning enough. “India now has close to 200 glacial lakes identified as high risk and almost a quarter being ‘very high risk,’ leaving millions exposed downstream,” Systemiq’s report found. Tipping points India is already feeling the deadly impact of this threat. Although Himalayan land constitutes only about 18% of Indian territory, the region now accounts for as much as 35% of the country’s natural disasters, based on Systemiq’s analysis, which was also conducted in coordination with the Integrated Mountain Initiative (IMI). One notably lethal flash flood in India’s northeast busted dams, buried traffic in mudslides, and killed at least 70 people when the glacial lake South Lhonak ruptured in 2023. But beyond the immediate spectacle of such damage, the report notes that the protracted economic fallout will be no less extreme: Himalayan water supports about 20% of India’s annual GDP, providing hydropower and irrigating wheat, rice, and tea crops, among other basic needs. “The Himalayas are one connected system,” the researchers noted, “but its benefits and its risks are distributed far beyond the mountains themselves, with ripple effects felt in South Asia, and potentially the entire world through supply chain disruptions, climate migrations or geopolitical risk.”

item.title: The ‘V/H/S: SCP’ Movie Doesn’t Involve the Actual SCP Foundation
item.description:
Source: Gizmodo Score: 3.11
Earlier this summer, we learned the V/H/S movies were expanding with a movie focused on the SCP Foundation. As it turns out, things are more complicated than that initial announcement. On Friday, Deadline announced A24 gained worldwide rights to the SCP movie and planned to give it a global theatrical release. Yes, Backrooms has been a hit this year, but the studio’s had other winners this decade, including Undertone from earlier this year and 2024’s Civil War. It’s a big get for the studio and V/H/S as a whole: since 2021, the films have released on Shudder, including this year’s Mixtape movie. The second and third V/H/S film had limited theatrical runs and made tens of thousands during that time, while the original film made $1.9 million. That was in 2012, though, and in that time, horror’s become a much bigger genre that can have some long legs. Given SCP is a collaborative sci-fi/horror project that’s been going on since 2008, the movie can be an easy entry point to theatregoers. It’s surprising, then, to hear the actual SCP Foundation doesn’t actually have anything to do with the film. In a statement to AVClub, the Foundation explained its people tried reaching out to the A24, the filmmakers, and producers, and never got a reply back. What’s more, it said Deadline’s “incorrect” in A24 having worldwide rights, citing terms from the wiki’s Creative Commons ShareAlike license that allows the entire enterprise to exist. Under the license, derivative projects made using the SCP name have to abide by ShareAlike’s rules. Specifically, for this movie to fit within those parameters, the studio would have release it DRM-free and without “any sort of exclusivity with respect to distribution,” aka on YouTube and other streaming platforms at no cost, without taking legal action. The SCP Foundation called out the V/H/S: SCP filmmakers for “having no interest in engaging with the authors or curators of the material they’re adapting.” Nonetheless, it’s open to sitting down and discussing what can be properly done to make the film comply with its license. Given the movie’s vague 2027 release window, there’s plenty of time for more developments and information on the situation to emerge. Want more io9 news?
