item.title: Scientists Warn This Year’s El Niño Could Create Brand New Extreme Weather Patterns
item.description:
Source: Gizmodo Score: 2.98
Something weird happened during the El Niño event of 2023 and 2024. Climate scientists with the National Science Foundation’s National Center for Atmospheric Research (NCAR) in Boulder, Colorado, noticed that the recurring global climate event somehow did not bring the expected wetter seasons to the United States’ southern tier, nor a dry season to its northern regions. But this El Niño’s powerful effects were still felt elsewhere—including punishing droughts in the Amazon, the likes of which Brazil had not seen in 120 years. The explanation, as NCAR’s researchers determined the next year, was that global warming’s slow roasting of tropical Indian and Atlantic Ocean waters had offset El Niño’s effects across North America, disrupting a once reliable pair of climate patterns known as a “teleconnection.” Now, scientists are worried that the current state of climate change is poised to make this year’s extreme El Niño conditions even more unpredictable, according to Bar-Ilan University climate scientist Eran Vos, who spoke to the journal Nature about the issue this month. “We know less about the teleconnections of the new atmosphere,” Vos told Nature, adding that perverse synergies between global warming effects, like rising sea surface temperature, and El Niño’s behavior will make it not only harder to forecast, but consequently harder to prepare for. A chaos theory Speaking to Science News, ecosystem scientist Sergio de Miguel at the University of Lleida and the Joint Research Unit CTFC-Agrotecnio in Spain, likened the phenomena of teleconnections in 2023 to “a kind of complex butterfly effect” where events “in one place have many derivatives very far away.” The recurring regularity of these paired events can last weeks or even years, and they include patterns like the El Niño/Southern Oscillation (ENSO) which has become much discussed as ENSO is the climate teleconnection whose warming helps produce El Niño. Vos and his colleagues have combed through historic meteorological records, hoping to track our warming climate’s countervailing impact on El Niño events. They found that warming patterns created by El Niño across southern Asia and northeast Africa between the years 1960 and 1990 have since bizarrely inverted, leading to colder temperatures in those regions during more modern bouts of El Niño. Elsewhere, in Western Europe, cold snaps tied to El Niño during those same decades have now flipped, consistently correlating to warmer seasons during modern El Niño events. “You change the patterns and the weather reacts,” as Vos told Nature. Uncharted waters But climate change isn’t the only factor leading to a more intense and unpredictable El Niño this year. The 2026 El Niño itself is the first since the late 1990s to be generated by warm ocean temperatures in the eastern Pacific as opposed to the central Pacific. There’s not a lot of precedent from the past three decades of warming years, in other words, to predict how it might behave or how climate teleconnections might alter. Clara Deser, a senior scientist at NCAR, and her coauthors on that study into the odd 2023-24 El Niño season spelled it out this way, “historical precedent may no longer be a reliable guide to ENSO teleconnections as anthropogenic warming patterns intensify.” The sea surface temperatures themselves create uncharted waters, with the atmosphere itself changing too. As Deser told The New York Times this May, “We are now in a different base line climate.”

item.title: In the Wild West of AI, Everybody Is Accusing Everybody Else of Theft
item.description:
Source: Gizmodo Score: 2.93
The AI boom has been fueled by the idea that all data is fair game, potential fodder for the training of new models. Little wonder then that ownership and intellectual property theft have become such sticky issues within the tech industry. On Thursday, Chinese robotics startup JoyIn—developer of a model called Aether—accused OpenAI of distilling its AI systems and stealing its website’s cosmic design aesthetic for the launch and branding of GPT-6 Astra. In an open letter written in Chinese, JoyIn CEO Guo Renjie said his company had started the process of filing a lawsuit, according to a translation from CNBC. (Gizmodo has not independently verified the report.) Distillation is a common industry practice in which developers use a larger, more advanced model as a sort of “teacher” to help train a smaller “student” model. But it’s become a controversial subject in recent months, as major American AI companies, including OpenAI and Anthropic, have repeatedly claimed that competitors in China have been using their proprietary models to conduct large-scale, illicit distillation efforts in order to gain a competitive edge. In a statement published Tuesday, the U.S. Cybersecurity & Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) said that some of the biggest Chinese AI firms—DeepSeek, Moonshot AI, Alibaba, MiniMax, StepFun, and Z.ai—“are conducting systematic extraction of proprietary functionalities and capabilities of U.S. AI companies’ models through industrial-scale knowledge distillation campaigns that form the core—not merely a supplement—of their AI development strategy.” All this was likely being carried out with the knowledge and blessing of the Chinese government, according to CISA. Anthropic also said in a Thursday report that Moonshot, developer of an AI model called Kimi, had been carrying out a mechanical Turk-style trick to make its customers think they were getting responses from Kimi, when in fact they’d been generated by Claude. Guo’s letter to OpenAI is the first known case of a Chinese developer accusing an American company of distillation. It’s far from the first time that OpenAI has been accused of theft, though. The company has had to fend off a litany of lawsuits since the launch of ChatGPT a little under four years ago, filed by artists and news publishers arguing that their copyrighted work was used illegally to train new AI models. (OpenAI has repeatedly defended itself by invoking the so-called “fair use” standard of U.S. copyright law.) In July, Apple sued the company, claiming it had stolen company secrets in order to get its newborn hardware business off the ground. (Again, OpenAI has denied any wrongdoing.) Earlier this week, a NYU mathematics professor questioned whether his work on Codex had been surreptitiously used to train the model that OpenAI used to solve the Navier-Stokes “Millennium Problem.” (OpenAI told the Australian Broadcasting Corporation it “can say categorically that it is impossible for Dr. Buckmaster’s Codex prompts over the last two months to have influenced the system in any way, including training.”) The irony of AI companies calling foul on “illicit” distillation when much of their business model depends on the nonconsensual scraping of online content seems to be lost on OpenAI and Anthropic, both of which are preparing for what are expected to be record-breaking IPOs. At least for the time being, the line between “fair use” and theft within the unregulated AI industry is as hazy as the inner-workings of models themselves.

item.title: Three Batman Movies Return to Theaters Next Week
item.description:
Source: Gizmodo Score: 2.64
Warner Bros. and DC have made Batman Day a September staple for a decade, and for 2026, the occasion means a trip to the movies. For Saturday, September 19 and Sunday, September 20, theatregoers can see Tim Burton’s Batman or the animated flicks Mask of the Phantasm or The Lego Batman Movie on the big screen again. The 1989 movie was back in theaters for its 35th anniversary in 2024, while Mask and Lego have only had their initial theatrical runs. Of the three, the 1989 movie is the highest-grossing ($411.6 million worldwide), followed by Lego ($312 million) and Phantasm ($5.8 million). Beyond money, each of the Batman movies are significant in some fashion. Burton’s movie kickstarted the character’s modern dominance, while Lego’s re-release is nicely timed, given the Legacy of the Dark Knight game from earlier this year. Meanwhile, Mask of the Phantasm wasn’t just the first movie of the DCAU—which Batman: The Animated Series helped kick off—it’s also the only of those films to get a theatrical release. If there’s anything else planned for Batman Day, like a look at The Batman Part II or something for next month’s Clayface, Warner Bros. is keeping that under wraps. Even if there’s not, three pretty good movies covering different parts of the character’s history is good on its own, especially if you were too young or weren’t alive to see these on the big screen when they first came out. Want more io9 news? Check out the best movies and TV shows to stream this month and all the upcoming sci-fi, fantasy, and horror books that should be on your radar.

item.title: Crypto’s Latest Stablecoin Innovation? Chargebacks.
item.description:
Source: Gizmodo Score: 2.32
For more than a decade, a core gospel of crypto has been permissionless, censorship-resistant transactions. If you send someone cryptocurrency, it is gone, and no central authority can force a refund. The industry spent years marketing this rigidity as a revolutionary feature that would liberate global commerce from the slow, expensive clawback mechanisms of credit cards and banks. incredible levels of innovation https://t.co/4PNtjXoJ64 — Alex B 👾 (@bergealex4) September 11, 2026 Now, that foundational ideology is colliding head-on with the messy reality of actual human commerce in the search for mainstream, widespread use cases. Earlier this month, a stablecoin payments startup called Payy announced a new product named Finality. Despite the uncompromising name, the entire pitch for Finality is that it adds a chargeback-like dispute layer directly onto stablecoin transactions, which themselves already reintroduce third-party trust through their behind-the-scenes use of the traditional banking system. Finality does not actually modify the underlying blockchain or magically reverse transactions on a public ledger. Instead, it places a dispute-resolution wrap around the settlement. But in many ways, it appears to simply be a technical bandage for the realization that when you remove all consumer protections from a payment rail, businesses and shoppers do not actually want to use it. In other words, there are sometimes good reasons for payments to be reversible or slow, like safety and security. What Payy Is Actually Announcing The mechanics of Payy’s new network, as detailed in its announcement thread on X, operate entirely through a combination of smart contracts and economic incentives. When a sender creates a stablecoin payment, they choose a “short clawback window”. The merchant receives the funds immediately, while liquidity providers step in to back the payment protection during that window. If a dispute arises over fraud, human error, or commercial disagreements, the sender can submit a claim alongside supporting evidence. A neutral arbitrator then reviews the case. If they approve the clawback, the system returns the protected funds to the sender without reversing the original blockchain transaction. Payy argues that this approach solves a massive obstacle for businesses. In its announcement, Payy claims that trillions of dollars are transacted annually without any way to dispute a single payment. But like most crypto industry metrics, that headline figure is almost certainly overblown. Stablecoin transaction volumes are heavily inflated due to the counting of every on-chain stablecoin transaction as a worthy data point, with only about 1% of those transfers actually representing real-world payments. The firm notes that while stablecoins make payments instant and global, irreversible settlement can turn a routine exception into a permanent loss. The Rediscovery of Traditional Finance Ultimately, the crypto industry is rediscovering why mainstream payment systems evolved the way they did. Building a credit card network or a commercial banking system requires dealing with the fact that people make mistakes and bad actors steal. Credit card chargebacks were not invented simply to enrich banks or payment processors. They were created to give consumers the confidence to spend money without worrying that a single typo or a fraudulent merchant would wipe out their savings. From a practical perspective, it’s worth asking whether Payy’s system that combines chargeback protections, neutral arbitrators, and liquidity pools is much different from the traditional systems crypto was supposed to destroy. For a consumer or merchant, a system that claws back funds through an arbitrator is a chargeback system, regardless of whether the technical settlement on the blockchain remains untouched. What the actual fuck? How can you use the name Finality for a chargeback program with a straight face? https://t.co/Jijqw5sL1a — Steven Roose (@stevenroose3) September 11, 2026 The irony of this technical workaround was not lost on observers. On X, Second CEO Steven Roose asked, “How can you use the name Finality for a chargeback program with a straight face?” Ark Labs Head of Ecosystem Alex Bergeron similarly mocked the announcement as representing “incredible levels of innovation.” Both Roose and Bergeron work on different implementations of Ark, a Bitcoin payments protocol. Payy’s Sid Gandhi responded to skepticism on X by explaining that the underlying blockchain transaction cannot be reversed and that Finality is an economic model, not a technical change. Technically, that is true, but it is also in some ways a distinction without a practical difference. It’s also worth pointing out that Payy referred to this as a system of “chargebacks for stablecoins” in their original announcement. This desire to build layers around stablecoins to mimic traditional finance looks even sillier when you realize stablecoin transactions are already far from final in their current form. Major stablecoin issuers like Tether and Circle maintain backdoors that allow them to freeze assets. For example, Tether froze $344 million in USDT in April after U.S. authorities identified links to Iranian activity, while Circle has been criticized for not using their power to freeze more proactively during security incidents. Indeed, traditional financial institutions, such as U.S. Bank, also find this level of central control incredibly appealing. More recently, tokenized stocks have been gaining traction as another reinvention of traditional finance on blockchain rails, and the blockchain rails themselves are also increasingly becoming corporation-operated technologies (see Robinhood’s Robinhood Chain). Why Blockchains are Used This pivot toward centralized control and consumer-friendly safety nets stands in stark contrast to the original ideals of the sector. During Bitcoin’s block size war, which raged from 2015 to 2017, participants fought a bitter philosophical battle over whether the network should prioritize cheap, fast payments or stricter decentralization. Developers and users resisted scaling changes that would increase node requirements, fearing the network would lose its censorship-resistant nature and mutate into a corporate-controlled “PayPal 2.0.” A decade later, those fears look prophetic. However, the compromise has occurred on alternative blockchains like Ethereum and Solana rather than Bitcoin itself. Instead of a peer-to-peer network of sovereign nodes, the modern landscape is dominated by centrally-issued stablecoins and tokenized assets running on corporate infrastructure. Now, the New York Stock Exchange is building its own tokenized stock platform, choosing to construct its own proprietary, private blockchain infrastructure for settlement rather than running on public crypto networks. Similarly, Circle is rolling out its own blockchain network to further centralize the crypto tech stack around its USDC stablecoin. On top of those examples, a 140-company consortium backed by Visa, Mastercard, and BlackRock recently launched the Open USD stablecoin project in an effort to create the stablecoin to end all stablecoins. Isn't that what they did with Base? — Kyle Torpey (@kyletorpey) December 9, 2024 These initiatives illustrate a broader, recurring crypto pattern. Startups and institutions take traditional financial concepts, strip them of their original regulatory obligations by placing them on a blockchain, and use that regulatory arbitrage to gain users and customers. Payy’s dispute-resolution overlay is an example of how much of the traditional system is then oftentimes effectively reinvented on top of those new blockchain rails at a later date. In reality, the closer crypto gets to offering a viable payments system for everyday commerce, the more it starts to resemble the legacy systems it was intended to replace. Indeed, the primary argument for using blockchain rails for stablecoins and tokenized stocks often boils down to regulatory arbitrage. Financial institutions can bypass conventional requirements by putting transactions on a ledger, even as they continue to extract the vast majority of the revenue. The end result is a new financial system that is just as centralized and intermediated as the old banking system, but with fewer regulatory burdens for those extracting value from it.

item.title: Your Ethernet adapter is negotiating itself down to 2003 speeds—here's how to fix it
item.description:
Source: How-To Geek Score: 5.95
Switching to Ethernet was simultaneously the best and the cheapest network upgrade I've ever gotten. Simply ditching Wi-Fi for a cable is fantastic, and in most cases, it improves your connection tremendously. But what if one Ethernet-related setting actually makes your PC feel slow? That can happen, and after some digging, I found the culprit. Speed & Duplex decides how fast your Ethernet link actually runs Auto Negotiation is doing more than you might think If you've never heard of Speed & Duplex, I won't blame you, but this is actually a pretty important setting. It controls how your Ethernet adapter talks to the device at the other end of the cable. Most of the time, that'll be your router. The "speed" part of the name determines whether that link runs at, say, 100Mbps, 1Gbps, or 2.5Gbps. Duplex, on the other hand, decides whether data can travel in both directions at the same time. It shouldn't surprise you that modern Ethernet usually uses full duplex. The reason I said that if you've never heard of this setting, I won't blame you, is that it's pretty niche. Under normal circumstances, you shouldn't have to choose any of this yourself, and that's because of Auto Negotiation, which lets your PC's network adapter and the router/switch compare what they both support and agree on the best compatible link speed and duplex mode. It's not much unlike what USB cables and ports do. To check this setting for yourself in Windows, go to the Device Manager, then expand network adapters. Right-click your Ethernet adapter, and choose Properties > Advanced. Then, dig for Speed & Duplex or a similarly named setting, and select Auto Negotiation. 99% of the time, Auto Negotiation is exactly what you want. This usually isn't the case of needing to tweak something manually, and forcing your connection to 1Gbps or 2.5Gbps doesn't make it faster if the connection (the entire connection, hardware and all) isn't prepared to handle it. Worse yet, doing so can actually mess things up instead of helping. The interesting thing is what happens when Auto Negotiation doesn't land on the speed you expected, and that's why this setting is worth checking. That'll be your first sign to dig deeper. A 2.5GbE PC can still end up crawling along You don't want to describe your connection as "crawling," right? So, what does Auto Negotiation have to do with your connection feeling slow? Quite a lot, because the speed it negotiates is the one your Ethernet connection actually runs at, so if something goes wrong along that whole line, your internet might feel incredibly sluggish. First, some numbers. A 2.5GbE connection tops out at 312.5MB/s, and 1Gbps has a raw ceiling of 125MB/s. Meanwhile, 100Mbps crawls along at around 12.5MB/s before overhead. So, if something in the link causes your network adapter to negotiate down to 100Mbps, you're missing out on so much internet speed you might as well hop in a time machine back to 2003. Such a slowdown is going to reverberate throughout your entire connection, unfortunately. Large downloads, streams, gaming—all of that stuff is majorly affected when suddenly the internet speeds you were meant to have just aren't there. Even with a fast PC, most tasks will crawl along at a snail's pace. There's a fix, of course. Don't fix it by forcing the biggest number That doesn't actually help Given what we now know about Speed & Duplex, your first instinct might be to go in there and force the highest number you possibly can, but I'm here to tell you not to do it. Auto Negotiation exists specifically for the purpose of two devices agreeing on a configuration that actually works on both ends. If you end up picking something that works on one end but not the other, it's not like one of the devices can force the other to just somehow learn how to negotiate at a higher speed. Doing this means that at best, you gain a big fat zero, zilch, nothing. At worst, the link can become unstable or fail to come up properly. So, if Auto Negotiation has landed you at 100Mbps even though you expected gigabit Ethernet or better, it means it's time to investigate instead of forcing it to do what you'd like to see. Check what speed was actually negotiated Link speed and internet speed are not one and the same Forcing it isn't the answer, then what is? You just need to check what Auto Negotiation actually gives you. In Windows, you'll find this under Settings > Network & internet > Ethernet if you look for link speed. You can also check your adapter's status in the Control Panel. If you have a gigabit or 2.5GbE connection but Windows reports a slower link, well, there you go. One thing to note: Don't confuse that number with your actual internet speed. Link speed only talks about the connection between your PC and the next device on your local network, which is most commonly a router. Your ISP determines how fast you can actually reach the internet, so that factors into the equation, too. If Auto Negotiation is disappointing, check the cable The setting may just be shining a light on the real problem On rare occasions, Auto Negotiation may indeed be the problem, in which case you can always force the link to follow a certain speed—but this will only work if all the devices involved, including the cable itself, can support that speed and are working properly. If not, you just got a pretty important hint as to where to look for the troublemaker. The first thing I'd check is the Ethernet cable itself. Unplug it and reseat both ends. Then, swap it out for a different cable that you know works perfectly well, and make sure it's Cat5e or better. There's a good reason cables can mess with this at times. Gigabit Ethernet needs all four twisted pairs inside the cable, while 100BASE-TX can get by with only two. A damaged pair can leave you with a connection that technically works, but doesn't perform the way you'd think. A fast PC is only as fast as its slowest link Any PC, aging or otherwise, is only as fast as its slowest link. If something is bottlenecking your connection, Speed & Duplex may expose it. Tweak the setting as needed, but if you're uncertain about the hardware's capabilities, you might have to start there first.

item.title: Windows 11 is running hidden tasks that drain your laptop battery—here's how to stop them
item.description:
Source: How-To Geek Score: 5.55
Your laptop had a full charge at the start of the day, but by noon, you're reaching for the outlet to refill the battery. The battery percentage kept dropping even though you didn’t stream anything or run a demanding task. That’s because Windows 11 isn’t sitting idle while you work. In the background, a quiet parade of apps, services, and sync routines run constantly in the background — none of which you ever asked for. The good news is that you can stop most of them. Some of the tasks are necessary for Windows to run properly. But several features and apps don’t need to run constantly. Here are the main culprits to look for if your Windows 11 laptop isn’t lasting as long as you want. Background apps Check battery usage before touching anything else Windows 11 allows apps to run in the background by default. Some have a legitimate reason and need to sync even when you’re not using them. However, the app you open once a week or a game launcher doesn’t deserve the same treatment. Battery Usage is the best place to improve your laptop’s battery efficiency. Windows 11 tracks which apps consumed the most power over the last 24 hours and seven days. This is accessible under Settings -> System -> Power and battery -> Battery usage. Instead of disabling background activity across the board, select the apps that consistently consume significant power and that you don’t need running constantly. To do this, you can go to Settings -> Apps -> Installed Apps, open each app’s settings, and set Background app permissions to Never. Startup apps Cut down what launches with Windows. When you boot Windows and sign in, the operating system launches certain apps, and those silently continue running in the background throughout the session. Furthermore, apps often add themselves to startup after an update or installation. Open Task Manager -> Startup apps tab, and you will see the programs that are configured to launch when Windows starts, along with information about their impact. You can right-click to disable anything you don’t need at boot. This action doesn’t uninstall the app or prevent you from opening it manually whenever you need it. Windows Search Your drive is crawled more than it needs to be Windows Search constantly crawls your files so the results appear instantly, making it easier to find something. Indexing happens in the background, so Windows doesn't have to scan your drive every time you search for something. There’s a fix for this — you can control which locations Windows indexes instead of turning it off entirely. Head to Settings -> Privacy and security -> Searching Windows to review the indexing options available on your PC. Limiting unnecessary locations and items that don’t need to be searchable can reduce the work Windows Search does in the background. Cloud sync Not everything needs to be synced. All the time Cloud storage apps are useful, but they do plenty of work in the background. OneDrive is the most common example on Windows 11. Your laptop may be doing more than you realize if you’re syncing a large folder, uploading or downloading a file. It uses additional system resources and network activity. If you don’t require real-time sync, you can pause cloud syncing instead of disabling it when you’re trying to squeeze more battery life out of your laptop. Syncing can be paused for 2, 8, or 24 hours by right-clicking the OneDrive icon in the system tray. If you want a permanent fix, head to OneDrive Settings -> Sync and backup -> Manage backup and then select the specific folders to sync rather than everything. Google and Dropbox also have similar sync options in their own settings menu. Widgets and notifications These stay active even when you ignore them The Windows widgets panel fetches live news, weather, and stock data even when you never open it. There’s no reason to keep it running if it’s not a part of your daily workflow. You can disable widgets from Settings -> Personalization -> Taskbar. Meanwhile, apps keep checking for new messages, updates, and other activity to send notifications you may not need. Each unnecessary notification is a small wake cycle for your PC. You can turn them off under Settings -> System -> Notifications. These are small changes, but they can eliminate another background activity you don’t need. Get more battery life from your Windows 11 laptop None of these changes are permanent. So, you can reverse them if something stops behaving the way you expect. You can also use Windows 11’s built-in energy recommendations under Settings -> System -> Power and battery -> Energy recommendations. Here, you can find screen and sleep settings that are worth checking before making any drastic changes. A few small adjustments won’t magically turn an aging laptop into an all-day machine, but together they can extend your laptop's battery life.

item.title: 7 pioneering Linux applications that never needed replacing
item.description:
Source: How-To Geek Score: 5.55
Linux has changed dramatically since the early days of the kernel. Desktops have gone from X11 environments with primitive window managers to polished graphical shells. Containers, cloud computing, virtualization, and immutable operating systems have transformed how people deploy Linux. Even the hardware running Linux today would have seemed extraordinary to many of its earliest users. Yet some applications have barely budged from their place in the Linux ecosystem. You can install a modern Linux distro in 2026 and still find yourself using software whose origins stretch back decades. Some of these programs are older than most Linux distros themselves. Others became popular during Linux’s formative years and simply refused to disappear: Vim The editor that started a feud Vim was developed in 1991 as an improved version of the classic vi editor. It eventually became one of the defining applications of the Unix and Linux world. Its staying power comes from an editing model that remains extremely efficient once learned. Vim lets users manipulate text almost entirely from the keyboard, making it particularly useful on remote machines where a graphical editor is unavailable. There is also a cultural reason Vim has remained so visible. The long-running Vim versus Emacs argument is one of the oldest rivalries in computing, with generations of users debating which editor deserves their loyalty. I have seen plenty of that debate over the years, but Vim has another advantage in internet culture: the infamous "How do I quit Vim?" problem. For decades, jokes about getting trapped inside Vim have turned into memes, tutorials, stickers, and even running gags among developers. The joke works because the problem is real, and a newcomer can open Vim, start typing, press a few unfamiliar keys, and suddenly have no idea how to get back to the shell. That combination of a genuinely different editing model and decades of community folklore has kept Vim remarkably visible even as newer editors have become easier for beginners to approach. Vim has also expanded well beyond the limitations of the original vi. Plugins, scripting, language integrations, syntax highlighting, and modern terminal capabilities have turned it into a remarkably capable development environment while preserving the core workflow that made it popular. OpenSSH Remote administration became a Linux superpower OpenSSH emerged in the late 1990s and became one of the most important pieces of software in Unix and Linux administration. SSH solved a fundamental problem of controlling remote servers securely. That need has only grown as servers moved into data centers, cloud platforms, and geographically distributed environments. OpenSSH is now used for much more than opening a remote shell. It supports secure file transfers, authentication, tunneling, port forwarding, automation, and connections used by development tools. A Linux installation can be stripped down to the essentials and still provide a secure administrative interface through SSH. That makes OpenSSH less like an ordinary application and more like a piece of the operating system’s infrastructure. rsync File synchronization that never became obsolete rsync was released in 1996 to solve a problem that remains familiar to Linux users. It provides an efficient way to synchronize files between two locations without repeatedly transferring data that has not changed. Rather than copying an entire directory every time, rsync compares the source and destination and transfers only the data required to bring them into sync. That made it useful for backups, migrations, website deployments, mirroring, and server administration. It also made the program exceptionally attractive to system administrators because it can be incorporated into shell scripts and automated workflows. Cloud storage has changed how many people think about backups and file synchronization, but it has not eliminated the need for direct filesystem operations. rsync remains particularly useful when you control both ends of the transfer and need predictable behavior. It understands permissions, timestamps, symbolic links, directory structures, and other Unix filesystem characteristics. Samba Linux learned to coexist with Windows networks Samba began in 1992 as an effort to implement Microsoft’s SMB networking protocol on Unix systems. That project became enormously important because Linux and Windows systems frequently need to coexist. A Linux server might provide shared storage to Windows workstations, participate in authentication infrastructure, or expose files using protocols familiar to Microsoft’s operating systems. As Microsoft introduced newer versions of SMB, Samba continued adding support for those changes, so Linux systems could keep participating in Windows-based networks. Its support eventually expanded from basic file and printer sharing to domain authentication, Windows domain membership, and Active Directory domain-controller functionality. The project therefore did not need to replace its original purpose, which allowed Samba to remain a practical part of Linux networking more than three decades after its initial release. GIMP An image editor that refused to disappear The Gimp appeared in 1995 and became one of the most prominent graphical applications in the Linux ecosystem. GIMP gave Linux users a serious local image editor at a time when proprietary graphics software dominated professional creative work. It supports image manipulation, retouching, compositing, format conversion, scripting, and plugins. The software industry has changed considerably since then. Subscription-based creative suites and browser-based applications are now common, while powerful image editing is available on almost every major platform. GIMP still has an important advantage for Linux users in that it remains a capable native application that can be installed locally and used without subscribing to a proprietary ecosystem. ImageMagick The command line still knows how to process pictures ImageMagick dates back to the early 1990s and became one of the most versatile command-line image-processing tools available on Linux and Unix systems. Its greatest strength is automation. A graphical editor is excellent when a person needs to make creative decisions about an individual image. ImageMagick becomes extremely useful when the same operation needs to happen hundreds or thousands of times. A script can resize an entire directory, convert images between formats, crop files, manipulate metadata, generate thumbnails, or perform more complicated transformations without requiring someone to sit in front of a graphical interface. That makes ImageMagick valuable to developers, publishers, system administrators, and anyone building automated media-processing workflows. Evolution The Linux email client that became a full productivity suite Evolution has been part of the Linux desktop for more than two decades. Originally developed for the GNOME desktop, it started as an email and personal information management application and grew into a broader groupware client. It handles email, calendars, contacts, tasks, and other information that users might otherwise manage through several separate applications. It also supports common enterprise email and collaboration systems, which helped make it useful beyond the typical home Linux desktop. Evolution's history is particularly interesting because email clients have gone through several major shifts since it appeared. Webmail became dominant, smartphones changed how people handled messages and calendars, and cloud services moved much of the underlying infrastructure away from desktop computers. Yet there are still Linux users who prefer having their email, calendar, contacts, and tasks in a native desktop application. Evolution continues to fill that role. It also demonstrates why some older Linux applications survive even when their category becomes less fashionable. Evolution does not need to compete with every web mail service. It simply needs to remain a capable desktop client for people who want one. That has been enough to keep it around through multiple generations of Linux desktops. These applications survived because their problems did The most interesting thing about these applications is not their age. It is the fact that modern Linux users can still encounter the same fundamental problems their creators were trying to solve. Technology has changed around these applications without eliminating the jobs they perform. Some have also benefited from an enormous ecosystem built around them. That does not mean every one of these programs is the best choice for every user. A new editor may be easier to learn, but the replacement has to provide enough additional value to justify changing a workflow that already works. A program written thirty years ago does not have to look modern to remain useful. It simply has to continue solving a problem that people still have.

item.title: Your mesh Wi-Fi's backhaul is destroying your NAS performance
item.description:
Source: How-To Geek Score: 4.11
If you've ever used a mesh Wi-Fi system, you've probably noticed that the satellite nodes usually have a spare Ethernet port. It is tempting to use that port to attach a NAS. After all, it seems like a good way to get your NAS connected without running a cable across the floor or through a wall. However, that port isn't really well-suited for use with a NAS. The wireless back haul may not be up to a NAS's demands Back haul may not have enough bandwidth available Wireless Wi-Fi nodes work using a second "back haul" connection. It is a special connection (usually Wi-Fi-based) that links the satellite node to your main router. So, even though your NAS is physically plugged into a node with a cable, the data it sends and receives instantly gets transmitted over the Wi-Fi to the main router anyway. It has all the same limitations and problems as a regular Wi-Fi network, like interference from other devices or physical obstructions. If you're backing up or streaming 4K media or a huge photo archive, you're almost certainly going to notice a bottleneck caused by whatever connection limitations the back haul network has. In most scenarios, you're better off just directly connecting your NAS to the Wi-Fi directly if your NAS supports that. At least then you have greater discretion over where you place it. Not all NAS units have Wi-Fi, and only some support Wi-Fi dongles. Wired is more stable Your wireless throughput is less stable than a wired connection Many consumer NAS units today have gigabit, 2.5 gigabit, or even 5 gigabit Ethernet ports. On a wired network, you can expect even Cat6 to hit those speeds easily over residential distances, and it'll likely be very stable too. With a wireless back haul on a budget mesh system, the situation is almost certainly going to be worse. Even if you see decent speeds, which I'd consider anything about 50 megabytes per second, those numbers are going to fluctuate depending on all sorts of external factors. In the times I've used a wireless back haul, I found that other devices on the back haul often caused pretty significant performance hits, and it isn't anything weird either. Even someone streaming video on their phone can be enough to impact the performance of wireless back hauls. That doesn't even begin to address other issues that may arise if you live in a crowded Wi-Fi environment, like an apartment building. Your NAS needs to be online almost 100% of the time Back haul drops and node reboots take the NAS offline A NAS needs to be online as much as possible. If it disconnects at an inopportune time, it can abort a massive backup mid-run, corrupt an open database, or leave your mapped network drives in a "broken" state until you manually reconnect. Unfortunately, mesh satellites are inherently a little volatile. Even if you don't mind the speed variability, satellites are prone to reconnecting, can sometimes automatically optimize their channels, or reboot for a firmware update. Every time one of those events happens, the NAS you have connected to the device will be offline. Unfortunately, automatic updates often roll out overnight—the exact same time that people schedule their backups. On more than one occasion, I had an automated backup fail when a mesh node was temporarily disrupted overnight. After that, I drilled some holes in the walls and ran an Ethernet cable directly to my router. Of course, your main router needs to reboot occasionally too, but that is still less common than an interruption caused by connectivity or renegotiation. Similarly, wired switches are usually extremely simple—many don't need updates and don't need to reboot. So long as the wire remains connected and undamaged, they'll run for years without interruption. If you have the option, try to ensure that your Wi-Fi system doesn't perform automated updates during your backup windows. Keep your NAS near your router if possible If you're just trying to connect something like a printer, the Ethernet port on a mesh node is fine. However, your NAS should really be connected via an Ethernet cable directly to your router. The best choice is to directly plug your NAS into your router's LAN port. If that isn't an option, attach it to a simple wired switch connected to your router instead. It is also a good idea to keep both devices attached to the same UPS if you have one—it ensures that your devices will usually both be online at the same time, and neither device is likely to try to reach the other while it is offline. If the NAS can't sit directly next to your router, run an Ethernet cable or use a MoCA (which allows internet over coax cable) instead. MoCA introduces some hiccups, but I've found it is more reliable across longer distances than most ISP-supplied mesh Wi-Fi systems are. And, finally, if the NAS cannot be wired to the router directly and your NAS has Wi-Fi functionality, just place it in the same room as the router. The Wi-Fi connection will be much more reliable than the back haul from a node.

item.title: This open-source Windows launcher does what Microsoft’s new Start menu should have done
item.description:
Source: How-To Geek Score: 3.29
After years of complaints about how little you could customize the Windows Start menu, Microsoft is finally overhauling it in the 26H2 update. In reality, though, they are only catching up to something an open-source app figured out years ago. Meet Flow Launcher, a keyboard-first app launcher that is superior to the current Start menu from all directions. Trying Flow Launcher for the first time The productivity boost felt like cheating To test this praised tool out myself, I went straight to the official Flow Launcher website to grab a copy. There were multiple download options, including a portable version, an EXE file, and also through package managers such as WinGet. I went for the portable version for a quick setup. Though that meant I had to create a shortcut myself. The setup process was intuitive, as the onboarding pages took you through some of the essential things you should know about the launcher, including shortcut keys, hotkeys, and explaining action keywords. On first launch, I'm welcomed by a search bar, followed by a list of commands. The UI looked nice and blended well with Windows 11. I also noticed a clicky sound every time I opened it with Alt+Space. The most common functionality for the launcher is searching, especially searching for and launching apps. I like to pin apps I use often to my Taskbar and the Start menu. However, that means I have to use the mouse to click the app to open it. With Flow Launcher, I only had to start typing its name and hit Enter. But that's not all. Searching for an app is blazing fast. By the time you finish typing the name halfway, the result is already there. It's not just apps, though. You can also search for files and open them in the default file opener. This is much more useful as I don't have to remember where I kept that one pesky file or use Windows File Explorer's slow search. As long as I remember the name, that's enough. If Windows search drives you crazy, this could be a lifesaver. Flow Launcher itself is highly customizable You'll get lost playing around its settings Talking about customizing the customizer. You can tweak General and Appearance settings. Let's explore both. The General settings tab contains the settings that shape the behavior and functionality of the launcher. For example, whether or not you want to start Flow Launcher on system startup, hide its tray icon, whether it should be on top of other windows, and more. One setting I liked a lot is Always Preview. It opens a new panel on the side that shows the icon of the searched app and some details. Not only does it enhance the overall look of the app, but it's also helpful when you need some quick details about the app or file. The Appearance tab is all about the look and feel. There are almost 20 themes to choose from. Mine was set to Windows 11 by default, which explains why it looked like a native app. I went with the Rider theme, which looked more polished to me. Other things you can customize are animation, sound effects, icons, badges, window size, and the color scheme, among others. If you turned on Always Preview, some of the results may not take effect since the preview panel takes up some space in the full launcher window. You can also adjust the clock and date here. I found that turning on both squishes them together, with no space in between. So I turned off the date. The plugin ecosystem is where it really pulls ahead Turning a launcher into a control center In the settings, you'll find a Plugins and a Plugin Store section. The Plugins section contains plugins you've already installed in Flow Launcher. The store has more you can try. And this is really where things turn more interesting as you keep extending what the launcher can do. In the Plugins section, you can turn a plugin on or off. Each plugin also has a dropdown menu that contains some settings regarding it. For example, the Browser Bookmarks plugin lets you choose the browser(s) you want to load from. Each plugin lets you set an action keyword for it. The Plugin Store was quite amusing to explore. There is an ocean of plugins to be installed in a wide range of categories, from productivity and study to gaming and development. You can search, update, and install plugins. You can also choose a plugin from your local path. Installing a plugin is also straightforward. You click on the plugin and click Install. Once installed, you'll need to restart Flow Launcher to use it. Some of the plugins I found useful are Speed Test, File Folder Opener, Google Translate, and some of the math plugins. One thing I wish is that each plugin had a dedicated page where I could check the details of the plugins. You can see them by clicking a link that opens the GitHub page of the plugin. However, having a page inside the Plugin Store would be much more intuitive. Microsoft still has some catching up to do While PowerToys Run and Command Palette have quite similar functions and capabilities, the Start menu still feels left behind. Moreover, Flow Launcher has an upper hand over the PowerToys tools if you love customization and you want to become a power user.

item.title: Milwaukee's real cost isn't the drill — it's everything that comes after
item.description:
Source: How-To Geek Score: 2.90
It's no secret that Milwaukee makes some of the best power tools, but buying into Team Red isn't as straightforward as it appears. The initial sticker price is only part of the story, and everything that comes after will inevitably cost a lot more. Like most brands, Milwaukee has an aggressive battery ecosystem lock-in, but then offers affordable common tools to lure you onto the platform. Soon after, you'll end up forking out a lot of cash. If you're trying to decide which brand to buy, here are some hidden expenses and things to keep in mind so you don't get caught off guard. Common tools or deals lock you into an expensive ecosystem Affordable drills and drivers, but niche tools will get you Like every major power tool brand, Milwaukee has its M18 (18-volt) battery platform that powers almost all of its tools. Once you buy one, you won't want to buy a different brand's battery or charger, so you'll end up buying more Milwaukee tools. However, that also means a single battery can power everything, which is extremely helpful. With that same logic, one thing that Milwaukee does better than most of the competition is lure customers onto the platform by offering common or popular tools at an aggressive price point, but then everything else quickly becomes more expensive. You can get a Milwaukee drill/driver or a drill-and-impact combo for roughly the same price as a DeWALT or Ryobi. For a newcomer who's heard Milwaukee is one of the best, they'll instantly jump on that combo kit. However, aside from drills, drivers, oscillating multi-tools, and a few other items, Milwaukee products are generally far more expensive than those from several other brands. Basically, outside of some of the most common items, Milwaukee quickly becomes more expensive, but by then, you've already committed. For example, Milwaukee's 10-inch brushless pole saw is $379 for the tool alone, with no battery, because you probably already have one. However, a comparable 18V Ryobi brushless pole saw is only $199. Homeowners everywhere use these, but one is far more expensive than the other. The same thing applies to something as basic as a Sawzall. Milwaukee's absolute cheapest model is $150, while you can get a Ryobi for $89, or a DeWALT for $129. Your first purchase, which is likely a drill or driver,. That said, they are excellent. Batteries can break the bank More expensive than the tools themselves Another hidden cost we need to talk about is the battery packs themselves. Now, don't get me wrong: every brand on the market has expensive battery packs, and they're almost always more than the tools themselves. There's a reason each combo kit usually comes with a tiny 2Ah battery: to get you into the tool and ecosystem. Eventually, you'll need a bigger 4.0Ah or 6.0Ah battery, and those are usually $200 each, if not more. Once you buy your first Milwaukee tool, the hidden cost that'll catch you off guard is upgrading or buying additional battery cells. The other trick each big-name brand plays is "tool-only" pricing. You'll see an awesome Milwaukee tool-only deal that makes the tool more affordable than the DeWALT you might already own, but now you need an expensive battery. Jumping to a different brand for a deal usually ends up costing you in the long run. However, once you own a few battery packs, this becomes a pro rather than a con, as you can save money on tool-only purchases since you already have the expensive batteries to power them. Just keep it in mind before you buy a cheap combo kit or a tool-only deal. The M12 vs M18 dilemma Pay attention to the battery platform And last but not least, you'll want to pay special attention to whether you're buying a Milwaukee M12 or M18 power tool. These tools might look the same, and the M12 models are usually more affordable because they're smaller and run on an M12 (12-volt) battery pack. Milwaukee M12 tools are not compatible with Milwaukee M18 tools. They're a different size and design, with a smaller battery pack geared for compact scenarios, DIY projects around the house, and the like. Milwaukee's bigger M18 models deliver additional power and performance. If you're new to power tools and buy a Milwaukee M12 drill, you'll be stuck with the smaller M12 platform, which offers around 125 tools that all run on that battery. However, Milwaukee's M18 lineup offers over 300 tools to take advantage of. Don't get me wrong, I know tons of homeowners and professionals who run both the Milwaukee M12 and M18, but it's something to be aware of and a potential hidden cost down the road. If you start with M12 but eventually need more power or a tool that's only available on the M18 platform, you'll need to buy a new battery and another charger, and those costs can add up quickly. And that's not all Milwaukee owners all over Reddit frequently mention other things, like repairs and maintenance, lights, and PACKOUT accessories, as big hurdles potential buyers need to consider. If you're a DIYer and want to repair or service your tool, Milwaukee often groups small components into larger assemblies or one wire/switch into an entire wire harness, driving up repair costs. And that's if you can even find them. Obviously, that's not a huge concern for most, but it's something to think about. In closing, Milwaukee certainly has some of the best tools on the market and caters to a ton of trades and professionals. There's a reason people everywhere swear by them, just know that things can and will get expensive.

item.title: I stopped using Word for simple notes after discovering this ridiculously capable text editor
item.description:
Source: How-To Geek Score: 2.35
Most of us learned Microsoft Word while growing up and never really questioned it. It was on most computers, so it became the default for everything, including notes that had no business being formatted like a printed document. You don't need an entire document to take a few notes; you should use an app built to manage them like databases. Word was built for printing, not real note-taking Notion treats your notes like data Microsoft Word is the go-to app for everyone. It's not hard to see why, because it's kind of built into so many of our childhoods. I was taught Word in elementary school, and Microsoft Office tended to be used in plenty of classrooms. However, it was never designed for quick, messy notes. It was built to make print-ready documents. The whole architecture is print-first, which means everything is built around wrapping text onto physical pages like A4 or Letter. That makes a ton of formatting overhead when you're just trying to write information in real time, so structuring text tends not to be the most important thing. The file system model doesn't help either. Documents live in folders, links break if you move or rename anything, and a note can only be in one folder at a time. Syncing across devices is its own issue that I don't even bother with anymore due to the bugs. Since Word is constantly doing layout calculations in the background because of things like page breaks and floating images, it's really bad at spatial organization and handling more complex additions to documents. I like the apps that treat the page like a page, and not like paper. One that does this well is Notion, because it treats your pages like a database. The workspace becomes a graph of linked blocks, and there's no real difference between a string of text, an image, a checklist, a database row, or a whole page. Every block is atomic, and you can move, nest, or transform things without losing data. So indenting a block changes the database render tree, not just the visual styling. Synced blocks solve the duplication problem too. A single block can exist on multiple pages, and edits can spread everywhere. It overall makes your life easier. Notion is built around little blocks instead of normal pages The block system makes writing a lot easier So Notion's whole workspace is a lot more complicated than it seems, but it makes a lot of sense when you get used to it. It's built around this editor, except instead of a normal document that just goes top to bottom, everything is a structured tree of little modular pieces that live on their own. Hitting Tab actually changes the underlying database relationships and moves that block's ID into the children list of the block above it. Since the data is decoupled from the style, everything survives type changes. Basically, if you have a checked to-do item and turn it into a heading, the rendering engine just ignores the checked flag. But the flag is still stored. If you turn it back into a to-do later, then the checkmark will come right back, because the metadata was never thrown away. For actually taking notes day to day, I've found that slash commands make things easier than Word does. You type /and a searchable menu pops up, so you don't have to grab the mouse and dig through toolbars. Start typing, and it filters in real time. /todo gives you a checkbox, /table drops in a grid, /toggle makes a collapsible section. There are also ones like /duplicate or /comment, and you can even do visual highlights like /red or /blue backgrounds without stopping your typing. While there are arguments as to why Microsoft Word doesn't make things this easy, it feels like these are the kinds of changes the company should push for. Instead, we have Copilot being forced into way too many apps. Notion has its fair share of problems You trade raw speed for way better organization Notion can be kind of annoying. It's cloud-dependent and runs on a huge JavaScript stack, so it's just not as fast as a blank Word document. The desktop app is built on Electron and React, which means it has to load a massive framework before you can even type. My computer is older, so it takes around five to ten seconds. Word opens in under a second because it's a native app, but even the online version loads incredibly quickly. It also takes a bit of time to learn Notion. I was initially turned off by it because it felt like I was setting up a Wikipedia page instead of taking notes. However, that tiny bit of lag and setup you get with Notion is a pretty small price for having everything you write easy to find and all connected in one system. That said, Word isn't going anywhere. Even with all the new AI features getting built in, it's still the standard. So if you genuinely like a notepad that feels like it was built for a printer, use Word. However, if you want to feel like your notes have a lot more depth and control, try out Notion. Notion is not an easy switch from Word Notion isn't a clean swap for Word, but that's a good thing in some ways. The learning curve is the hardest part to get through, but once you know how to use Notion, it's a lot of fun to pair with AI and other things. I use Antigravity to help organize the random notes I have, and it works like a charm. The setup cost is a few hours, and what you get at the end is a really good app. Notion - OS - Windows, macOS, iOS, Android, and web browsers - Supported Desktop Browsers - Web Clipper Extension for Chrome, Firefox, Safari This customizable workspace simplifies and combines the processes of note-taking, task creation, and date planning to create an all-in-one productivity workspace.

item.title: This $15 ESP32 made Apple Music and Spotify discovery way better
item.description:
Source: How-To Geek Score: 2.24
With so much music on streaming services, and more and more being added daily, it's not always easy to find music I really love among the millions of tracks. I use a cheap ESP32 board to make the process much easier. I really struggle to find new music I really love Discovery playlists are often a mixed bag One of the things that makes discovering new music that I genuinely love so hard is that I have pretty eclectic tastes. I listen to everything from classical music and 80s pop to hip-hop and crank wave. If I like it, I like it. This means that recommendations from apps such as Spotify and Apple Music are often a bit hit-or-miss, since they have to cover a wide range of genres with no obvious link. These playlists will usually contain some songs that I like the sound of, but also a lot that really don't fit the bill. The problem is that when I listen to these playlists, I often zone out during the mediocre songs, and by the time I realize that I actually like a song, it's moved on to another. I then have to skip back, find the song, note the artist, then search for that artist on Spotify or Apple Music and add some of their music to my library so I can listen to it later, before going back to the discovery playlist and restarting it. The whole process felt really awkward. I wanted to find a better way. A Cheap Yellow Display offered a solution A single tap saves the current song to a new playlist When I'm trying to find a tech-based solution to a problem, there are two places I almost always turn first: Home Assistant and ESP32 boards. The two work really well together, and ESP32 boards are usually fairly cheap. One very useful ESP32 board is a Cheap Yellow Display (CYD). This is an ESP32 connected to a small touchscreen display, making it incredibly versatile for tech projects. The touchscreen was what gave me the idea I ended up going with. I set up the ESP32 to display the artwork of the current song being played through Music Assistant. I can play both Spotify and Apple Music discovery playlists through Music Assistant by linking my accounts. On a Monday, I listen to my discovery playlists, and when I like the current song, I just tap the screen, and the song is added to a new custom playlist in Music Assistant. There are usually enough interesting songs in Apple Music and Spotify discovery playlists to end up with a playlist of about 10–20 songs that I like the sound of. Using the CYD means I can instantly mark a song as having potential with just a single tap. The second pass adds selected songs to my library I can add albums from artists I want to hear more of Once I've added all the songs I like the sound of to my custom playlist, I listen to that playlist, with the album art appearing on the CYD again. This time, if I like a song, tapping adds the entire album to my library. I will play the custom playlist a few times, as some songs only really hit on the second or third listen. I will often end up with maybe five new albums added to my library. I will then spend the rest of the week listening to these albums. At the start of the next week, the whole process starts again. Home Assistant and Music Assistant make recommendations better I've discovered some great albums The system works really well. Using the CYD means that the only things I need to do are listen to the songs and tap the screen when I like the sound of a song, which is so much easier than what I was doing before. A lot of the albums that get added to my library turn out to be disappointing, with the playlist song being easily the best song on the album. Some albums, however, turn out to be genuinely awesome, and I'd likely have missed many of them without my CYD setup. While the CYD is the interface that makes it all work, the real magic comes from Home Assistant and Music Assistant. They do all the hard work in the background. Music Assistant . Sometimes a cheap fix can be the best fix A CYD can cost as little as $15, but the tiny board can be incredibly useful. It's made a huge improvement to how I find new music to listen to, and for me, that's something that's priceless.

item.title: Android makes switching password managers much easier
item.description:
Source: Latest from Android Central Score: 6.47
What you need to know - You can now move passwords and passkeys directly between supported apps on Android without exporting sensitive data to an unencrypted file. - Your new password manager hands the process to Android, which detects compatible managers installed on your phone and coordinates the transfer. - Once authorized, Android moves the credentials between apps without requiring manual file handling. Android has always made it a pain to switch password managers. Moving passwords usually involved exporting your data into an unencrypted text file, and passkeys were pretty much stuck in place. Android is tackling both of those issues with a new transfer experience that makes moving your credentials much more secure and simple. In a blog post, Google said the new system lets you transfer passwords and passkeys directly between password managers, without first having to download a file. That eliminates one of the biggest security hassles of the old process, which was that sensitive credentials were sitting unprotected on your device for a while. Furthermore, passkeys weren’t transferable, so you had to manually recreate them across websites and apps. The process is built to be mostly out of your way. Start in your new password manager and select the option to import or copy credentials from another provider. The app then hands the job to Android, which knows which compatible password managers you have already installed on your phone and shows you where the data can come from. You are then sent back to the password manager you already use to select, review, and approve the transfer. Once approved, the passwords and passkeys move between the apps in just a few seconds. The feature is already available with Google Password Manager, 1Password, Bitwarden Password Manager, and Dashlane. Dashlane notes that CXP is compatible with devices running Android 10 or newer with the latest Play Services update. Bitwarden needs Android 14+ with Play services 26.21+. It is not merely a matter of convenience. Passkeys are more secure than passwords and resistant to phishing. Adoption has been stalled in part due to user concerns around vendor lock-in. CXP removes that barrier. Get the latest news from Android Central, your trusted companion in the world of Android Bitwarden says the creation of passkeys peaked this summer at over 500% compared to early 2024, with nearly half of all passkeys created in the past three months alone. Google says more partners are on the way. If you’ve been waiting to change password managers because of the hassle, that excuse just went out the window. Jay Bonggolto always keeps a nose for news. item.title: iQOO 16 display leaks were true: Samsung's 2K 165Hz panel is official
item.description:
Source: Latest from Android Central Score: 5.40
What you need to know - The iQOO 16 is set to debut as the first smartphone with a 2K resolution OLED display running at a 165Hz refresh rate. - Co-developed with Samsung Display on a dedicated production line, the panel marks the Android debut of Samsung's latest M16 luminescent material and LEAD 2.0 architecture. - The screen reaches 2,800 nits global peak brightness (10,000 nits local peak), features 508 PPI, and delivers sub-pixel-level calibration for color accuracy. Rumor has it that the iQOO 16 will be released soon, and iQOO has now confirmed one of the upgrades that could make this gaming-focused flagship stand out from the crowd. The next phone from the company is said to be the first to sport a 2K OLED panel with a 165Hz refresh rate from Samsung, which iQOO is calling a smartphone first. The announcement also confirms earlier reports that the iQOO 16 would sport Samsung’s newer M16 OLED technology. The company says the phone will be the first Android smartphone to use the material, along with its new 2K LEAD 2.0 technology. For context, we saw the original LEAD OLED panel debut with the iQOO 15. LEAD 2.0 has been developed in partnership with Samsung, built on a dedicated production line just for iQOO’s flagship. The two companies also designed a custom high-refresh-rate display IC and a dedicated production line for the phone. The panel is rated at 2,800 nits for global brightness and 10,000 nits for local brightness. It also offers 508 ppi, wide P3 color coverage, DC dimming, and better brightness and color uniformity than the iQOO 15. iQOO also claims sub-pixel-level calibration leads to extremely tight color accuracy. There is also a less obvious upgrade here: Samsung recently said the new display uses roughly 31 percent less power at 150 nits than a similarly sized 1.5K panel. That’s particularly useful, as improving both resolution and refresh rate often comes with a battery cost. The target is clearly gaming. The display features 500Hz multi-touch sampling and 5,000Hz instantaneous sampling rate, while iQOO’s Q-Flex technology focuses on reducing input lag. There’s also 3,300Hz PWM dimming and many eye-comfort features. Get the latest news from Android Central, your trusted companion in the world of Android The iQOO 16 is expected to launch in China sometime near the end of September. If the rest of the hardware is up to the mark as this display, the top gaming flagships out there will have a serious new competitor on their hands. Jay Bonggolto always keeps a nose for news. item.title: Rokid wants anyone to build AI agents for its smart glasses
item.description:
Source: Latest from Android Central Score: 5.31
What you need to know - Rokid's AIUI Studio is a browser-based platform that lets anyone build spatial AI apps for Rokid Glasses, with no coding experience or dev kit required. - Developers can describe an idea, while the AI-native workflow helps turn it into a working app. - The built-in smart glasses simulator lets developers create and test projects before getting physical hardware involved. Rokid is making it easier to build apps for its AI glasses, and you won't need a coding background or even to own a pair of the glasses. The company has launched AIUI Studio globally at IFA Berlin 2026, giving developers a browser-based platform for creating and publishing spatial AI applications. Much of the development process takes place via an AI-native workflow in AIUI Studio. You can say what you want to build in plain language, and the platform can take that idea and build an app without the traditional coding skills. It also offers a simulation of Rokid’s smart glasses, enabling developers to work on their projects without having to purchase the hardware. There’s still a reason to get the real hardware involved eventually, though. Rokid’s developer documentation advises testing agents in its Interactive Inview simulator before performing a final check on the actual glasses. For developers who want to have more control, Rokid pairs its AIUI Skills Library framework with AIUI Code assistance. The company says this helps creators make better use of the glasses’ hardware while also optimizing apps for less latency, less memory use, and less power consumption. The move is the latest as Rokid’s developer ecosystem continues to grow. The company says it now has some 35,000 registered developers and more than 500 agents available through its Agent Store. Get the latest news from Android Central, your trusted companion in the world of Android AIUI Studio is now available worldwide. If Rokid can take advantage of that growing developer base to create a steady stream of useful agents, its glasses might just become a platform that people actively build around. item.title: These popular Samsung phones just received their final software update
item.description:
Source: Latest from Android Central Score: 4.91
What you need to know - Samsung has officially ended software support for the Galaxy Z Fold 3 and Galaxy Z Flip 3 after five years. - Both foldables received four years of OS upgrades and five years of security updates, as Samsung originally promised. - Samsung has removed both phones from its security update page, meaning they won't receive regular security patches anymore. Samsung's foldable phones that launched in the summer of 2021 have officially reached the end of their software support cycle. Most Samsung flagship smartphones today, including the Galaxy S26 Ultra and even 2024's Galaxy S24 Ultra, come with seven years of software support. But Samsung hasn't always offered updates for this long. Older flagships came with shorter support promises, and now the Galaxy Z Fold 3 and Galaxy Z Flip 3 have officially reached the end of theirs. As spotted by Android Authority, the Galaxy Z Fold 3 and Galaxy Z Flip 3 have received their final software updates. At launch, Samsung promised four years of OS upgrades and five years of security updates for both foldables, and the company has now fulfilled that promise. Samsung has also removed both devices from its security updates page. This means Samsung won't be releasing any further regular software or security updates for these devices. The oldest foldables officially supported by the company are now the Galaxy Z Fold 4 and Galaxy Z Flip 4. Even those devices have moved to a quarterly update schedule, unlike newer Samsung phones that continue to receive monthly updates. So, if you're still using a Galaxy Z Fold 3 or Galaxy Z Flip 3, your phone won't receive any new regular security patches from Samsung going forward. That means any new security vulnerabilities discovered from here on may remain unpatched on these devices. If you're still holding onto one of these foldables, this might finally be the time to start thinking about an upgrade. Samsung recently introduced a completely new form factor with the Galaxy Z Fold 8, while its latest foldables also come with a much longer software support promise. If you've managed to keep your Fold 3 or Flip 3 running for five years, one of Samsung's newer foldables should last you considerably longer. item.title: Ray-Ban Meta glasses update makes them more useful on the go
item.description:
Source: Latest from Android Central Score: 4.72
What you need to know - Meta AI glasses v28 update adds pedestrian navigation, Spatial Audio, expanded language support, and camera anti-tampering improvements. - With hands-free walking directions, you can ask Meta to navigate to nearby destinations, with driving directions sent to your phone for farther trips. - Spatial Audio makes listening richer and adds a more immersive layer to music and podcasts on supported Ray-Ban Meta glasses. Meta has been steadily expanding what its AI glasses can do, and the latest v28 update adds several practical upgrades, including pedestrian navigation, Spatial Audio, and broader language support. Perhaps the headline addition is pedestrian navigation. You can now ask the smart glasses to guide you on foot to nearby destinations using voice commands such as “Hey Meta, navigate to Times Square.” If you’re farther away, the glasses can send driving directions to your phone. There’s also a new way to begin navigation from your phone: Find a destination in your mapping app, tap Share, and select Meta AI, and navigation will start on your connected glasses. The update also broadens where walking directions work. Meta says it now offers walking directions in the U.S., Puerto Rico, Canada, and some cities across the world. Audio gets an upgrade as well. Now, Spatial Audio can make a more immersive version of the stereo sound you’re already getting, whether that’s music or a podcast. You can find this option in Settings > Audio > Spatial. It works with Ray-Ban Meta Gen 2 Optics and the Meta Glasses collection. Meta is also adding Mandarin Chinese (zh_CN) support across Device Controls, calls and messaging, media capture and music controls, Meta AI, and MMAI. Finally, v28 has ongoing anti-tampering improvements to protect the cameras on the glasses. item.title: Arm's upcoming GPU for Android claims it can deliver 'desktop-class' graphics—I hope it's true
item.description:
Source: Latest from Android Central Score: 4.34
What you need to know - Arm revealed the work put into empowering its new Mali G2-Ultra NX GPU, which is said to bring "desktop-class" graphics to phones. - Arm states it's leaning on an AI-native Mali GPU with a Neural Accelerator and more to handle demanding graphics, while maintaining smooth frame rates for mobile gamers. - Qualcomm also teased its upcoming Adreno GPU for the next Snapdragon chips, stating it will also lean on AI to help with graphics rendering and frame rate generation. Arm is highlighting what mobile users can expect from its next GPU. It states everything it's worked to implement is due to growing user demands for "richer visuals" and better frame rates. Arm revealed the Mali G2-Ultra NX GPU in a newsroom post this week. According to its data, Arm says mobile users want a few things: "They want richer visuals, smoother frame rates, and increasingly immersive experiences." However, there are certain challenges it reportedly needs to overcome to help consumers (and developers, too). The Mali G2-Ultra NX is purportedly the answer to everyone's problems. Arm states it built the GPU for "neural graphics." This is an AI-native Mali GPU—its first-ever—which brings the Neural Accelerator into shader cores. This reportedly aids better teamwork between the graphics and computing workloads. What's more, performance is said to increase. Arm states its Neural Accelerator helps the GPU "handle increasingly demanding scenes more efficiently." This would give developers creating more pleasing visuals more room without the cost of reduced frame rates. Arm's third-generation ray tracing technology will also assist the graphics department. The Mali G2-Ultra NX support for this ray tracing software will facilitate advancements in shadows, complex lighting, reflections, and more. At a hardware level, Arm states devices with Opacity Micromaps support can produce "richer foliage, more detailed fabrics, layered surfaces, and more." Better graphics are nothing without smooth frame rates. Arm says "architectural improvements" in the GPU can support longer gaming sessions at "up to" 120FPS. AI comes to the aid of mobile graphics? We've been hearing about AI's involvement with mobile phone graphics since earlier this month. Qualcomm highlighted its Adreno "Neural Fusion" GPU, stating that it will lean on AI to upgrade mobile gaming graphics. The chip reportedly utilizes AI-driven rendering tech. This new tech will put better gaming resolution and frame generation in the graphics pipeline. Console-like graphics were a major detail for Qualcomm in that announcement. The company claims its new chip, coupled with AI, will reduce the work the chip needs to do to produce the graphics mobile users have been asking for. All of this is en route to the Dual 8 Elites from Qualcomm during the Snapdragon Summit from September 22-24.
