item.title: Powering AI is an architecture problem
item.description:
Source: MIT Technology Review Score: 3.39
Sponsored Provided byON.energy On July 22, 2026, a transmission line fault in Ashburn, Virginia—the heart of the world's largest data center cluster—knocked more than 3 gigawatts of load off the grid in seconds. And it wasn't the first time. Two years earlier, a single failed surge arrester dropped roughly 60 Virginia facilities and 1,500 megawatts at once. No one could anticipate so much uniform load responding to grid faults the same way, at the same time. The AI power debate is mostly about generation: more turbines, more solar, more transmission. The grid needs more electrons. But the outages in Virginia weren't supply failures; they were architecture failures. And a giant wave of interconnections is arriving on that same architecture, putting grid reliability at risk. It's a problem nobody wants to own. Asking more from the grid The grid was built around predictable loads: steel mills, refineries, and houses at dinnertime. Different load sizes, same process—drawing power smoothly, misbehaving occasionally, and recovering gracefully. But AI data centers don't behave that way. An AI campus can swing 70% of its load in milliseconds during a training run, then trip offline just as fast at the first sign of trouble upstream to protect billions in compute. Each is rational alone. Together, at gigawatt scale, they're a problem the grid has never solved—and the next wave of data center campuses is planned at exactly that scale. Where the old stack breaks The standard data center power stack hasn't changed in decades. Medium-voltage power arrives, transformers step it down, low-voltage uninterruptible power supply (UPS) units condition it, and it reaches the racks. Push that design to AI scale, and it cracks in three places. First, the UPS sits deep inside the building, close to the racks. But its batteries are an undersized spare tire, designed to handle an outage for a few minutes, not to absorb load swings this fast and volatile around the clock. Second, the UPS spends most of its life in bypass. Legacy converters waste enough power that operators run in eco-mode: A static switch feeds the racks directly from the grid and nothing filters in either direction. The compute's swings go out raw, and grid transients—sub-millisecond events that can damage or take down equipment—come in too fast for any switch to catch. Third, the protection logic was written when "large load" meant 50 megawatts. This protection logic can't see the grid it is now a part of, so when trouble hits upstream, it does exactly the wrong thing: it drops out. In the 2024 Virginia event, most of the lost load traced to protection schemes that count voltage dips and disconnect on the third one—as designed, at the worst moment. This isn't sloppy engineering. It's careful engineering the load has outgrown. Moving into the path The fix is three moves, made together. Move it up—from 480 volts to medium voltage (13.8 kilovolts and higher), the voltage large sites draw from the grid. Move it out—from the data hall to modular enclosures near the substation so the building holds only compute and the cooling that keeps it alive. Move it into the path—instead of a battery that watches and reacts, a system every electron runs through, all the time. There's nothing to detect and nothing to switch because nothing was ever routed around it. On paper, three straightforward upgrades. In practice, they rewrite every line item downstream. Making the change When thousands of GPUs spin up together, the system absorbs the swing and hands the grid a flat load profile. When a disturbance hits, the equipment behind it never notices. A difficult neighbor becomes a predictable one. And when the utility needs help, it becomes a useful one. Interconnection changes, too. The utility certifies one medium-voltage box instead of untangling every transformer, UPS, chiller, pump, and switchgear lineup behind it. Engineers swap chip generations without a fresh interconnection study. Months come off the permitting timeline. Inside the fence, UPS rooms become compute or cooling space. Density per construction dollar climbs. And the economics flip. Equipment that runs at medium voltage, sits outside, and stores its own energy can qualify for tax credits, and earn revenue in grid programs like peak shaving and demand response. Backup power stops being insurance and starts paying for itself. The architecture test In early 2026, we tested a full-scale system at the National Laboratory of the Rockies, a U.S. Department of Energy facility and the only place in the Western Hemisphere that can replicate real grid faults and AI-scale load swings concurrently in the same loop. We hit it from both directions: real AI load profiles hit the compute side at full medium voltage. Grid faults hit the utility side, including a full zero-voltage event. The compute side didn't flinch. Neither did the grid side. It cleared the large-load voltage ride-through requirements from the Electric Reliability Council of Texas (ERCOT), the grid operator, with room to spare. Those rules exist because operators no longer take facilities this size on faith, and more are coming. Most of the industry treats them as hurdles. A medium-voltage, inline system clears them out of the box. Compliance isn't an added feature. It's what the architecture does. The new layer Much of what looks like a grid problem in the AI buildout sits inside the fence, in equipment sized for a load that no longer exists. Move the right pieces up, out, and into the path, and a grid liability becomes a grid asset. Density goes up. Permitting time comes down. Backup power earns its keep. The engineering works—and the next wave of AI factories is being built on it. The industry hasn't named this layer yet. We call it the medium-voltage AI UPS. The name matters less than the choice: those factories can arrive as a strain on the grid or as strength for it. We already know how to build the second kind. This content was produced by ON.energy. It was not written by MIT Technology Review’s editorial staff. Deep Dive Artificial intelligence A fundamental flaw leaves LLMs strikingly vulnerable to attack It makes it easy to trick them into doing things they shouldn’t, such as telling you how to sabotage an aircraft’s navigation system. AI is more likely than humans to form biases when hiring AI doesn’t just learn stereotypes from its training. It can cook up new ones, too. item.title: Healthcare AI’s next test is integration
item.description:
Source: MIT Technology Review Score: 3.33
Sponsored Provided byEnsemble The entrance of major AI companies into healthcare is a meaningful and welcome development, accelerating the technical foundation available to the industry. Their models are increasingly capable of processing long clinical records, interpreting complex terminology, comparing documentation against evidence and generating coherent summaries from large volumes of information. For clinicians, operators, and administrative teams who spend significant time searching through fragmented data, these advances are helping reduce cognitive burden and make high-value information easier to access. But healthcare leaders should not confuse model capability with operational capability. Healthcare’s administrative challenges are caused by fragmented information, fragmented workflows, and fragmented accountability, not a lack of information. The industry has spent decades investing in systems that capture activity: electronic health records, billing platforms, payer portals, scheduling systems, call center platforms, and analytics applications. Each system records something important. But few were designed to reason across the full chain of decisions that determines whether patients get timely access, clinicians have the right documentation and providers are reimbursed appropriately. This is the problem that AI must now confront. Revenue cycle is becoming one of healthcare AI’s proving grounds The revenue cycle is the process healthcare providers use to get paid for care — from scheduling and registration through coding, billing, payer follow-up, and payment collection. It is unusually suited to rigorous AI deployment because it combines high transaction volume, complex reasoning, structured and unstructured data, measurable outcomes, and significant operational variation. It also sits at the intersection of financial performance, patient access, and administrative workload. A single claim can be influenced by patient insurance information, clinical documentation, coding rules, payer-specific policies, prior authorization requirements, medical necessity criteria, and many other data sources and operational processes. A breakdown in any one of those areas can create downstream consequences weeks or months later. This is why generic automation has often fallen short. Traditional robotic process automation works well when workflows are stable and rules are predictable, but healthcare administration is neither. Payer requirements change. Documentation expectations evolve. Exceptions are common and often material. Large language models improve part of the equation, extracting meaning from narrative text, summarizing records and supporting reasoning over complex documentation. But when used alone, they inherit important limitations. They may produce plausible outputs without sufficient traceability. They may lack awareness of local workflow constraints. They may miss payer-specific history or context that determines whether an action is likely to change an outcome. Why foundation models will become necessary but insufficient The major AI firms are solving real technical problems for healthcare. Better context windows make it easier to process longitudinal records. Stronger reasoning improves the interpretation of complex clinical scenarios. Better multimodal capabilities may eventually help connect text, imaging, structured data, and clinical signals in more useful ways. Safer model behavior and healthcare-specific tuning will continue to improve adoption. These capabilities will make healthcare work faster, more consistent and easier to navigate. But they will not, on their own, solve deep-rooted administrative complexity. Much of healthcare’s operational knowledge does not live in general medical literature, coding manuals, or public payer guidance. It lives in the accumulated experience of what actually happens after decisions are made. For example: - Why does one appeal strategy outperform another? - Which documentation gaps are most likely to cause reimbursement delay? - How does a specific payer respond to a particular clinical argument? These insights are behavioral, operational, and longitudinal. They emerge from years of transactions, outcomes, exceptions, and human judgment. As foundation models become more capable, access to baseline healthcare knowledge will become less differentiating. Most leading systems will be able to interpret ICD-10 codes, recognize medical terminology, summarize payer policies, and reason over public clinical criteria. The durable advantage will come from how organizations combine that model intelligence with proprietary operational data, structured knowledge, workflow context, and governance. The technical shift: From automation to orchestration Agentic orchestration turns foundation model understanding into coordinated action — intelligence that can follow work across systems, apply the right rules, adapt when something changes, and keep learning from what happens next. A prior authorization workflow, for example, may require retrieving clinical documentation through fast healthcare interoperability resources (FHIR) APIs, mapping patient history to payer criteria, identifying missing evidence, generating a submission packet, routing exceptions to a specialist, monitoring payer response, adjusting patient care pathways, and learning from the outcome. This type of workflow requires coordination. It also requires guardrails: regulatory requirements, privacy standards, clinical policies, coding rules, payer criteria, and organizational risk thresholds. One promising approach is hybrid architecture that combines LLMs with structured knowledge bases, symbolic logic, reinforcement learning, and deterministic validation layers. At Ensemble, this is the design principle behind EIQ, our revenue cycle intelligence engine. EIQ brings together operational activity, clinical documentation, payer behavior, and reimbursement outcomes into a continuously learning intelligence layer that’s integrated with the hospital’s electronic health record (EHR). It supplements the system of record with a system of intelligence, designed to connect information and surface actions most likely to improve outcomes. EIQ uses a neuro-symbolic approach that combines LLMs and custom small language models with rules-based reasoning. That architecture is built on one of the most robust datasets in healthcare, informed by more than a decade of award-winning operational performance, transaction history, payer behavior, and operator decision-making. The language models help interpret information and generate human-readable outputs. The symbolic layer represents policies, rules, payer requirements, and workflow constraints so the system can apply guardrails, make reasoning steps more traceable and recommend actions that fit the specific operational context. What the next decade will reward The contribution of major AI firms to healthcare will be significant. Their models will become faster, safer, more capable, and more accessible. But the next decade of healthcare AI will be defined by integration, not model capability alone. The organizations that create the most value will be those that connect models to governed data, operational workflows, domain expertise, human oversight, and measurable outcomes. They will understand that healthcare intelligence cannot live in a separate interface. It has to exist inside the decisions that shape access, documentation reimbursement, and patient experience. This content was produced by Ensemble. It was not written by MIT Technology Review’s editorial staff. item.title: The AI industry has taken a doomer turn. What now?
item.description:
Source: MIT Technology Review Score: 2.76
This story appeared in The Algorithm, our weekly newsletter on AI. To get stories like this in your inbox first, sign up here. This weekend, Dario Amodei, CEO of Anthropic, posted an essay calling for a brake on the pace of development of LLMs. Amodei cites the looming dangers he sees from the technology, from its use in cyberattacks and bioterrorism to its potential to wreck the economy. The heads of the other three top US AI labs—OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, Google DeepMind chairman Demis Hassabis, and SpaceXAI CEO Elon Musk—voiced their support. “Dario is right,” Musk wrote on X. Think about how surreal that agreement is for a moment. Just a few months ago, Musk and Altman sat in court attacking each other’s reputations in a (failed) lawsuit that Musk brought against his former OpenAI colleague that was—on paper at least—about whether or not Altman was a trustworthy steward of such dangerous technology. Amodei’s rift with OpenAI is even deeper. Anthropic was founded in 2021 because Amodei didn’t think Altman took the risks of the technology they were building seriously enough. Anthropic and OpenAI have been competing in a winner-takes-all race ever since. (Hassabis has stayed out of the drama, but his company remains a rival.) Now, it seems, they’re all in agreement: The latest generation of LLMs aren’t safe and everyone needs to figure out what to do about it. The public messaging from the top AI labs has taken a doomer turn. It’s easy to be cynical. It’s not at all clear what any of them mean by a slowdown or how it would work. These companies also care a lot about how they come across. With trillion-dollar IPOs in their sights, OpenAI and Anthropic need to reassure investors that they’re the grown-ups in the room while at the same time hinting at the power of the monsters they have created—and intend to tame. Calling for a slowdown does both. And yet the vibe at the top of these firms really does appear to have shifted. Amodei’s latest post landed six days after OpenAI published an essay by Jakub Pachocki, the firm’s chief scientist, in which he also laid out why he’s concerned about what will happen if the pace of development of LLMs continues unchecked. In short, Pachocki is worried that OpenAI’s ability to build powerful models now far outstrips its ability to monitor and control them. Amodei and Pachocki each cite the cyberattack against AI firm Hugging Face by a swarm of OpenAI’s agents in July—a hack that OpenAI did not even realize had taken place until days after it was all over—as a wake-up call. But their exact position is hard to pin down. Pachocki both calls for a slowdown and highlights an urgent need to stay ahead: “The strongest argument I see for continuing to train much smarter models quickly is the need to build defensive systems against the dangers posed by other AI,” he writes. As Pachocki frames it, AI firms are locked in a literal arms race. Slowing down is good, winning is better. (Don’t forget: OpenAI just spent millions of dollars and a staggering amount of computer power to rush out a controversial math result a few days ahead of Anthropic.) But let’s assume a slowdown happens. Top labs agree to spend more time and resources on finding ways to monitor and control existing models instead of making more capable ones. They invite outside auditors in to help evaluate those models. What might this coordinated effort actually achieve? Consider the Hugging Face attack again. OpenAI has said that the model that drove most of the rogue agents was a “highly persistent” next-generation model that it was testing in-house. Their implication appears to be that OpenAI has built a model so good it’s dangerous. But if you read the reports about the Hugging Face hack published by OpenAI and METR, a third-party firm that OpenAI called in to help them understand what happened, what you come away with is the impression not of a model that was too powerful for OpenAI to keep up with, but of a broken model that OpenAI failed to train properly. The agents did what they did—including leaving messages for one another, delegating work to other agents, and scouring their environment for any means possible to complete their tasks—because they had been rewarded during training for doing exactly those things. There were also errors in the training setup, such as tasks that were impossible to complete, which pushed the models to find unexpected workarounds that were also rewarded. At the time, many of these issues went overlooked or unreported. OpenAI says it has stopped training this new model and locked it down. That makes it sound like it has caged a dangerous beast. In fact, OpenAI has shelved a faulty product. That’s not to say a faulty product can’t be dangerous. Broken software has even killed people in the past. But as the discussion of a slowdown gathers steam, it’s worth remembering that all of this is self-inflicted. A slowdown might have some altruistic side effects. But it’ll mostly give these tech titans a chance to clean up the mess on their own assembly lines. Transparency from these frontier labs will be key to any meaningful effort to reform, restrain, or regulate AI. Otherwise, the rest of us will still only have their word for exactly what they’ve built and how safe it is—whatever pace they’re going. To continue this discussion about AI’s latest doomer moment, join me and my colleagues for a subscriber-exclusive Roundtable discussion tomorrow, September 15, at 11 a.m. US eastern time. We hope to see you there! Deep Dive Artificial intelligence A fundamental flaw leaves LLMs strikingly vulnerable to attack It makes it easy to trick them into doing things they shouldn’t, such as telling you how to sabotage an aircraft’s navigation system. AI is more likely than humans to form biases when hiring AI doesn’t just learn stereotypes from its training. It can cook up new ones, too. item.title: Time to Patch: Nintendo Switch Can Be Hacked Using QR Codes
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 6.26
Nintendo is warning about a security flaw in the first-gen Switch console related to the feature that lets you send game screenshots to a smartphone. It turns out you can hack the function to run malicious computer code or leak console data. Nintendo has issued a security advisory about the vulnerability. It involves the Send to Smartphone function, which displays a QR code on the handheld that a smartphone can scan to initiate the wireless transfer of a game screenshot or in-game footage. According to Nintendo, unnamed security researchers recently discovered a way to exploit QR codes to carry out a Proximity-Based Remote Attack. “If a third party can directly scan the QR code, they could run unauthorized code on your Nintendo Switch console or obtain information stored on the console,” the advisory says. The vulnerability can also be exploited with the displayed QR code when pairing the kart accessory to play Mario Kart Live: Home Circuit. Details about the bug, dubbed CVE-2026-82079, are thin. But it involves a “stack-based buffer overflow,” where data copied into a memory buffer exceeds the buffer's size, overwriting adjacent memory and potentially leading to software crashes or a path to hack the system. Fortunately, exploiting the flaw isn't easy since the hacker would need to be nearby. Nintendo also patched the issue last week with version 23.0.0. So, it's recommended that users download and install the update. “You can check the current system version applied to your Nintendo Switch. From the HOME Menu, select System Settings > System. You can also update the system version,” the company says. Nintendo adds that “this vulnerability cannot be exploited to obtain console information on Nintendo Switch 2,” which seems to have phased out QR codes in favor of transferring screenshot via the Nintendo app. About Our Expert I've been a journalist for over 15 years. I got my start as a schools and cities reporter in Kansas City and joined PCMag in 2017, where I cover satellite internet services, cybersecurity, PC hardware, and more. I'm currently based in San Francisco, but previously spent over five years in China, covering the country's technology sector. Since 2020, I've covered the launch and explosive growth of SpaceX's Starlink satellite internet service, writing 600+ stories on availability and feature launches, but also the regulatory battles over the expansion of satellite constellations, fights with rival providers like AST SpaceMobile and Amazon, and the effort to expand into satellite-based mobile service. I've combed through FCC filings for the latest news and driven to remote corners of California to test Starlink's cellular service. I also cover cyber threats, from ransomware gangs to the emergence of AI-based malware. In 2024 and 2025, the FTC forced Avast to pay consumers $16.5 million for secretly harvesting and selling their personal information to third-party clients, as revealed in my joint investigation with Motherboard. I also cover the PC graphics card market. Pandemic-era shortages led me to camp out in front of a Best Buy to get an RTX 3000. I'm now following how the AI-driven memory shortage is impacting the entire consumer electronics market. I'm always eager to learn more, so please jump in the comments with feedback and send me tips.

item.title: Google Just Made It Way Easier to Move Your Keys Between Password Managers
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 6.25
Google has made it easier to swap your saved passwords between different password managers on Android, and will now allow you to transfer passkeys across different managers for the first time. When you open up your password manager app, you can now click on a new option to import or copy your passwords and passkeys from another provider. The password manager will then hand the task over to Android, which will detect existing password managers on your device and show you which one it supports. Tap Continue and Android will bring you to your existing password manager to select, review, and authorize the transfer. After verifying your identity, Android will complete the migration automatically, meaning there is no need to manually import and export your logins via a CSV file (which can open up security issues of its own). The new feature uses the Credential Exchange Format (CXF), a standardized data structure published by the FIDO Alliance, designed to help users move log-ins between different password managers. The feature is already available for Google Password Manager, 1Password, Bitwarden Password Manager, and Dashlane. Google says it will roll out integrations with more password managers in the future, though it didn't give a firm timeline. You don't need a modern device to get the feature to work; any device running 2017's Android 8 and above is supported. Password managers are becoming increasingly mainstream. As of 2023, more than one third (34%) of Americans say they're using some kind of password management tool, according to a study from Security.org, though the majority (63%) are opting for free services. About Our Expert I’m a reporter covering weekend news. Before joining PCMag in 2024, I picked up bylines in BBC News, The Guardian, The Times of London, The Daily Beast, Vice, Slate, Fast Company, The Evening Standard, The i, TechRadar, and Decrypt Media. I’ve been a PC gamer since you had to install games from multiple CD-ROMs by hand. As a reporter, I’m passionate about the intersection of tech and human lives. I’ve covered everything from crypto scandals to the art world, as well as conspiracy theories, UK politics, and Russia and foreign affairs.

item.title: Apple Watch Series 12 vs. Ultra 4: 7 Key Differences You Need to Know Before Buying
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 5.40
Table of Contents The foldable iPhone stole the headlines, but Apple's newest wearables quietly packed the biggest upgrades. Both the Apple Watch Series 12 and Apple Watch Ultra 4 boast the powerful S11 chip, upgraded heart rate tracking, and new Audio Intelligence. Yet with massive gaps in battery life, materials, and off-grid durability, choosing between them comes down to a few critical trade-offs. Read on for a detailed breakdown of exactly what's different to help you determine which watch is right for you. Full Specs | Apple Watch Series 12 | Apple Watch Ultra 4 | | |---|---|---| | Phone OS Compatibility | | | | Phone OS Compatibility | iOS | iOS | | Watch OS | | | | Watch OS | watchOS | watchOS | | Processor | | | | Processor | Apple S11 | Apple S11 | | Display Size | | | | Display Size | 1.65 inches/1.81 inches | 1.9 inches | | Display Type | | | | Display Type | Always-on LTPO3 OLED | Always-on LTPO3 OLED | | Fitness Features | | | | Fitness Features | Heart Rate Monitor, ECG, Blood Oxygen Monitor, Temperature Sensor, Pedometer, Gyroscope, Pulse Oximeter, Accelerometer, GPS, Barometer | Blood Oxygen Monitor, ECG, Heart Rate Monitor, Accelerometer, GPS, Temperature Sensor, Pedometer, Gyroscope, Light Sensor, Barometer, Pulse Oximeter | | Battery Life | | | | Battery Life | 24 hours (estimated) | 50 hours (estimated) | | Separate App Store | | | | Separate App Store | | | | Phone Call Capacity | | | | Phone Call Capacity | | | Price: One Ultra 4 Costs the Same as Two Series 12s At first glance, the pricing structure is straightforward: the Series 12 starts at an accessible $399 (42mm, aluminum, GPS), while adding larger sizing (an additional $50) or cellular (an additional $100) tops out the standard titanium model at $749. That makes it significantly cheaper than the $799 Ultra 4, which comes standard in a single 49mm titanium cellular configuration. But there's a wildcard: material upgrades. Choose the fancy new Ceramic Series 12, and the price jumps to $899 (42mm) or $949 (46mm). Add in the ultra-luxury Hermès editions ($1,399 for Series 12; $1,499 for Ultra 4), and both lines can climb into true luxury territory. But for everyday buyers watching their wallet, the Series 12 remains the clear entry-level choice. Winner: Apple Watch Series 12 Design: Massive Variety vs. Single-Frame Utility If you want your pick of finishes, sizes, and materials, you should go with the Apple Watch Series 12. It comes in aluminum, titanium, or all-new ceramic versions, each in two sizes (42mm and 46mm). Aluminum is available in black, gray, gold, or bronze finishes; titanium in radiant gold or natural; and ceramic in white or blue. The Ultra 4, on the other hand, is just one size with two flavors: black or natural titanium. If you want some color or have smaller wrists, the Series 12 is the watch to go with. Winner: Apple Watch Series 12 AI Features: Audio Intelligence Is Always Listening (If You Want) Both the Series 12 and the Ultra 4 use Apple's new S11 chip, which enables some new AI tricks their predecessors won't get. The biggest one is Audio Intelligence, an Apple Intelligence feature that lets the watch listen to you, your conversations, and your surroundings all day, providing AI summaries and other information. It can rewind a live conversation with a 15-second text snippet, or give a full summary afterward with a title and key points. It can also notify you of sounds like alarms and doorbells, if you're hard of hearing. Apple says it approaches Audio Intelligence with privacy in mind, and that the S11 chip has a dedicated hardware section for locally processing and then deleting any audio it records. It also claims that speakers aren't identified or attributed, and that sensitive information isn't kept. I'm leery of any always-on AI, but you should be able to just turn it off on either watch if you don't want to engage with it. Winner: Tie Health and Fitness: All-Day Heart Rate Tracking Even if you don't want to use Audio Intelligence, AI powers some of the Series 12 and Ultra 4's new health features. They can provide a holistic readiness score, ranging from zero to 10, to let you know how much energy you have, and give you a recommendation of just how hard you should train that day. The iPhone Health app has also been redesigned and offers even more holistic information, including a Longevity tab that can tell you your body's Health Age. The S11 chip also improves the pedometer function on both watches, providing more accurate distance measurements and allowing you to monitor individual steps in real time. Beyond AI analysis, both new Apple Watch models have redesigned always-on heart rate sensors. They can measure your heart rate every five seconds throughout the day, rather than just periodically, as previous models did. They also measure heart rate variability (HRV) up to 24 times more often than before. For general health and fitness, the Series 12 and Ultra 4 are on equal footing. When you get into more extreme outdoor activities, though, that changes, and that brings us to the next section. Winner: Tie Connectivity and Navigation: Satellite Emergency Messaging vs. Standard Cellular The core connection features of the Series 12 and Ultra 4 are the same, with support for dual-band Wi-Fi 4, Bluetooth 5.3, and 5G and LTE cellular connectivity. The Ultra 4 builds on that with satellite connectivity for messages and emergency signals, even if you're outside of cellular coverage, which could prove useful if you enjoy long hikes on remote trails. It also has dual L1/L5 GPS compared with the Series 12's L1 GPS, enabling more precise location tracking. Winner: Apple Watch Ultra 4 Durability: City-Proof Ratings vs. Extreme Dive Certification Once again, while the Series 12 and Ultra 4 are on equal footing for day-to-day work and play, the Ultra 4 wins when you look to the extremes. Both are IP6X-rated for dustproof and waterproof protection, but the Series 12 is only rated for submersion to a depth of 164 feet and is not recommended for diving. The Ultra 4 is water-resistant to 328 feet and safe for diving to 141 feet, and has EN13319 certification to prove it. It's also tested to MIL-STD 810H, which means it can be put through environmental peril that the Series 12 might not survive. Winner: Apple Watch Ultra 4 Battery Life: 24 Hours vs. Multi-Day Endurance We still need to test them ourselves, but based on Apple's estimates, the Ultra 4 can last more than twice as long as the Series 12. Apple estimates a battery life of 50 hours for the Ultra 4 with normal use compared with 24 hours for the Series 12. Those numbers might diverge even wider based on what we've seen with previous models. Apple is usually conservative with its battery life estimates, and both the Apple Watch Series 11 and the Ultra 3 lasted far longer than Apple said they would. In testing, the Series 11 lasted 43 hours, compared with a claimed 24 hours, and the Ultra 4 lasted 63 hours, compared with a claimed 42 hours. Considering the always-on heart rate monitors in the newest models, the Series 12 and Ultra 4's real-world battery lives might be closer to Apple's estimates this time around, but either way, it's safe to say that the Ultra 4 will last much longer than the Series 12. Winner: Apple Watch Series 12 Verdict: Everyday Versatility or Extreme Performance? It's hardly shocking that the Apple Watch Ultra 4 looks like the superior device—it's always been Apple’s top-tier feature showcase. But that premium performance comes with a premium price tag (unless you have your eye on a luxury ceramic Series 12). Since both watches share the same S11 chip and continuous heart rate tracking, their everyday performance is virtually identical. If you need multi-day battery life, off-grid navigation, or ocean diving specs, spend the extra money on the Ultra 4. Otherwise, the Series 12 offers all the smarts you actually need in a far more wrist-friendly design.

item.title: OpenAI CEO Warns of 2 Ways AI Could Go 'Very Badly' If Tech Doesn't Slow Down
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 5.30
AI CEOs took to social media this weekend to discuss a collective slowdown in large language model development following a series of security incidents involving agentic AI and a viral resignation warning about the risks posed by self-improving LLMs. After a brief tweet on Saturday afternoon concurring with his sometimes-nemesis Dario Amodei, CEO of Anthropic, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman posted a longer message early this morning, warning of ways "AI progress could go very badly." He didn’t outline what losing control means for OpenAI, but there's been a lot of talk about superintelligence, or AI that surpasses humans. It comes after an Anthropic researcher resigned last week over safety concerns, saying OpenAI and Anthropic are both “gambling with our lives" on the development of self-improving AI. Altman says losing control of the future to AI is unacceptable, adding, "We are unapologetically on Team Humanity, and AI must always serve people. To ensure that, we need ways to ensure that alignment and safety techniques stay ahead of progress in model capabilities.” He also warned about “too much concentration of power." He alluded to the idea that one country may eventually have too much control due to access to advanced AI, or that one development lab may have significantly more power over another. “If an extraordinarily powerful AI is used by one person or company to impress their worldview onto everyone else, the results could be extremely dystopian," Altman said. This comes as Altman and his rivals try to control the conversation about the future of AI development. Amodei called for collective action to slow development and suggested government intervention may ensure firms comply with any new rules. In addition to Altman, Elon Musk and Demis Hassabis, co-founder of Google DeepMind, also expressed interest. Altman claims OpenAI would “welcome a federal framework that sets consistent safety requirements,” but says work could begin without Congress. He called for “shared standards for misalignment, monitoring, and safety,” saying it would “lead to better outcomes. “We look forward to collaborating with our colleagues across the industry to formulate the best version of these," he said, without sharing specifics. Amodei outlined a three-stage plan for AI companies such as Anthropic and OpenAI to limit the risks posed by new models. That included adding third-party evaluators to each company, a new set of standards across firms, and deals with foreign nations to limit potentially dangerous use cases of models. David Sacks, chair of the President's Council of Advisors on Science and Technology, suggested each AI firm should slow down of its own accord if necessary, rather than waiting for government oversight. "I don’t see what you see in the lab. If the unreleased models are scary enough that you think you should slow down, I support your decision to be responsible," Sacks said. "But stop pretending you need anyone else’s permission. Stop pretending antitrust law has to be suspended so you can form a cartel. Stop pretending you need a regulatory approval process that supersedes product liability." Meanwhile, President Trump took to Truth Social this morning to tout his own brainpower. "The only control or 'guardrails' that AI needs is a STRONG AND SMART (High IQ!) PRESIDENT, and the U.S.A. has that, in spades!" he wrote. Trump says Amodei, who tangled with the Pentagon over using Claude for military operations, is "pretending to be a 'perfect little angel,'" and reiterated his irritation at data center protests. "Conspiracy Theorists, Treasonists, Traitors, and Leakers, BEWARE!" Vice President JD Vance also said it's "weird" that "so many frontier AI tech companies [are] coming to the government and begging the government to regulate them. It feels a little bit to me like a bit of a Trojan horse." Disclosure: Ziff Davis, PCMag's parent company, filed a lawsuit against OpenAI in April 2025, alleging it infringed Ziff Davis copyrights in training and operating its AI systems. About Our Expert I’ve been a journalist for over a decade after getting my start in tech reporting back in 2013. I joined PCMag in 2025, where I cover the latest developments across the tech sphere, writing about the gadgets and services you use every day. Be sure to send me any tips you think PCMag would be interested in.

item.title: Apple's New OSes Hide an Easter Egg That Old-School Mac Users Should Appreciate
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 5.14
Apple’s newest operating systems, out today, hide a throwback reference to one of the more whimsical bits of one of the company’s oldest OS releases: Clarus the dogcow. Mac users with enough gray hair (or no hair left at all) should remember Clarus as a bitmapped animal with the spots of a cow and approximately the head and the tail of a dog, which would visualize how your choice of print settings affected how your text appeared on a page. More than four decades after the dogcow’s debut in a page-setup dialog for Apple's LaserWriter printer—with a moniker nodding to the firm’s Claris productivity-software subsidiary—you can now catch this critter in settings dialogs for Apple’s less-than-universally-beloved Liquid Glass interface-transparency option. To see this Easter egg in iOS 27, iPadOS 27, and macOS 27 Golden Gate, open Settings > Appearance > Liquid Glass, and keep scrolling down repeatedly until the word “Moof!” starts to appear in the sample image’s search box. As longtime Mac types can attest, “Moof!” is the sound a dogcow makes instead of “woof” or “moo,” since it’s part dog and part cow. Here, the word appears, at first in rainbow colors, below a picture of a non-bitmapped dogcow next to a pool. While you’re in this dialog, you can also adjust the slider to control how transparent menus and other interface elements appear, a source of considerable grumbling among users of macOS 26 Tahoe. The definitive description of Clarus appears in a mock technical note written by Apple developer-support staffer Mark Harlan in 1989 that has long since vanished from the web. “Dogcows, by their nature, are not all dog, nor are they all cow, but they are a special genetic hybrid,” Harlan wrote. “They are rarely seen in the wild. Since dogcows are two-dimensional, they will stand facing a viewer ‘on edge’ to avoid being seen.” The note also alludes to the dogcow’s role in illustrating which way your text would appear on the page if you adjusted various dialogs. “Like any talented dog, it can do flips,” he praised the dogcow. “Like any talented cow, it can do precision bitmap alignment.” In a 2019 interview recorded for the Computer History Museum in Mountain View, graphic designer Annette Wagner explained how she created the dogcow by adopting a dog icon created by Susan Kare for the original Mac’s Cairo symbols-only font. “We needed some kind of graphic that would show flipping horizontal, flipping vertical, 2% reduction,” she said. With significant alterations to make it clear to the user when this icon was reversed, flipped, or shrunk by a specific percentage, her work survived an unnamed marketing type’s initial thumbs-down: “Everyone’s going to think this is doggy software!” For years, a Clarus sculpture held a prominent spot in the icon garden outside the Apple headquarters buildings, predating Apple Park’s spaceship structure. But this icon fell out of favor over Apple’s long series of reinventions. The dogcow, however, made a reappearance in page-setup dialogs in 2022’s macOS Ventura as a smoothly drawn figurine and continues to adorn those dialogs in Golden Gate. To see one, choose “Page Setup” from the File menu in a writing app like Apple’s built-in TextEdit. A year ago, Clarus also resurfaced in an optional face for the Apple Watch Series 11’s Hermès edition. We don’t know when this Mac mascot began showing up in beta versions of Apple’s newest operating systems, but MacRumors analyst Aaron Perris shared a video of it on X on Sept. 9, after which Macworld’s Roman Loyola wrote up that finding and offered this conclusion: “It’s fun to see Apple add a little whimsy to its software.” True. About Our Expert Rob Pegoraro writes about interesting problems and possibilities in computers, gadgets, apps, services, telecom, and other things that beep or blink. He’s covered such developments as the evolution of the cell phone from 1G to 5G, the fall and rise of Apple, Google’s growth from obscure Yahoo rival to verb status, and the transformation of social media from CompuServe forums to Facebook’s billions of users. Pegoraro has met most of the founders of the internet and once received a single-word email reply from Steve Jobs.

item.title: You Can Get Up to $1,200 for an iPhone 18 Pro with Apple's Carrier Trade-in Incentives
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 5.07
The iPhone 18 Pro will release on September 18, and if you can't stomach the starting $1,199 price tag, there is some good news. Apple recently increased its trade-in values for the second time this year, making it a little easier to afford one of its new rumored iPhones. And, following the September 9 Apple Event, the tech giant also unveiled new trade-in partner incentives for anyone buying the iPhone 18 Pro. Preorders open today, so if you're preparing to trade in your old device to shave some cost off the upfront price, here's everything you need to know about Apple's trade-in deals and values, and how to make sure your old phone is ready to ship, so you can get the highest value in exchange. Apple's New Carrier Trade-in Incentives for the iPhone 18 Pro Max Apple has partnered with AT&T and T-Mobile to offer up to $1,200 in trade-in credits when you trade in an iPhone 14 or later to put toward a new iPhone 18 Pro or iPhone 18 Pro Max. Preorder Deals: - Save $1,200 when you preorder with T-Mobile and trade in an eligible device - Save $1,200 when you preorder with AT&T and trade in an eligible device You can also trade in your device through Apple, but the maximum trade-in value you can get this way is $885. What's the Trade-in Value for Older iPhones? Apple recently announced its trade-in values for the iPhone 17 line. It also boosted trade-in values for older devices twice this past summer. Here's the max value you can get for each type of iPhone through Apple Trade In: - iPhone 17 Pro Max: $885 - iPhone 17 Pro: $785 - iPhone Air: $585 - iPhone 17: $585 - iPhone 16 Pro Max: $720 (previously $695) - iPhone 16 Pro: $630 (previously $560) - iPhone 16 Plus: $485 (previously $465) - iPhone 16: $480 (previously $460) - iPhone 16e: $310 (no change) - iPhone 15 Pro Max: $530 (previously $490) - iPhone 15 Pro: $420 (previously $410) - iPhone 15 Plus: $340 (previously $325) - iPhone 15: $335 (previously $320) - iPhone 14 Pro Max: $405 (previously $375) - iPhone 14 Pro: $335 (previously $320) - iPhone 14 Plus: $235 (unchanged) - iPhone 14: $235 (previously $225) What to Do Before Trading in Your Old iPhone Now that you know the maximum trade-in value of your old phone, you'll want to take some steps to make sure it's backed up, unpaired, and cleaned up. Here are the steps you should take before you send in your old device. 1. Back Up Everything First, make sure you don't lose your data. Back everything up before you wipe it from your phone. To back up to iCloud from your device, go to Settings, select your name, and then choose iCloud > iCloud Backup > Back Up Now. To back up to your Mac, connect your iPhone and your computer via a cable or Wi-Fi. If you have macOS Catalina or later, go to Finder, select your iPhone, and then choose General > Back Up All of the Data on Your iPhone to This Mac > Back Up Now. If you have an earlier version or a Windows PC, you'd use iTunes. Open the program, click on the image of your phone, then select Summary > Back Up Now. 2. Unfind Your iPhone Apple’s Find My app can sometimes block activation by a new owner, so you should deactivate the app before you ditch the device. Though Find My is automatically deactivated when you erase all content and settings, which you'll do below, this is still a good step to take as a precaution. Go to Settings, select your name, then choose Find My and disable it for that device. Enter your Apple Account password and tap Turn Off. 3. Sign Out of Messages More than a decade ago, people who switched from iOS to Android without logging out of Messages on their iPhone found that texts were going to the old phone. The problem has since been fixed, but those still scarred by "iMessage purgatory" may want to go to Settings > Apps > Messages and disable iMessage. 4. Unpair Your AirPods Similarly, you can still connect your AirPods to a new iPhone without unpairing them from the old one, but it can't hurt to wipe the slate clean. Place your AirPods and iPhone near each other, then go to Settings > Bluetooth. Tap the information icon next to your AirPods, and select Forget this Device. 5. Unpair Your Apple Watch If you have an Apple Watch, save yourself a potential headache and unpair it from the iPhone you'll be selling. Place them near each other, then open the Apple Watch app on your phone. Go to My Watch > All Watches and select the info circle next to the watch you want to unpair. Tap Unpair Apple Watch and then confirm, which may require you to enter your Apple Account password. With a GPS + Cellular model, you're asked whether you want to keep or remove your cellular plan. Since you're selling the iPhone, you'll want to remove it. (If you don't plan to pair your watch with a new iPhone, you might need to contact your carrier to cancel.) Tap to confirm; you might need to enter your Apple Account password to disable Activation Lock. 6. Sign Out of iCloud You should sign out of iCloud, iTunes, and the App Store before selling your device. Tap Settings, select your name, and choose Sign Out. Enter your Apple Account password and tap Turn Off. 7. Wipe Your iPhone and Delete Data When your new phone is set up and you're ready to trade in or sell your old iPhone, head to Settings > General > Transfer or Reset iPhone > Erase All Content and Settings, then approve all subsequent prompts. 8. Remove the SIM Card (If You Have One) Apple went the eSIM route starting with the iPhone 14 lineup, but older devices will have a physical SIM card. In most cases, you can just deactivate your cellphone service on the device and trade it in with the SIM card intact. But that SIM card is the repository of your phone number, various bits of security data, and all the info needed for billing. It identifies you, your phone, and a lot of your activity on your phone. So you should remove it before you sell the phone. Fortunately, it's simple. Locate the SIM ejector on your phone, then insert a paper clip until the tray pops out. Remove the SIM card, replace the tray, and say goodbye to your old iPhone. The Best Places to Sell Your Phone I've also included some of the best sites for selling or trading in your phone. Some make it easy to send in your phone and get immediate cash, others let you control the price through bidding, and there are even options for receiving store credit from places you shop. To give you an idea of your trade-in power, I priced out what you can expect to get for an iPhone 15 Pro across all of them, and it varies wildly, as you'll see below. You can also trade your phone in with your existing carrier or switch to a new one. Many offer compelling trade-in promotions, so be sure to check out AT&T, T-Mobile, Verizon, and others. Apple Trade In The Apple Trade In program pays you with a credit or gift card. If you pay for an Apple device in full up-front, a credit will be applied to your payment card once Apple receives your trade-in device and verifies its condition. If you're paying on an installment plan, the credit will be applied right away. Turning in an iPhone 15 Pro, for example, can get you up to $410 on a new iPhone now that Apple has increased some trade-in values by as much as $35. Best Buy If you're selling your iPhone and just want cash to buy electronics, you can cut out a step at Best Buy: Trade in your phone at a store or mail it in for a digital gift card. For a Black Titanium 512GB iPhone 15 Pro on Verizon in good condition, expect to get about $275. eBay To sell your device yourself, there's always eBay. The site has a quick walkthrough where you can input your phone's stats. After entering my example device, a Black Titanium 512GB iPhone 15 Pro in good condition on Verizon, the page recommended that I list the phone at $510. GameStop Are most of your iPhone apps games? Then you'll probably do well to turn in your iPhone in for some store credit at GameStop. You can also get cold, hard cash for it there. Bring your device to your nearest GameStop, get a price quote from a sales associate, and then receive store credit or cash on the spot. I recommend getting an estimate on the site before you make the trip. I found that a 512GB iPhone 15 Pro from Verizon in very good condition will get you $267.30 in cash or $297.00 in store credit. Swappa Swappa is a marketplace where you can sell your iPhone directly. Select your phone model on the site, upload some photos, and set a price. Once someone buys it, you're paid immediately via PayPal. You're responsible for safely shipping your phone to the buyer. According to the site, an iPhone 15 Pro is selling for an average price of $544, while a trade-in to one of Swappa's partners could get me $311. uSell Want to sell your iPhone fast? One option is uSell. Select your model, carrier, capacity, and condition to receive an offer. If you choose to accept it, you ship your iPhone to uSell for free. If your device is in the condition you said it was, you're paid by check or PayPal. A 512GB iPhone 15 Pro on Verizon in good condition is currently worth about $268. Editors' Note: Trade-in values were accurate at the time of publication. Your mileage may vary. Chandra Steele contributed to this story About Our Expert As PCMag's editor of how to content, I have to cover a wide variety of topics and also make our stories accessible to everyday users. Considering my history as a technical writer, copywriter, and all-around freelancer covering baseball, comics, and more at various outlets, I am used to making myself into an expert. I believe tech corporations are bad, but you might as well know how to use technology in everyday life. Want more how to content delivered right to your inbox? Sign up for the tips and tricks newsletter that I curate three times a week. My job as how-to guru means I use just about every gadget under the sun, so I can figure out how everything works. I work from a Lenovo ThinkPad running Windows 11, but also have a very large Dell Inspiron 17 3000 and Apple silicon MacBook. I have a Google Pixel 6a for personal use and use a Galaxy Z Flip 4 for additional Samsung-related testing. For iOS coverage, an iPhone 13 mini works like a charm, though it's already becoming a little long in the tooth. My desktop situation includes a dual monitor setup with a modest Acer monitor. I also use a Logitech vertical mouse (who can use these ThinkPad trackpads) and a Havit keyboard (my first mechanical keyboard; I love it but my wife hates it!). I'm a recent convert from wired headphones; I have Anker Soundcore Liberty Air wireless earbuds for personal use and have taken to the Sennheiser HD 450BT headphones for work. Whenever I have a second to myself, I'm probably gaming on my Nintendo Switch 2, Steam Deck, or Xbox Series S. I also still have a bunch of classic consoles lying around as well.

item.title: HBO Max's Reddit Account Was Hijacked to Spread Malware
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 5.02
A hacker hijacked an HBO Max-focused account on Reddit to trick users into installing malware that can infect Windows PCs and Macs. The hacker circulated 46 official-looking but fake ads via the u/hbomax account, according to security researchers at Hudson Rock and Adam Networks. Some of the ads promoted a fraudulent desktop app for the streaming service. A user on Reddit first flagged the threat earlier this month after noticing that many of the ads led to a fake domain at hbomaxx[.]us. The site was offering three months of free HBO Max for downloading HBO on macOS. However, clicking the offer triggered a ClickFix-style attack, or a list of seemingly harmless instructions to perform on a Windows PC or Mac. Hackers often dress up ClickFix attacks to look like CAPTCHA or error screens that can pop up on an internet browser, nudging the users to execute the instructions to resolve the issue. Computer-savvy users will immediately understand the nature of the threat. But the trick can fool casual users who are unaware they're triggering their own computer system to download and execute malware. Hudson Rock and Adam Networks took a closer look at the HBO Max-Reddit incident and noted that "by hijacking a verified corporate account, [the attacker] bypassed the initial skepticism many users apply to internet advertisements.” The attack used macOS malware designed to steal browser passwords, along with cookies, wallet data, and login credentials from password managers. If the user visited the malicious site on a Windows computer, the domain served a ClickFix-style attack meant for the Microsoft OS. In addition, the hacker behind the scheme used the same HBO Max account to distribute dozens of other ads and fake apps, including AI tools Claude and Codex, along with a macOS system cleaner. This created a “massive 48-hour malvertising blitz,” an indication that the hacker tried to exploit the HBO Max account for as long as possible before users caught on. So far, HBO Max hasn’t responded to a request for comment. But an admin at Reddit said last week that the social media platform had “paused the affected ads and are looking into what happened with our Security and Safety teams.” The incident is a reminder to be vigilant around any websites or pop-ups that ask you to perform seemingly random instructions. Ars Technica reports that ClickFix-style attacks continue to evolve and grow by finding new ways to circulate on the internet. About Our Expert I've been a journalist for over 15 years. I got my start as a schools and cities reporter in Kansas City and joined PCMag in 2017, where I cover satellite internet services, cybersecurity, PC hardware, and more. I'm currently based in San Francisco, but previously spent over five years in China, covering the country's technology sector. Since 2020, I've covered the launch and explosive growth of SpaceX's Starlink satellite internet service, writing 600+ stories on availability and feature launches, but also the regulatory battles over the expansion of satellite constellations, fights with rival providers like AST SpaceMobile and Amazon, and the effort to expand into satellite-based mobile service. I've combed through FCC filings for the latest news and driven to remote corners of California to test Starlink's cellular service. I also cover cyber threats, from ransomware gangs to the emergence of AI-based malware. In 2024 and 2025, the FTC forced Avast to pay consumers $16.5 million for secretly harvesting and selling their personal information to third-party clients, as revealed in my joint investigation with Motherboard. I also cover the PC graphics card market. Pandemic-era shortages led me to camp out in front of a Best Buy to get an RTX 3000. I'm now following how the AI-driven memory shortage is impacting the entire consumer electronics market. I'm always eager to learn more, so please jump in the comments with feedback and send me tips.

item.title: Valve's Steam Frame VR Headset Finally Arrives for $1,059
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 4.81
Following a memory-related delay, Valve’s Steam Frame is finally ready to launch. The company will begin taking orders for the VR headset later this week. A 256GB version will be $1,059, and a 1TB model will cost $1,299. Both come with 16GB of Unified LPDDR5X RAM. To thwart resellers and bots, interested buyers will need to join a waitlist/reservation system; Valve is accepting sign-ups now through Thursday, Sept. 17, at 10 a.m. PT. They will then be randomized “to determine reservation and waitlist order.” “Based on the results of that randomization, you'll receive an email on September 17th letting you know you're either in the reservation queue or on the waitlist,” the company says. “If you're in the reservation queue, the model you signed up for has been reserved in your name. As units become available to ship, you'll receive an email with the option to purchase. The first batch of these emails will begin going out on September 18th. “You'll then have 72 hours to complete the purchase before we cancel your reservation and move on to the next person in the queue,” the company added. Although the Steam Frame isn’t cheap, Valve is touting an array of enhancements and capabilities, including its design for both VR titles and non-VR games. “Designed for streaming, it can handle your entire Steam library. And it supports standalone play too, with over 100 games (and growing) already Steam Frame Standalone Verified,” it wrote in a blog post. The headset also features a 4-nanometer Snapdragon 8 Gen 3 processor and two 2,160-by-2,160 LCDs, each with a 72-144Hz refresh rate. In addition, the product relies on “inside-out tracking,” ditching external sensors, unlike the older Valve Index headset. The product will be available on the Steam store for buyers in the US, Canada, Europe, and Australia. Customers in Japan, Taiwan, and Hong Kong will be able to purchase through Valve’s partner, Komodo. The company has also created an FAQ about the reservation system, which is open only to Steam accounts that have made at least one purchase prior to April 27, 2026. “Limit one signup per household. We will use payment method, shipping address, and other information to eliminate multiple entries,” it says. If you decide to buy after Sept. 17, your order will be placed at the end of the waitlist. Ahead of the launch, a few tech publications reviewed the headset. IGN notes, “The Steam Frame is probably one of the first VR headsets that can do everything right out of the box, from standalone gaming to streaming 2D games from your PC.” However, both IGN and CNET flagged the short battery life as a weakness. item.title: This Free Tool Unlocks 500+ Hidden Windows 11 Features, and Even Microsoft Execs Are Fans
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 4.80
Windhawk is a free and open-source tool that helps you tweak aspects of Windows and your apps in ways that Microsoft and developers would never allow, combining a sophisticated code injection technique with an intuitive interface. The project's developer, Michael Maltsev, says it now has 1.5 million users, and Microsoft employees are increasingly enthusiastic about it, too. March Rogers, partner director of design at Microsoft, recently called it "amazing." Simply put, Windhawk is the most powerful customization program I've come across in my decades of writing about Windows. But before you install it, here's how this groundbreaking tool actually works, what it can do for your PC, and the safety rules you should follow. How Windhawk Modifies Windows Under the Hood Maltsev, who also goes by m417z and publishes under the Ramen Software name, is well-known in the Windows tweaking community for previous projects, including 7+ Taskbar Tweaker. He describes Windhawk as a “customization marketplace for Windows programs," and offers it as a free download for PCs running Windows 10 or 11. The app lets you download and configure a variety of Windows mods from Maltsev and other developers. How does it work? His original announcement post from 2022 explains that it modifies running programs in memory by injecting code into their processes. The technique lets you change nearly any aspect of any app or operating system component. Windhawk users have long had the option to move Windows 11’s taskbar to the top of the screen, for example. Mods can also apply themes to the taskbar, Start menu, and other Windows OS components, changing how they look. But Maltsev says "Windhawk is not just about styling Windows," pointing out that the marketplace now has over 500 mods that add new functionality. The Safety Risks (And Why Most Users Don't Mind) Yes, Windhawk’s code injection technique is potentially dangerous. Antivirus software sometimes flags it because malware often uses a similar method to tamper with running processes. Still, Maltsev says this is becoming less common: "Mainstream antivirus products don't usually conflict with it." He does note, however, that enterprise security tools typically block code injection, making Windhawk a poor fit for corporate environments. A poorly written mod or a problem with Windhawk itself could, of course, cause apps or your OS to malfunction, but Maltsev claims that complaints from the project's one-and-a-half million users are rare. "The most common complaints are about mods that stop working, which usually happens when Microsoft makes [OS-]breaking changes." The program displays a warning if a mod crashes and gives you the option to disable it. "Most mods only make temporary changes to the memory of the target process, so there's no permanent impact, and exiting Windhawk undoes all of them," Maltsev explains. "So far, no malicious mods and no malicious submission attempts have been spotted in the Windhawk marketplace."
Anti-cheat protections in multiplayer PC games might also flag Windhawk for tampering with PC game processes, potentially resulting in cheating-related bans. To counteract this problem, Windhawk avoids injecting its code into programs located in common PC game folders. I haven’t seen any reports of bans from multiplayer games for simply using this tool, but the risk is real. "Windhawk is intrusive, but it doesn't do anything non-standard or try to hide itself, so an anti-cheat that objects to it can detect it and refuse to run," says Maltsev, explaining that he hasn't seen evidence that this is a problem. He continues, "I'm not too concerned about anti-cheat bans, but I wish games handled this more transparently so it wouldn't be an issue in the first place." As with any software, a Windhawk mod could potentially include malicious code. The source code for each mod is public, but most people can't read C++, let alone identify vulnerabilities. The program wisely warns you to run mods only from developers you trust. "So far, no malicious mods and no malicious submission attempts have been spotted in the Windhawk marketplace," according to Maltsev. He continues, "Every submission, both new mods and updates to existing mods, goes through a thorough AI-based systematic review process." He also says he manually examines each one before it goes live to check for security and stability issues. 7 Essential Mods to Try First Windhawk lets you install mods in a few clicks, and Maltsev says it's designed to be as simple as installing a browser extension. Here’s just a taste of what’s available in Windhawk’s mod marketplace, in order of popularity: - Windows 11 Taskbar Styler: Customize your taskbar with themes, including everything from a transparent dock-style design to a classic Windows XP-style taskbar. - Windows 11 Start Menu Styler: Transform your Start menu with visual themes that can also change its layout. - Taskbar Clock Customization: Add information to your taskbar’s system clock, including CPU and RAM usage, news headlines, or the weather. - Taskbar Volume Control Per-App: Control an application’s volume by placing your mouse cursor over its taskbar icon and rotating your mouse’s scroll wheel. - Chrome/Edge Scroll Tabs With Mouse Wheel: Use your mouse wheel on a browser’s tab bar to move between tabs. - Windows Animations: Choose custom animations for closing and minimizing application windows. - Taskbar Music Lounge: View and control music playback with a widget on your taskbar. The list of mods is extensive. Microsoft continues to add more customization tools to Windows, but the company still isn’t scratching the surface of what’s possible with Windhawk. Running 20+ Mods Without Slowing Down Your PC As mentioned, Windhawk is a free and open-source application, so it doesn't come with a guarantee of stability. However, despite running Windhawk on and off for several years, I’ve never encountered real problems aside from some minor visual bugs. And when those pop up, I can easily turn off any offending mods. Maltsev says, "My priority is for it to be extremely reliable, with no noticeable stability or performance impact. Windhawk runs on my computer all the time with about 20 mods, and I'd say it lives up to that standard." Windhawk is remarkably user-friendly for an app that injects DLLs into processes on your system. After installation, it automatically starts at boot and runs in the background. The app uses about 800MB of disk space and under 20MB of RAM in my experience. Simply launch the program window to search for and install mods. After installing a mod, click the Details button and use the options in the Configure tab to customize any available options. Windhawk warns you about security before installing a mod. As mentioned, mods that show m417z as the author are from Windhawk’s creator and should be just as trustworthy as the main application. An Open Community Makes Windows Better for Everyone Windhawk or a similar system could also make it easier to customize Windows with AI. I’ve used AI tools to vibe code custom AutoHotkey scripts for my workflows, and the same would be possible for custom mods. "Nowadays, it's amazing to see how people with little to no programming experience can create impressive mods," says Maltsev, mentioning a recent mod submission that creates a highly customized taskbar layout with the Start button always positioned in the middle. He continues, "Microsoft is unlikely to ever provide this level of customization (maybe for a good reason), but Windhawk makes it possible." Maltsev points out that the author noted they were not a software developer, but that they developed the mod for personal use with Claude Code and were sharing it with the community for further development. "Windhawk's goal is to make customization accessible to everyone, and this is a great example of how it can be done." Why Even Microsoft Execs Are Paying Attention While Microsoft is focused on OpenClaw AI agents, I’m more excited about the ability to customize the software I use regularly. Windhawk is much closer to what I had in mind for tools to customize and personalize Windows. Meanwhile, Copilot still can't enable dark mode on my Windows 11 PC. Thankfully, as mentioned, Windhawk is on Microsoft's radar. In a Microsoft podcast from earlier this year, Marcus Ash, who leads design and research for Windows and devices, recalled speaking to a student who was enthusiastic about their Windhawk setup. "We see people just light up," Ash noted when discussing the passion he sees for desktop customization among enthusiasts. But whether and when Microsoft will give users significantly more control over Windows remains an open question, so Windhawk is an excellent alternative in the meantime. About Our Expert I've been writing about technology for more than 15 years and using it in earnest for over twice as long. As a member of PCMag's software team, I focus on Windows coverage, but also write about other key desktop operating systems and system apps. (I used Windows 3.1 upon its release and have followed every subsequent release closely). Prior to joining PCMag, I wrote for How-To Geek starting in 2011, and my articles amassed over a billion page views. I went on to run the publication as editor-in-chief for four and a half years. I have also contributed to Computerworld, Fast Company, PCWorld, Reader's Digest, The New York Times, and many other outlets about everything from AI to PC hardware to Windows. I founded and ran my own direct-to-reader Windows-focused newsletters, Windows Intelligence and The Windows ReadMe, working in partnership with Thurrott.com.

item.title: UK Lawmaker Proposes AI 'Kill Switch' to Stop Artificial Superintelligence
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 4.79
The UK is just behind China and the US when it comes to the level of funding it is pouring into AI development. Following Sen. Bernie Sanders introducing a bill to preemptively stop the creation of artificial superintelligence (ASI), lawmakers in the UK are now making similar proposals. Over 70 British lawmakers, in collaboration with lobbying group ControlAI, have written to Prime Minister Andy Burnham calling on him to back a ban on the creation of ASI, a theoretical AI system that would significantly outperform all humans on essentially all cognitive tasks. MP Alex Sobel introduced an Artificial Superintelligence Security Bill in collaboration with ControlAI in the British parliament last week. The bill suggests a basket of measures, including restricting the supply chain of materials such as semiconductors. Meanwhile, Lord Tim Clement-Jones separately proposed an amendment to the UK's upcoming Cyber Security and Resilience Bill, currently being voted on by lawmakers, which would create a “kill switch” that could be activated in an emergency to shut down a rogue AI. (This could mean shutting down the UK's data centers.) This comes after a former Anthropic employee went viral earlier this week for alleging the company is "gambling" with human lives by "racing straight to self-improving superintelligence." Lawmakers are calling on the UK to lead "an international agreement prohibiting the development of superintelligent AI, while preserving strategic AI ambitions," citing recent incidents of "rogue AI systems taking unsanctioned action on the internet." This may be a reference to July's Hugging Face attack, where 700 OpenAI agents breached the security of the open-source AI platform, making 17,000 separate actions, according to the forensic logs. "There is no question that AI is the crucial technology of the 21st century, vital to military and scientific applications," wrote the letter. "Superintelligent AI, however, is different. These systems would be so autonomous and capable that they would replace and outcompete humans across domains." Critics have already pointed out issues with the recent proposals. Unlike the US, Britain has no major frontier AI lab of its own, causing some UK think tanks to question the UK’s ability to regulate AI development. The UK government's Cabinet Office told the BBC that the UK "cannot simply turn AI off," in reference to demands for a kill switch, adding that "blocking access to models in the UK would not prevent them being developed or misused elsewhere." About Our Expert I’m a reporter covering weekend news. Before joining PCMag in 2024, I picked up bylines in BBC News, The Guardian, The Times of London, The Daily Beast, Vice, Slate, Fast Company, The Evening Standard, The i, TechRadar, and Decrypt Media. I’ve been a PC gamer since you had to install games from multiple CD-ROMs by hand. As a reporter, I’m passionate about the intersection of tech and human lives. I’ve covered everything from crypto scandals to the art world, as well as conspiracy theories, UK politics, and Russia and foreign affairs.

item.title: Not a Fan of Liquid Glass? You'll Love the New Slider in iOS 27
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 4.49
Apple unveiled a new Liquid Glass design in 2025 that added translucent UI elements for icons, toolbars, and menus, as if you were looking through glass. The problem? Not everyone loves the look of it. I’ll confess that I’ve been on the fence. I like some aspects of Liquid Glass, such as the way it renders icons and folders, but I’m not crazy about how it can obscure menu items and controls, making them more difficult to see. Some people have even complained that Liquid Glass makes them feel sick when their device is in dark mode. While you can't disable Liquid Glass, you can modify it. And now, with iOS 27, you can vary the look between ultra-clear and fully tinted using a convenient slider. You can play with Liquid Glass on an iPhone, Mac, and Apple Watch; here are a few ways to control it, no matter which system or device you’re running. 1. Customize the Look of Liquid Glass Starting in iOS 27 and iPadOS 27, you’re able to fine-tune the look of Liquid Glass. Head to Settings > Appearance > Liquid Glass and move the slider accordingly. Pulling it all the way to the left makes your icons, menus, and other elements more clear, while bringing it to the right gives everything a more tinted look. An image of a Search field and button shows a UI preview. Don’t like the extremes? Move the slider along the bar until it’s nestled where you want it. A similar slider bar has been added to macOS 27 Golden Gate. If you're on a Mac, you can go to System Settings > Appearance. Under the Liquid Glass section, move the slider until you find the look you like. If you don't yet have iOS 27, you'll still have a few options. In iOS 26.1 and iPadOS 26.1, Apple introduced Clear and Tinted styles for Liquid Glass. Head to Settings > Display & Brightness > Liquid Glass, and choose either Clear (more transparent) or Tinted (more opaque). The latter option is recommended if you want more contrast. In macOS 26.1, you'll need to open System Settings > Appearance, then choose between Clear and Tinted. 2. Reduce Transparency on Liquid Glass You can further tone down the effect on an iPhone or iPad by going to Settings > Accessibility > Display & Text Size and enabling Reduce Transparency. Now, when you look back at the folders and menus on your Home screen, you should see that the translucent look has been replaced by a more opaque one. To do the same thing on a Mac, go to System Settings > Accessibility > Display and turn on the switch next to Reduce Transparency. You'll notice that the icons, folders, menu bar, dock, and widgets are now less transparent than before. To adjust Liquid Glass on an Apple Watch, open the Watch app on your iPhone and go to My Watch > Accessibility> Reduce Transparency. You can also go to Settings > Accessibility directly on the watch and turn on Reduce Transparency. You should notice the difference, especially in the Notification panels and Control Center. 3. Enable Dark Mode I've also found that Liquid Glass looks better in dark mode instead of light mode because it hides much of the new design. On a phone or tablet, go to Settings > Display & Brightness and set the appearance to Dark. You can do the same on a Mac by going to System Settings > Appearance > Dark. Just be sure you're not one of the unlucky people who suffer motion sickness from the theme. 4. Reduce Bright Effects Starting in iOS 26.4, you’re able to tone down some of the lighting effects that come with the Liquid Glass redesign. Head to Settings > Accessibility > Display & Text Size, then turn on Reduce Bright Effects to make the change. It's a subtle difference, but one that might help make the theme more tolerable. Apple has also enhanced its Reduce Motion option to incorporate Liquid Glass effects. Just go to Settings > Accessibility > Motion and enable Reduce Motion. 5. Customize the Home Screen Thanks to the Home screen customization options introduced with iOS 18, you can also adjust the color and lighting of icons and widgets to improve readability. To do this, press down on any open area of the Home screen, tap the Edit button at the top, and then select Customize. Now, you have several options for adjusting the screen's appearance. Tap the small sun icon on the left side of the bottom pane to switch the screen and widgets between light and dark modes. Tap the square icon on the right of the page to increase the size of the icons and folders. The only drawback with the larger size is that the names disappear. Looking at the bottom of the pane, tap the Dark icon to paint the Home screen with a darker tone. You can also switch the option from Always to Auto, in which case the icons and widgets appear dark at night and light during the day. Tap the Clear icon to give Home screen icons and widgets a clear look similar to Liquid Glass, but without color. Here, you can also switch from Light to Dark to give the screen a darker look, or to Auto to make it dark at night and light during the day. Tap the Tinted icon to open multiple sliders to tweak the screen's appearance. By moving the first slider left or right, you can change the tint color. By moving the second slider, you can modify the lightness of the tint. Under the sliders, you can pick specific colors (including those from your wallpaper). About Our Expert I've been working for PCMag since early 2016 writing tutorials, how-to pieces, and other articles on consumer technology. Beyond PCMag, I've written news stories and tutorials for a variety of other websites and publications, including CNET, ZDNet, TechRepublic, Macworld, PC World, Time, US News & World Report, and AARP Magazine. I spent seven years writing breaking news for CNET as one of the site’s East Coast reporters. I've also written two books for Wiley & Sons—Windows 8: Five Minutes at a Time and Teach Yourself Visually LinkedIn. I've used Windows, Office, and other Microsoft products for years so I'm well versed in that world. I also know the Mac quite well.
