Some other new features I enjoy seeing include: - Better-organized information on the artist pages in Music. - Full-resolution images in shared albums from Photos. - Handwritten notes and sketches in the Notes app. - Improved touch support for iPhone and iPad apps via the Sidecar feature, including markup and one-finger scrolling; this is another hint in support of a touch-screen Mac. - Keynote-like slideshow creation in Photos. - More compact, informative menu bar icons (with the battery percentage inside the icon, as in iOS). - New Tapback options in Messages. - Photo albums are shareable with Android and Windows users who don’t have iCloud accounts. - Refined support for dark mode, notably in Freeform, where black text on a white background becomes white-on-black in dark mode. - Resizable apps via iPhone Mirroring, so you can view them larger than they look in the small screen on your phone; you must update these apps for iOS 27. - Sharper flyover imagery in Maps. - The hard drive icon in Finder used to be a spinning-platter disk, but now it's more accurately an SSD. - Video podcasts in the macOS Podcasts app. When Apple announced Golden Gate, it promised snappier performance throughout the OS, and the release version delivers on that promise. Access to networked Windows machines and other Macs, file transfers, and messaging all work much faster than in earlier versions. In the Golden Gate beta versions, some apps seemed to open more slowly than they did in Tahoe, but in the final release, the whole system feels more responsive than before. Final Thoughts Apple macOS Golden Gate - 5.0 - Exemplary: Near perfection, ground-breaking - 4.5 - Outstanding: Best in class, acts as a benchmark for measuring competitors - 4.0 - Excellent: A performance, feature, or value leader in its class, with few shortfalls - 3.5 - Good: Does what the product should do, and does so better than many competitors - 3.0 - Average: Does what the product should do, and sits in the middle of the pack - 2.5 - Fair: We have some reservations, buy with caution - 2.0 - Subpar: We do not recommend, buy with extreme caution - 1.5 - Poor: Do not buy this product - 1.0 - Dismal: Don't even think about buying this product Read Our Editorial Mission Statement and Testing Methodologies. macOS Golden Gate succeeds where past releases stumbled, delivering an operating system that feels both modern and genuinely useful. Apple Intelligence is no longer just a headline—it is a deeply integrated, highly functional set of tools that leaves Microsoft's Copilot feeling disjointed by comparison. Moreover, Golden Gate lets you tone down many of the most distracting elements of the Liquid Glass experience. Factor in top-tier child safety features and noticeable performance gains, and this release becomes an essential upgrade that's well worthy of our Editors' Choice award. About Our Expert I've been writing about software and hardware for PCMag for more than 40 years, focusing on operating systems, office suites, and communication and utility apps. I've specialized in everything related to word and document processing, including format conversion, OCR, and PDF apps. In my spare time, I build apps for Macs and Windows PCs that make it easy to run legacy operating systems (such as old versions of macOS and Windows) and work with legacy documents. I've also written about technology for non-technical publications, such as The New York Review of Books. Before joining PCMag, I reviewed music and sound equipment for audio magazines. In my other career, I'm the Lionel Trilling Professor in the Humanities at Columbia University and write books about modern literature.

item.title: 10 New iOS 27 Features You Should Try Right Now
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 2.67
The impressive but eye-watering $1,999 iPhone Duo is dominating the headlines, but the best Apple-related news of the week is a massive software upgrade that won’t cost you a dime. Out now, iOS 27 officially brings next-generation customization and desktop-grade workflows to millions of users worldwide. The update supports the iPhone 11 and newer (including the second-generation iPhone SE). Whether you are rocking an older device or are preordering the brand-new iPhone 18 Pro ahead of its Sept. 18 release date, you can start experimenting with these 10 game-changing features on day one. Note: Although everyone gets access to the core platform features, you will need an iPhone 15 Pro or newer to unlock the first four Siri AI upgrades listed below. 1. Agentic Siri Siri has now gone full agentic AI in iOS 27. You can now command the assistant to execute autonomous, multi-step tasks across different applications, like locating a fresh PDF download, renaming it, and immediately drafting it into an email. This removes the tedious process of manually opening, closing, and copying/pasting data across multiple apps. iOS 27 finally transforms Siri from a simple voice-trigger tool into a true, autonomous productivity assistant. 2. Siri App Adds a Dedicated Workspace The Siri screen overlay remains, but iOS 27 also introduces a dedicated, persistent Siri chat application. This new space preserves a history of your research conversations and syncs them across your iPhone, iPad, and Mac via iCloud. It is incredibly useful for deep-dive research sessions where you need to track complex thought threads over several days. 3. Visual Intelligence Adds On-Screen Context Apple Intelligence allows you to activate Siri inside any active image, web page, or text thread to instantly query whatever is currently displayed on your screen. Siri can now parse context dynamically, allowing you to ask "Where was this photo taken?" or "Summarize this article link" without any manual typing. This brings a powerful, seamless visual search tool straight into the core architecture of iOS. 4. Reframe Your Photos With AI Apple's new Spatial Reframing feature is a generative AI system that can fix tightly cropped or poorly framed shots. Built directly into the native Photos app, the software analyzes your image and contextually "outpaints" the background borders to intelligently expand the canvas. This is a lifesaver for salvaging great family photos or landscapes where you accidentally cropped out a key detail. 5. Freeform Icon Placement Break completely free from the rigid, top-to-bottom layout grid that has governed the iPhone interface for nearly two decades. You can now anchor application icons and widgets anywhere along the sides or bottom of the screen, leaving intentional blank spaces wherever you like. It finally gives you total aesthetic control to properly frame your favorite lock screen wallpapers and custom themes. 6. Extra-Large Home Screen Widgets You can now dedicate massive, high-density screen blocks to unified multi-app widgets on your display grid. These expanded containers let you blend interactive calendar schedules, live weather tracking, and active media playback into a single, beautifully organized module. It drastically reduces the need to constantly flip between separate app pages just to check your basic daily stats. 7. Dynamic Lock Screen Shortcuts Swap out the permanent, legacy Flashlight and Camera buttons at the bottom of your lock screen for entirely custom alternatives. You can map these quick-access triggers to activate specific system settings, open third-party apps, or launch custom workflows. This makes your phone much faster to navigate, the literal second you pick it up. 8. In-App Drawing Canvas Tap the plus sign directly inside an active Messages thread to open a revamped, ultra-low-latency layout board. This tool lets you sketch custom graphics, diagram an idea, or handwrite a quick note mid-conversation without leaving the chat interface. It makes visual communication feel completely native and fluid, especially for collaborative brainstorming sessions. 9. Increased Liquid Glass Customization Although Apple introduced the Liquid Glass design language last year, iOS 27 adds a dedicated customization slider to fix its legibility issues. This new toggle lets you manually dial in your preferred level of background translucency. You can shift seamlessly from an ultra-clear crystal design to a solid, high-contrast tinted layout, giving you absolute, pixel-level control to ensure your text and menus remain sharp over any custom wallpaper. 10. Safari live page tracking Safari now lets you set automated "Notify Me" tracking flags to monitor visual or text changes on selected webpages. Safari will silently monitor the targeted page in the background and ping you the exact moment the content updates, completely eliminating the need to manually refresh the tab. This is exceptionally useful for tracking moving shipping statuses, fluctuating ticket prices, or flash online sales. About Our Expert In 2014, I began my career at PCMag as a freelancer. That blossomed into a full-time position in 2021, and I now review email marketing apps, mobile operating systems, web hosting services, streaming music platforms, and video games as a senior writer. I'm a graduate of Hunter College, a hard-core gamer, and an Apple enthusiast.

item.title: September's Desktop Deals Bring Powerful PCs at Deep Discounts From Dell, HP, Lenovo, and More
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 2.66
There are lots of different kinds of computers out there, from palm-sized productivity machines to desktop towers. While we do a lot of stuff on a laptop, there's no substitute for a full-bore PC with all of the trimmings, and major manufacturers build and release numerous different models every year. If you're shopping for one, it's a tough time for prices, but deals are out there if you know where to look—and we do. At PCMag, we review desktops more thoroughly than anywhere else, and with over 40 years in the business, our system can't be topped. We evaluate desktops using a transparent system of metrics, factoring in price, features, design, and performance for work and play. We compare capabilities with ever-evolving benchmark tests, as well as run real-world applications and games, to determine the real value of each system and how the deals compare. Best Home and Office Desktop Deals These desktop towers prioritize reliability and value over high-octane gaming performance. Major brands like Dell, HP, and Lenovo specialize in these PCs, which usually cost around $1,000 for worthwhile models. If you have nostalgia for the glory days of wood-paneled computer rooms and the AOL dial-up noise, HP's OmniDesk towers combine vintage aesthetics with current-gen performance in an affordable package. We have a CES preview of this line, where we noted that the wood-grain front panel conceals surprisingly effective cooling fans and tons of ports. The footprint is also relatively small, but a ton of tech is packed inside, so it's not lightweight enough to be considered portable. Inside the case, you get a capable Intel Core Ultra 7 processor that easily tackles everyday productivity and entertainment. RAM and storage are light, but the price is right, as Best Buy has a nice discount on this configuration right now. For a slightly slimmer profile with solid performance, Lenovo's IdeaCentre tower PCs have always been a good option. We don't have a full review of this model, but we were impressed by its 2023 iteration, with top features including a compact chassis, good connectivity, and an install refreshingly free of bloatware. This loadout ships with an Intel Core Ultra 7 265 processor, coupled with 16GB of RAM for smooth operation on most major productivity apps. Port selection is another strong point, with seven USB ports and an HDMI 2.1 output for your monitor of choice. While the integrated Intel UHD graphics aren't cutting-edge, it even works for casual gaming. Best All-In-One Desktop Deals All-in-one desktops pack all of the computing components inside the monitor housing for easier setup and less cable management, and what they lose in customization, they make up for in convenience. We have discounts on a few solid Windows all-in-ones for work and play. We gave an Editors' Choice award to the latest iteration of Dell's all-in-one desktop in our review, commenting that it hit all the marks we expect for a general-purpose home desktop with ease, starting with a cutting-edge Intel Core Ultra Series 3 processor and following it up with plenty of RAM and storage for everyday productivity. The 27-inch FHD screen is touch-enabled, bright, and crisp, with surprisingly assertive stereo speakers. Connectivity is also terrific, with Wi-Fi 7 and Bluetooth 6 along with plenty of ports, although we wish more of them were on the front edge of the screen. The included wireless mouse and keyboard are high quality, and it comes with Windows 11 Pro installed. For a Windows alternative, Lenovo's IdeaCentre has a bigger screen and more onboard storage than the iMac above. We had a mixed but ultimately positive time reviewing this all-in-one. Our reviewer noted that it was well-constructed with lots of ports on multiple sides, and the included wireless keyboard and mouse were comfortable. The 10-core Intel Core i7-13620H processor is suited for everyday productivity, as well as streaming video and surfing the web. Although the FHD screen isn't the highest resolution, it's pleasurable to use for long stretches thanks to an antiglare coating and hardware-based blue light reduction. Snagging this one for under $900 is a fantastic bargain. Best Mini PC Deals Squeezed for space? A mini PC might be the answer. They pack tons of power into cases around the size of a stack of CDs, and are surprisingly capable. We have a Dell compact that's designed for businesses, as well as a creative powerhouse from Kamrui. More mainstream companies also make compact PCs, and this Dell OptiPlex is a solid choice for most productivity-oriented applications. It tackles spreadsheets and presentations with ease, and a plethora of ports let you connect up to four individual monitors in up to 4K resolution (not all at once, of course). It comes with Windows 11 Pro installed and virtually no manufacturer bloatware, so you can have it up and running in minutes. The 14th-generation Intel i3 processor isn't the most impressive chip on the market, but it's capable enough for most everyday office use. Chinese company Kamrui produces a wide range of mini desktop loadouts, and they're impressive from a value proposition, with high-quality components and sturdy design. Amazon has a 19% price cut on the Hyper H2 Mini, which is targeted toward content creators with 32GB of RAM and a full 1TB SSD, along with multi-monitor 4K support thanks to HDMI, USB-C, and DisplayPort outputs. The cooling system is up to the task as well, with centrifugal fans, twin copper heat pipes, and two fin-stack cooling modules. See where it clocks in on our rundown of the best Windows mini PCs. Finally, here's a nicely-priced MSI mini that really gets the job done. You can read our extensive review of the Cubi NUC to see how it performed in our benchmarking tests, but the short version is that it's got a speedy 14-core processor with integrated neural processing unit for Copilot AI, and solid design to work in tight spaces with peak efficiency. Port selection is diverse, with plenty of USB connections on the front and Thunderbolt, HDMI, and a pair of 2.5G Ethernet ports on the back. It even has a corded power button so you can mount it on a wall or in a hard-to-reach spot and still turn it on and off easily. For the money, this is one of the better mini PCs on the market. Best Home and Office Desktop Deals - HP OmniDesk Intel Ultra 7 2TB SSD 16GB RAM Desktop — $1,374.99 With Code "JULY4PC25" - HP OmniDesk Ryzen 7 RTX 3050 2TB SSD 16GB RAM Desktop — $649.99 ($1,969.99) Save $1,320.00 - Dell Tower Plus Intel Ultra 7 RTX 5060 1TB SSD 16G... — $1,579.99 ($2,129.99) Save $550.00 - Dell Tower Intel Ultra 7 1TB SSD 16GB RAM Desktop — $1,249.99 ($1,449.99) Save $200.00 - HP All-in-One 27 Ryzen AI 7 512GB SSD 16GB RAM Desktop — $799.99 ($1,349.99) Save $550.00 - Dell 24 All-in-One Intel i5 512GB SSD 16GB RAM Desktop — $1,049.99 ($1,249.99) Save $200.00 - Dell 27 All-in-One Intel 5 512GB SSD 16GB RAM Desktop — $949.99 ($1,149.99) Save $200.00 Best Gaming Desktop Deals Gaming desktops need high-capability components to be worthwhile, including dedicated GPUs, lots of onboard RAM, and powerful fans to keep it all cool. We've got a few good gaming tower offers right now, notably a pair of battlestations from iBuyPower and HP. HP might not be the first name you think of when it comes to gaming hardware, but its Omen line consistently tests well in the midrange space, with cost-effective builds perfect for 1440p play. We gave an Editors' Choice award to the Omen 35L desktop in our review, noting that it had an ultra-efficient cooling system that kept it running silently even under heavy load, and the easy-access case and industry-standard part selection made it a great pick for upgrading and customizing. The Blackwell-series GeForce 5060 is tuned for medium-resolution performance at fast frame rates, and a full 1TB SSD is beefy enough for your save files. It looks cool, too, with a ceramic white metal case and tempered glass side panels. For an AMD-powered gaming machine that pushes the envelope at a reasonable price, this prebuilt from iBuyPower is worth a look, especially with a $300 price drop from Walmart. We gave the RX 9070XT graphics card an Editors' Choice award in our review, noting that it combined vastly improved ray-tracing performance with great cooling and a reasonable price, competing very capably with Nvidia's current-generation cards. The rest of the silicon loadout is solid for the price, including a speedy Ryzen 9 processor and 32GB of DDR5 RAM for seamless multitasking and content creation. The liquid CPU cooling system and RGB fans keep the whole enterprise stable under pressure. Walmart is really bringing the smoke this week with gaming desktop deals, and snagging a potent performer like MSI's Codex Z2 with the new RTX 5070 Ti at a $500 price drop is worth the final spot on our list. Running off of the Ryzen 7 8700F processor, it's absolutely fast enough to handle all of today's latest games, and the GPU and RAM combination will give you fast framerates at 1440p and even stretch into 4K for aspirational resolution hounds looking to overclock a bit. The chassis is a cool piece of tech as well, with attractive RGB lighting and well-designed airflow, although the fans can run a bit loud. Best Gaming Desktop Deals - HP Omen 35L Intel Ultra 9 RTX 5080 2TB SSD 64GB RAM Desktop — $4,699.99 ($6,499.99) Save $1,800.00 - HP Omen 45L Intel Ultra 7 RTX 5070 1TB SSD Desktop — $2,699.99 ($3,599.99) Save $900.00 - Alienware Aurora Intel Ultra 7 RTX 5060 Ti 1TB SSD... — $2,149.99 ($2,459.99) Save $310.00 - Alienware Area-51 Intel Ultra 7 RTX 5080 1TB SSD 3... — $3,899.99 ($4,299.99) Save $400.00 - Alienware Area-51 Intel Ultra 9 RTX 5090 2TB SSD 3... — $5,999.99 ($6,199.99) Save $200.00 - HP Omen 16L Ryzen 7 RTX 5060 1TB SSD 16GB RAM Desktop — $1,012.49 With Code "BACK2SCHOOL25" How Much Should I Pay for a Desktop Computer? Your money goes further with desktop PCs and their components than with laptops. You can find complete mini PCs for less than $400 and perfectly serviceable small towers for $500 to $600. Gaming desktops with dedicated graphics cards start at around $700. You can also find all-in-one (AIO) desktops, with the display and all of the computing components built into a single device, starting at around $600. The sky's the limit once you get into high-end gaming PCs and business-workstation power desktops, but the prices above are in the right range for most mainstream buyers. How Much Does a Good Budget PC Cost? Expect to pay at least $500 for a basic, competent small tower for day-in/day-out productivity and web work. You'll find plenty of models for less than $500, especially in the mini PC class, but you should insist on at least 8GB of system memory for any PC, with 16GB required at minimum for AI tasks. For anything beyond basic productivity work, look for an Intel Core i5 (or Ultra 5) or AMD Ryzen 5 processor at least. Which Brands Offer the Best Desktop Discounts? Some brands post deals and discounts on their products more often than others, particularly Acer. Dell, HP, and Lenovo also do this, but you should always double-check exactly what you're getting and whether you can buy it for less at other retailers. Brands like Lenovo adjust their prices frequently, making assessing the raw value of deals you see there difficult. Notably, Apple has improved its image as a value-focused brand, permanently dropping prices on some of its laptops and often hosting limited deals on shopping holidays. What Is the Best Desktop Under $800? Our experts have named the Acer Aspire TC-1775-UR11 their top budget pick for, "packing a 14th Gen Core i7 processor, Wi-Fi 6E, USB-C, and a compact design that tucks under your desk." We've seen this model go for as low as $557 on Amazon. For more budget options, check out our top picks for the best cheap desktop PCs. What Is the Best Gaming Desktop Under $1,000? Finding a really good model under a grand is a big ask. Your best bet is going to be the Asus TUF Gaming T500, which pairs a mobile processor with a discrete graphics card inside a small-footprint desktop. Our experts said, "This cute, efficient rig excels for 1080p gaming, but its CPU, motherboard, power supply, and cooling scheme limit its future upgradability." Right now it's going for around $959.99 at Best Buy. About Our Experts K. Thor Jensen is a writer and cartoonist living in the Pacific Northwest. He has contributed to dozens of prestigious outlets, including PCMag, Tested, Clickhole, and Newsweek. His second graphic novel, Cloud Stories, was released in 2017. After starting my career at PCMag as an intern more than a decade ago, I’m back as one of its editors, focused on managing laptops, desktops, and components coverage. With 15 years of experience, I have been on staff and published in technology review publications, including PCMag (of course!), Laptop Magazine, Tom’s Guide, TechRadar, and IGN. Along the way, I’ve tested and reviewed hundreds of laptops and helped develop testing protocols. I have expertise in testing all forms of laptops and desktops using the latest tools. I’m also well-versed in video game hardware and software coverage. When she isn't perusing online stores for deals, Jade enjoys playing video games (mostly JRPGs and roguelikes), sorting board game components neatly into containers, and building Gundam models. Her love of electronics has persisted through her youth and has resulted in a collection of gaming peripherals including keyboards and controllers, scale figures, and art work. Jade lives in blissful harmony with her wife, cat, and two chinchillas—as well as a host of houseplants.

item.title: I’ve Tested Hundreds of Cameras: Here Are My 10 Best Pro Photography Tips
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 2.51
Are you ready to step up your photography to the next level? Regardless of whether you're just starting out with a camera or if you've been taking snapshots for years, there's always room to learn and grow as a creator. I've reviewed cameras at PCMag for 15 years and have taken countless photos in that time. That's let me try out different techniques, learn from my mistakes, and really get to know how to squeeze the best results out of the newest gear—read on for some of the best tips and tricks that I've learned along the way. 1. Learn to Process Raw Images Digital cameras are set up to record images in an 8-bit JPG format out of the box. These pictures are "developed" from the sensor by your camera's image processor and leave little headroom to adjust exposure or color balance. They also suffer from lossy noise reduction and compression. Almost all interchangeable lens cameras and many advanced compacts support a Raw format, either with 12-bit or 14-bit color sampling. The extra data lets you open shadows to save poorly exposed backlit shots, or apply an artistic color grade to a photo without losing any picture quality. Raw photos aren't meant to be shared right out of the camera, however, so it's up to you to learn how to process them. You'll need software to do so, but you can start out with the software that came with your PC (Microsoft Photos) or Mac (Apple Photos) to handle the basics. If you like the creative freedom you get with these apps, consider upgrading to a professional workflow application with more features like Adobe Lightroom, Capture One, or Skylum Luminar. The Best Raw Processors We've Tested One more thing: If you're nervous about using Raw format, don't fret. Your camera almost certainly has a Raw+JPG setting that will save each picture in both file types. This takes up more space on your memory card, but is a useful safety net. 2. Move Your Flash Off Camera Most serious cameras omit an in-body flash, so chances are you'll end up shopping for an add-on flash soon. On-camera flash is good for filling in shadows when taking portraits outdoors on a sunny day, and more powerful flashguns like the Godox V1 can brighten dimly lit interiors. With flash, the direction of the light is as important as its power. At minimum, you should get a flash that lets you point its light up, back, or to the side to bounce off of a wall. This will give you softer, more diffused light and help avoid the harsh look of direct flash. But if you want to get fancy, pick up a flash that works with a wireless transmitter. I use Godox R2 TTL transmitters with my cameras and have found them reliable, versatile, and more affordable than high-end options from industry leader Profoto. With an R2 transmitter on my camera, I can simultaneously trigger multiple off-camera strobes with manual or automatic Through the Lens (TTL) power to light a scene. The Best Off-Camera Lights We've Tested I prefer Godox over a first-party solution simply because I can use one set of lights for several brands of cameras. If you end up switching camera brands later on it's just a matter of switching transmitters, not replacing your entire lighting kit. One note, Godox R2 TTL flashes are also sold under other brand names, and are thankfully cross-compatible. I've reviewed several some Godox lights sold under the Flashpoint brand and they work together seamlessly. 3. Try Some Weird Lenses Chances are you've already moved away from your 18-55mm kit lens, either opting for a better quality zoom or a fast prime lens. But if you're stuck in a creative rut, or just want to experiment with some new types of photography, a specialized lens can really come in handy. You can opt for a super-sharp macro lens that can focus close and fill your frame with small objects. You can also go in the opposite direction and experiment with Lensbaby, a creative lens system that allows you to adjust the plane of focus. They let you create photos that have a sharp point of focus that gives way to soft, swirly dreaminess. My Favorite Artsy Lenses If you have a mirrorless camera your choices are even more vast. Numerous lens adapters are available that allow you to mount virtually any lens to these cameras for use in manual focus mode. I love using antique lenses with cameras simply because of their character and value. Check out How to Use Vintage Lenses on Mirrorless Cameras for more ideas. If you want to try a lens before you buy, you can rent online from Lensrentals. 4. Clean Your Image Sensor Sensor dust. If you use a mirrorless camera, you're likely familiar, as it's far easier to get a few specks of detritus on your image sensor versus an SLR, simply because there is no mirror to protect it, so the sensor is exposed when you swap lenses. Some good practices can help reduce the chance of dust getting onto the sensor. First, make sure the camera is turned off when you change lenses as dust is more prone to stick on a powered, electrified sensor. Some newer, pro-level mirrorless cameras include a shield that protects the sensor when powered down, but most do not, so you should also try to avoid changing lenses outdoors in rough weather. But even if you're the most careful, meticulous photographer in the world, you will end up with dust on your image sensor at some point. You might not notice if you use your lenses at wide apertures, but the spots are apparent at smaller f-stops. Many mirrorless cameras include automatic dust reduction systems that vibrate the sensor to shake smaller particles away, but they're not foolproof. If you have a dust spot that won't go away, blowing it off with an air puffer typically works. For more persistent spots, consider a cleaning kit from Visible Dust and Lenspen or, if you aren't comfortable doing it yourself, a professional cleaning is in order. 5. Throw Away the Bundled Neck Strap If you're going to carry your camera around all day, you should do it in comfort. Most mirrorless cameras come with a basic nylon strap without any padding. Even worse, the strap is typically covered with brand logos, so you turn into a walking advertisement, and it attaches using a confounding set of loops and grommets. I've been taking pictures for decades, and I still haven't figured out how to properly secure them. Third-party straps come in all shapes and sizes, so you've got freedom to choose between different styles. Some photographers swear by wrist straps; others may prefer a cross-body sling to support telephoto lenses. My favorite is the Peak Design Slide Lite, which is comfortable to wear cross-body and attaches to your camera with a simple loop and anchor. Sling straps, like those from BlackRapid, are often used by event photographers who carry multiple bodies with heavy lenses attached. They're a good match if you have a telephoto lens with its own tripod collar, too. I still reach for one when using a big zoom lens. You can also go the classic route with a wide, fabric strap—readily available via Etsy shops, or go full hipster with an artisanal, handcrafted leather strap like those made in Brooklyn by Tap & Dye. 6. Get a Tripod, Monopod, or Gimbal There are some scenes where holding the camera in your hand doesn't make the most sense. If you are interested in taking pictures of landscapes, cityscapes, or architecture, a tripod is a handy tool for careful, deliberate composition. A tripod isn't your only option for camera support. Sports and wildlife photogs who use big lenses and need to move around frequently are better off with a single leg, a monopod, to give arm muscles a rest without sacrificing freedom of movement. And if you're more interested in video, consider getting a powered gimbal for smooth handheld footage. Tripods I Recommend Lightweight options like the Peak Design Travel Tripod sacrifice some stability and features in favor of size, but are a great option if you spend more time at airports than at home. Photographers who use heavy telephoto lenses or medium-format gear will want something beefier. If you haven't shopped for a tripod before, it's worth reading my buying guide to help you decide how much to spend and what type to target for your gear and photo interests. 7. Experiment With New Techniques If you find yourself in a creative rut, or simply bored with the images you're taking, take it as a sign to move outside your comfort zone. You can make so many types of images with your camera, so try something new if you're looking for a new challenge. My first advice is to try different shutter speeds. You can use long exposures (1/4-second or longer) to smooth out flowing water or to add motion blur to moving subjects. If you want to bend time even further, check if your camera has a time-lapse capture mode. You can also try different angles or scenes. If you usually take landscapes outdoors, consider adding a telephoto for wildlife opportunities. If you often use a macro lens to hone on on the little details, switch over to a wide angle. You should expect some growing pains when trying something new, and perhaps a memory card of images that aren't up to your usual standards, but missed photos are a part of improving your craft. 8. Fly a Drone You don't have to just take images when standing on level ground. Adding a drone to your toolkit makes it possible to grab shots from perspectives you'd never be able to get otherwise. Most drones can capture 4K video and Raw format images, and current models are safe to fly (assuming you follow the rules). Check out our top picks in the category. The Best Drones for Photographers 9. Print Your Work It's easy to share your photos online or view them on a digital picture frame, but if you take a photo you truly love, it deserves to be printed. You can print at home on an inkjet, but for the best results, you'll want to go with a dedicated printing service. Many of our favorite photo printing services offer fun ways to display your work, including prints on canvas, metallic paper, and true black and white photo paper for a classic look. You can also opt for a custom photo book, an update on the classic family album with your photos printed directly onto the pages. The Best Photo Printing Services We've Tried 10. Upgrade Your Camera for the Right Reasons If you're enthusiastic about your photos, you might be itching to buy a new camera. There are plenty of reasons to upgrade, but you don't always have to have the latest camera to take good photos. That said, most newer mirrorless cameras include far better autofocus systems and video features versus older DSLRs, so there are good reasons to get a new camera. Before you spend money, ask yourself, "What frustrates me about my current camera?" and make sure a replacement addresses your gripes head-on. The Best Cameras We've Tested For more inspiration and guidance, check out our explainers on photographing lightning and fireworks. If you're looking for a new camera or lens, be sure to peruse our digital cameras product guide for the latest reviews, and our roundup of the best digital cameras for the top products we've tested. About Our Expert Images, and the devices that capture them, are my focus. I've covered cameras at PCMag for the past 15 years, which has given me a front row seat for the changeover from DSLRs to mirrorless cameras, the smartphone camera revolution, and the emergence of drones for aerial imaging. I have extensive experience with every major mirrorless and SLR system, and am also comfortable using point-and-shoot and action cameras. As a Part 107 Certified drone pilot, I’m licensed to fly unmanned aircraft systems (UAS) for commercial and editorial purposes, and am knowledgeable about federal rules and regulations regarding drones.

item.title: HP OmniBook Ultra 14 (2026) Review: A Top-Tier Ultraportable With Good Looks, Better Power
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 2.23
We're in a golden age for luxe ultraportables, which makes it seriously challenging to stand out in this increasingly crowded segment. HP's OmniBook Ultra 14 does just that. From its sleek aluminum chassis and vibrant OLED display to its excellent webcam, impressive speakers, and all-day battery life, nearly every aspect of this 14-incher feels carefully considered. Though the OmniBook Ultra 14 is undeniably pricey, starting at $1,799.99 and reaching $4,049.99 as tested, it delivers exactly the kind of experience that power users expect in this elite tier. Alongside rivals like Apple's 14-inch MacBook Pro and Dell's XPS 14, the OmniBook Ultra 14 earns its place among the best premium ultraportables available today, earning an Editors' Choice award alongside the best of its kind. HP’s OmniBook Ultra 14 brings Intel’s latest "Panther Lake" silicon to the premium ultraportable market. Every configuration is built around a 16-core Core Ultra Series 3 processor, starting with the Core Ultra 7 356H and scaling to the flagship Core Ultra X9 388H featured in our test unit. Systems equipped with the Core Ultra X7 and X9 house Intel's highly capable Arc B390 integrated graphics. The memory and storage options are also impressive. You can configure the system with up to 64GB of LPDDR5X memory running at 9,600 megatransfers per second and a 2TB PCI Express 5.0 SSD, though the highest RAM allotment is reserved for configurations with the Core Ultra X9 chip. Those specs make the OmniBook Ultra 14 a good fit for demanding multitasking and content-creation workloads. Naturally, the premium components come at a cost, and the ongoing component shortages don't help much. With prices ranging from $1,799.99 to more than $4,000 for my test machine, the OmniBook Ultra 14 competes directly with flagship machines like Apple’s 14-inch MacBook Pro and Dell’s XPS 14. Offered in Eclipse Gray or the Silk Sand colorway of our review unit (the Sand shade is an extra $20), the OmniBook Ultra 14 looks every bit the flagship. Its all-aluminum chassis feels exceptionally rigid, with virtually no flex in the lid or keyboard deck. The laptop even passed MIL-STD durability testing. Then you get subtle touches—machined edges, a responsive haptic touchpad, and understated reflective logos—that elevate the overall experience. At just 0.42 inches thick and 2.81 pounds, the OmniBook is exceptionally sleek and remarkably easy to carry, undercutting Dell's XPS 14 and Apple's 14-inch MacBook Pro in both measurements. The only major drawback is connectivity: HP has three Thunderbolt 4 ports and a headphone jack, but omits USB-A altogether, which can be frustrating if you're juggling older peripherals. Even so, the system boasts a bunch of modern conveniences that help make up for the missing ports: Wi-Fi 7, a super-sharp 5MP webcam with privacy shutter, and a compact GaN wall charger. HP covers the system with a one-year warranty, with multiyear extensions and accidental damage coverage available. In our testing, the OmniBook Ultra 14 offered up a premium experience, with a lot of strong points that worked together brilliantly. From its design to its input devices and everything in between, the system feels thoughtfully executed. The 3K (2,880-by-1,800-pixel) display makes for one of the system’s leading features—this is the type of screen that you’ll think about long after you’ve seen it. Sharp detail, rich color, and punchy contrast bring any content to life, with touch input and a smooth 120Hz refresh rate augmenting everyday practicality. It pairs well with the quad-speaker system, which sounds closer to a small Bluetooth speaker than a typical laptop. HP's webcam also impresses, offering a crisp, well-exposed picture that outclasses the usual laptop fare. The laptop's input devices are just as impressive. The lattice-free keyboard design looks clean, and the sloped key edges help preserve a sense of spacing. You also get nice key travel and a quiet, cushioned feel. I also appreciated the status LEDs integrated into the mute, microphone, function lock, and power keys, which make it easy to confirm key system states at a glance. The white key backlighting could stand out a bit more under ordinary lighting conditions, but it'll do in the dark. The system gets another usability boost from effective thermal management. The laptop runs quietly day to day and stays comfortable to the touch under heavier workloads. Though the lack of USB-C ports might force you to pack some adapters, the OmniBook Ultra 14 remains a polished, dependable premium ultraportable that nails the core experience. I tested HP’s OmniBook Ultra 14 in a flagship configuration featuring Intel’s Core Ultra X9 388H (16 cores, 5.1GHz turbo), Intel Arc B390 integrated graphics, 64GB of LPDDR5X-9600 memory, and a 2TB PCI Express 5.0 solid-state drive. The system runs Windows 11 Pro and represents the most powerful version of the OmniBook Ultra 14 currently available. To see how well that hardware translates into real-world performance, we compared the OmniBook to similarly upscale systems, including Apple's 14-inch MacBook Pro ($2,349), the Asus ExpertBook Ultra ($3,599.99 as tested), the Dell XPS 14 ($2,199.99), and the Framework Laptop 13 Pro ($2,932). All of those models target power users seeking a premium experience. While the OmniBook’s Core Ultra X9 388H sits at the top of Intel’s lineup, it delivers only a marginal edge over the Core Ultra X7 358H silicon its competitors use: a higher boost clock of 5.1GHz versus 4.8GHz. The more illuminating comparison will be against Apple's 10-core M5 chip. Our primary overall benchmark, UL's PCMark 10, puts a system through its paces in productivity apps ranging from web browsing to word processing and spreadsheet work. Its Full System Drive subtest measures a PC's storage throughput. Three more tests we rely on are CPU-centric or processor-intensive: Maxon's Cinebench 2024 uses that company's Cinema 4D engine to render a complex scene; Primate Labs' Geekbench 6.3 Pro simulates popular apps ranging from PDF rendering and speech recognition to machine learning; and we see how long it takes the video transcoder HandBrake 1.8 to convert a 12-minute clip from 4K to 1080p resolution. Finally, workstation maker Puget Systems' PugetBench for Creators rates a PC's image-editing prowess through a variety of automated operations in the seminal photo editor Adobe Photoshop 25. The OmniBook Ultra 14 delivered consistently strong productivity results. Its 9,736-point showing in PCMark 10 ranks among the best we've seen from any laptop, trailing only the ExpertBook Ultra by a narrow margin. The OmniBook also impressed us with its storage performance, as HP’s PCIe 5.0 SSD delivered a top-tier score. The OmniBook came down to Earth in our CPU-focused tests, proving itself competitive rather than class-leading. It traded blows with the ExpertBook Ultra, XPS 14, and Framework Laptop 13 Pro, notably excelling in Handbrake while falling slightly behind in Cinebench multi-core testing. These results are hardly surprising, given the Core Ultra X9 388H's modest clock-speed advantage over its competitors' Core Ultra X7 processors. Apple’s M5-powered MacBook Pro proved to be the system to beat, though its performance advantages aren’t large enough to diminish HP’s excellent overall results. We challenge all systems' graphics with a quintet of animations or gaming simulations from UL's 3DMark test suite. The first two, Wild Life (1440p) and Wild Life Extreme (4K), use the Vulkan graphics API to measure GPU speeds. The next pair, Steel Nomad's regular and Light subtests, focuses on APIs more commonly used for game development to assess gaming geometry and particle effects. Last up, we turn to 3DMark Solar Bay to measure ray-tracing performance. Intel's Arc B390 integrated GPU doesn't transform the OmniBook Ultra 14 outright into a great gaming laptop, though we've seen how the Arc B390, in other tests, is more than up to the task of casual gaming. (That's largely beside the point with any premium ultraportable, of course.) However, the silicon kept the laptop competitive with the rest of the pack, delivering strong results throughout our graphics testing. The XPS 14, ExpertBook Ultra, and Laptop 13 Pro performed similarly, which you'd expect considering that they also rely on the Arc B390 in the configurations we tested. Apple’s MacBook Pro remained formidable, but the OmniBook nosed ahead of it in two out of the three tests the MacBook was compatible with. We test each laptop and tablet's battery life by playing a locally stored 720p video file (the open-source Blender movie Tears of Steel) with the display brightness set to 50% and the audio volume at 100%. We make sure the battery is fully charged before the test, with Wi-Fi and keyboard backlighting turned off. To gauge display performance, we use a Datacolor SpyderX Elite monitor calibration sensor and its software to measure a laptop screen's color saturation—what percentage of the sRGB, Adobe RGB, and DCI-P3 color gamuts or palettes the display can show—and its 50% and peak brightness in nits (candelas per square meter). It’s tough to fault the OmniBook Ultra 14’s battery life, which should comfortably power through a cross-country flight or a full day off the outlet. If you want to quibble, several of its rivals showed the same outstanding stamina. HP's OLED display also deserves praise. While it didn't match the searing brightness of the ExpertBook Ultra or Framework Laptop 13 Pro, HP still chose well. Its sharp resolution, near-complete DCI-P3 color coverage, and high brightness offer the premium viewing experience expected at this price. While brighter screens are available, few people will walk away disappointed by this panel. Final Thoughts HP OmniBook Ultra 14 (2026) - 5.0 - Exemplary: Near perfection, ground-breaking - 4.5 - Outstanding: Best in class, acts as a benchmark for measuring competitors - 4.0 - Excellent: A performance, feature, or value leader in its class, with few shortfalls - 3.5 - Good: Does what the product should do, and does so better than many competitors - 3.0 - Average: Does what the product should do, and sits in the middle of the pack - 2.5 - Fair: We have some reservations, buy with caution - 2.0 - Subpar: We do not recommend, buy with extreme caution - 1.5 - Poor: Do not buy this product - 1.0 - Dismal: Don't even think about buying this product Read Our Editorial Mission Statement and Testing Methodologies. Few laptops feel as complete as the HP OmniBook Ultra 14. Its premium design, OLED screen, excellent webcam and speakers, strong performance, and long battery life make this a compelling package that’s worthy of its flagship status. Naturally, it's priced to match, but no more so than rivals like Dell's XPS 14 and Apple's 14-inch MacBook Pro. Its balance of style, refinement, and everyday usability earns it an easy Editors' Choice recommendation as one of the finest premium Windows ultraportables. About Our Expert Computers are my lifelong obsession. I wrote my first laptop review in 2005 for NotebookReview.com, continued with a consistent PC-reviewing gig at Computer Shopper in 2014, and moved to PCMag in 2018. Here, I test and review the latest high-performance laptops and desktops, and sometimes a key core PC component or two. I also review enterprise computing solutions for StorageReview. I work full-time as a technical analyst for a business software and services company. My hobbies are digital photography, fitness, two-stroke engines, and reading. I’m a graduate of the Rochester Institute of Technology.

item.title: Gmail’s hidden trick: One inbox, endless custom addresses
item.description:
Source: PCWorld Score: 5.28
For those who read this newsletter, you’re probably aware that Gmail can do a lot more than most people think. But there’s one neat trick you may not know about and it’s called “plus addressing.” Add a plus sign and a word of your choosing after your address, and Gmail will deliver the message to your main inbox. Go ahead and give it a try: send a test email to [email protected]. It lands right where your regular mail does. So that’s cool, but what’s the point? First, you can sort your mail without lifting a finger. Gmail’s filters let you search for a specific plus address and route it straight to a label or folder. Set up a filter for “+shopping,” and every receipt and promo lands in one place, out of your main inbox. Second (this is why I use it), you can catch companies that sell your address info. If [email protected] starts getting spam from unrelated senders, you know exactly which website sold or leaked your information—not that they’d ever do such a thing, of course. There’s a catch, though. Not every website accepts a plus sign in an email address. Some sign-up forms will reject it outright or throw an error. When that happens, you can fall back to a temporary email service or just use your regular address instead. Plus, addressing is really easy to set up and you don’t have to create new accounts. Give it a try next time you sign up for something new. For more fun and helpful tips, tricks, website and app recommendations, be sure to subscribe to our PCWorld Try This newsletter.

item.title: Windows 11’s September patch breaks USB audio, and there’s no fix yet
item.description:
Source: PCWorld Score: 4.56
Microsoft recently confirmed that the September Patch Tuesday security update (KB5124008) is causing problems with USB audio on some Windows 11 systems. However, Microsoft did not disclose how many users are affected, only stating that some computers with USB Audio Class 1.0 devices are reportedly affected. On the support page for the update, Microsoft has listed this under its “Known issues in this update” section: After installing the September 8, 2026, Windows security update, some USB Audio Class 1.0 devices might fail to start or produce audio. Affected devices might experience one or more of the following symptoms: - The device displays an error in Device Manager: “This device cannot start (Code 10).” - No audio output. - Volume controls are unresponsive or remain at zero. - Sound settings are unresponsive or unavailable. - Some devices might function in standard stereo configurations but fail when using multichannel audio features, including 8-channel or 3D audio modes. Some customers have reported that they’re able to restore audio in these cases by switching to 2-channel mode. This issue is limited to USB Audio Class 1.0 devices. Unfortunately, there’s no known workaround for this problem as of this writing. The issue affects Windows 11 versions 25H2 and 24H2, as well as 26H1 via update KB5124012. Microsoft says it’s working on a resolution and will update the support page once more information is available.

item.title: Windows 11 has a secret way to skip the Microsoft account requirement
item.description:
Source: PCWorld Score: 4.56
Microsoft really wants you to use a Microsoft account when setting up Windows 11, and that’s why the company has been killing the workarounds for using Windows 11 with only a local account. Even so, a new trick—one that’s incredibly simple—has just been discovered. This newly discovered trick allows you to bypass the mandatory Microsoft account requirement when installing Windows 11, and it doesn’t involve any complicated workarounds, terminal commands, tampered installation files, or fancy maneuvers. All it takes is a mouse click. When you’re setting up Windows 11 on a new PC, click on “Sign in” on the login screen. A window will appear where you’re asked to enter your Microsoft account. However, both in the descriptive text and at the bottom of the screen, you’ll also see the “Learn more” option. Click on that text without entering a Microsoft account. You’ll then see a screen where you can create a local username and password. After that, if you wish, you can disable a few options that allow Microsoft to gather data like your location and diagnostic information, and all you have to do is click “Next” and “Accept.” It’ll take a few minutes for Windows 11 to set up your local user account and finish the rest of the installation process. You can then use this Windows 11 PC without a Microsoft account. A user named @TheBobPony shared and demonstrated the procedure via this social media post, in which he reports that this method does in fact work reliably with a current Windows 11 Home installation. Why does it work? Well, it’s most likely a bug. Microsoft will probably remove this method of setting up a Windows 11 PC without a Microsoft account in the near future. But for now, you can take advantage.

item.title: This free PowerToys command bar replaces several Windows search features
item.description:
Source: PCWorld Score: 4.30
The Microsoft PowerToys suite for Windows include the Command Palette, a tool that is often overlooked but actually offers a vast range of functions. For example, the program includes a search function that combines several other Windows search features into a single interface. The easiest way to install the PowerToys is via the Microsoft Store. Once the installation is complete, launch the software, then open the ‘System’ section on the left-hand side of the window and click on ‘Command Palette.’ You can accept the default settings. To access the tool’s command line, press the Windows-Alt-Space key combination. Now you’re ready to go: By typing the > (greater than) symbol, a command line opens, allowing you to search for Windows commands. Foundry For example, type ping here and click ‘Run’ at the bottom of the window. Many users now use the Windows package manager Winget to install programs. The Command Palette can show you which apps Winget supports. To do this, type winget into the input bar and click ‘Search for apps with Winget.’ Type the name of a program, such as vlc, and click on the name of the software in the results list to install it directly. You can also use the Command Palette to search for Windows settings. To do this, type $ (dollar sign) followed by the setting you want, such as keyboard. The program also monitors the Registry. Type : (colon) followed by the name of a registry folder, such as HKEY_Local_Machine\Software\Microsoft, to open the Registry Editor directly at this path. Finally, typing ?? will launch a web search. The Command Palette will open your default browser and load your preferred search engine.

The 24-inch touchscreen is a nice touch that keeps things simple accessible. I do think that the 128GB SSD is pretty limited, though, so be aware that you’ll probably need to invest in external storage at some point. Computer deals FAQ What are good websites to find computer deals? There are a ton of sites that sell computers, and scouring through all of them would take you a lot of time—that’s why we do it for you here and highlight the best deals we find. However, to save you some time and frustration, you need to be smart about where you look at any given time of the year. If you’re looking for a new computer during the holidays or around popular sale periods such as Black Friday or back-to-school, then you are likely to find great deals directly through first party vendor websites. These include the retail storefronts of popular computer manufacturers such as HP, Dell, and Lenovo. However, if you are looking in between sales periods, it’s generally a good idea to search through large third-party retailers such as Amazon, Adorama, Walmart, BestBuy, and Newegg. Oftentimes these websites will offer limited Deals of the Day type sales in hopes of getting rid of excess stock. On the upside, you can score still-decent PCs at a steep discount. When’s the best time to shop for a PC computer? Typically you’ll want to time your PC computer shopping around a prominent sales period. The biggest sales periods are Black Friday/Cyber Monday in late November and Amazon Prime Day in early-to-mid July. The best sales often occur leading up to and during these two events and they are great times to snag a new PC computer for cheap. Other holiday shopping periods such as the New Year sales in January, President’s Day sales in February, and the back-to-school sales event in August are also good times to find discounts on computers. What type of desktop should I get? You’ll see a ton of options when searching for a desktop computer, but they all mainly fit into four main categories: productivity tower PCs, gaming PCs, mini PCS, and all-in-ones (AiO). Which you should end up buying is entirely dependent upon what your needs are and what you want to do with your computer. If you are looking for something that will work in a home office or family room, then a productivity PC or AiO with a solid CPU and lots of RAM and storage is probably the way to go. If gaming is your main concern, a gaming PC can offer a lot more bang for your buck than a laptop and you should focus on getting the best GPU possible. Or if you just want something that can fit anywhere and provide basic computing then a mini PC is a good bet. What CPU and GPU should I get? When looking at your new computer’s CPU, get at least an Intel Core i5 or AMD Ryzen 5, both of which will provide plenty of processing power for everyday computing tasks. If you don’t intend to do any PC gaming, then feel free to save some money by going with integrated graphics. However, if you are looking to get your game on, we recommend at least an Nvidia GeForce 3060 or AMD Radeon RX 6600 XT, as these are the least expensive discrete graphics cards that can handle ray tracing well. If you aren’t interested in those cutting-edge lighting effects, however, the RTX 3050 and Radeon RX 6600 also provide decent 1080p gaming performance at even lower prices. The RTX 5070 is a strong midrange card that will allow for high settings at 1440p while the RTX 5080 is capable of decent 4K gaming if that’s more your speed. For those who won’t compromise for anything besides the best, the RTX 5090 is really your only option currently. How much memory and storage does my PC need? As for RAM, we think its best to shoot for 16GB at the minimum for productivity and gaming, but for family computers and internet browsing, 8GB should suffice. Storage size is dependent upon your personal needs, but it is generally a good idea to opt for an SSD over an standard HDD as they are much faster and don’t significantly affect the price of a desktop. Before deciding, it’s best to consider what your intended use of the computer will be. Are you just doing work or web browsing? Then something like 512GB will be plenty. If you want to load up a lot of large files such as games or content creation projects, then you’ll need at least 1 or 2TB or storage. However, just remember that even if your computer doesn’t have enough storage built-in you can always upgrade your SSD or go with an external drive to increase your available storage options. Is it a good idea to buy a refurbished computer? Refurbished computers are used machines that have been repaired, upgraded, and cleaned for the purpose of reselling. They’re usually open-box returns, overstock, or models with minor cosmetic damage (scratches, scuffs, etc). Refurbished computers can be a bargain hunter’s dream as they’re likely still in good (or great) condition and you can save a lot of money. That being said, refurbished computers can have their downsides as well. In addition to cosmetic blemishes, some of the internal components might be a little older or outdated and they might not be in peak condition due to previous usage. If you do consider buying a refurbished computer I recommend looking at eBay as they offer a one-year warranty. You can also check out manufacturer’s retail storefronts like Dell’s Outlet Store and Apple’s Refurbished Store—just be sure to look at the terms of warranty offered before purchasing.

Best deals on Intel mini PCs ACEMAGIC K1, Core i5-12600H/16GB DDR4 RAM/512GB SSD/triple 4K support—$440 (24% off on Amazon) My favorite Intel-powered mini PC deal right now is the ACEMAGIC K1 for $139 off on Amazon. The Core i5-12600H is a modern, capable processor that should have no trouble handling demanding productivity and multitasking work. Beelink Mini S12 Pro, Intel N100/16GB DDR4 RAM/500GB SSD/dual 4K support—$369 (14% off on Amazon) The Beelink Mini S12 Pro is $70 off on Amazon, making this compact PC a decent pick for basic everyday use. Its Intel N100 processor is modest, but it has more than enough power for web browsing, streaming, office apps, and other light tasks. You also get 16GB of DDR4 RAM and a 500GB SSD, so there’s plenty of memory and storage for a budget machine. GMKtec G3 Pro, Core i3-10110U/16GB DDR4 RAM/512GB SSD/dual 4K support—$330 (28% off on Amazon) At $130 off on Amazon, the GMKtec G3 Pro is a solid budget mini PC for everyday tasks. Admittedly, its Core i3-10110U is getting a little long in the tooth, but it still has enough power for web browsing, office work, streaming, and other light productivity. You also get 16GB of DDR4 RAM and a 512GB SSD, which is a decent setup for the price. Dual 4K display support, Wi-Fi 6, and 2.5Gb Ethernet add surprisingly nice connectivity at this price point as well. GMKtec Mini PC, Core i7-1185G7/16GB DDR4 RAM/512GB SSD/triple 4K support—$470 (27% off on Amazon) At $180 off on Amazon, this GMKtec Mini PC is worth a look if you want an affordable Intel system with plenty of connectivity. The Core i7-1185G7 is getting a little long in the tooth, but it still has enough muscle for everyday productivity, multitasking, and general home or office use. It comes with 16GB of DDR4 RAM and a 512GB SSD, which is a sensible (and affordable) setup for most people. You also get an unusually good selection of ports and networking options, including USB4, 2.5Gb Ethernet, HDMI, DisplayPort, and Wi-Fi 6. Mini PC deals FAQ What should you look for when buying a mini PC? The first thing you have to check off your list is just what configuration you need to get your job done. Are you going to use your new mini PC for browsing only? Then a cheap budget-friendly device with a decent CPU and 16GB of RAM will do the trick. Do you want it to be able to juggle a bunch of apps and not choke on 50 browser tabs? Then a more powerful CPU and at least 32GB of RAM would be better. Do you want to do some light gaming in your downtime? Look for a device that comes with a GPU or Occulink connectivity to hook up an external GPU instead. Are you looking to utilize the mini PC as a home server? Your priority then should be a large SSD—2TB or more. There are devices for each and every one of these scenarios, and they’re all quite affordable. The best part is that mini PCs are… well, small, so they can be placed practically anywhere depending on your intended use and available space. They also support multiple monitors out of the box, which makes it easy to replace your old, larger desktop and you won’t even need to pay for extra hubs. Can a mini PC replace a desktop computer? For most people, the answer is “yes”! Mini PCs are definitely powerful enough to replace desktops for most users, especially if you’re going to use it for work, browsing, or streaming movies. If you want something for photo and video editing, or even gaming, there are models that allow you to do that, but they’ll cost a bit more. If you’re into hardcore gaming, however, you’re still better off with a proper gaming PC or laptop. Can a mini PC run modern games? Mostly, yes. But it will ultimately depend upon the mini PC you buy and which modern games you want to play. Some high-performance mini PCs can run modern AAA games. You might not be able to run them at the highest settings though, and performance will depend heavily on the specific hardware. If you do want to game on a mini PC, look for powerful models with dedicated discrete GPUs such as an Nvidia RTX or AMD Radeon rather than integrated graphics. Alternatively, you can opt for cloud streaming services to game on less powerful mini PCs, which bypasses the need for high-end hardware. Which mini PC brands are reliable? Some of the most reliable mini PC brands are Minisforum, Beelink, GMKtec, and Geekom. Of course Apple’s Mac minis are also excellent computers if you prefer using macOS. Brands such as Asus, Lenovo, HP, and Dell all make high-quality smaller-footprint PCs, but they might not fill the same niche and/or they are typically more expensive.

item.title: Your PC knows your age. Your TV knows what you watch. Privacy is disappearing
item.description:
Source: PCWorld Score: 2.94
Privacy used to be a default feature of technology. Computers didn’t know who you were. Nor did any of the other appliances and devices living in our homes. I can’t say the same in 2026. Convenience is now eating privacy alive—and few people are aware. (Who can blame my friends and family for tuning me out when I sound like gloom and doom?) But this past week, we’ve had two examples that show just how times have changed. Welcome to Safe Mode, your weekly report for pressing security and privacy news—and what steps to take next. Want this newsletter to come directly to your inbox? Sign up on our website! Most recently, Microsoft announced a new API for Windows—”Windows Age API.” Normally, developer talk lacks buzz for us consumers, but this embedded support for age verification upends decades of expectations. Before, user anonymity was the baseline. Windows had no centralized system for checking age. But now, this API will unify and streamline that process across everything Windows touches, including apps and services. The idea is to simplify age protections for parents and developers—reducing the need for parents to comb through individual app settings, and for developers to program their own age verification systems. Apps and services can query Windows to see if a Microsoft account owner is old enough. But to set that age, Microsoft will require information it’s never previously asked for—either a selfie (for estimation of age based on your face), document upload, or logging into a government digital identity platform (e.g., Singpass) where applicable. And that data may pass through multiple hands—Microsoft lists two partners who handle the verification process, Yoti and Verifymy. Meanwhile, on the less personal yet creepier side of the spectrum, LG found itself as hot news, thanks to an investigative report focused on its smart TVs. Just before Labor Day, YouTube channel Gamers Nexus published a two-hour video detailing how LG televisions capture info on all devices connected to your home network; record audio conversations; and monitor what you watch on the TV. And none of the behavior requires an internet connection to activate. LG In response to these damning accusations, LG released a statement to defend its TV features. The scanning helps with connecting to nearby devices. The other features must be opted into by users. Otherwise, its TVs do not collect or record conversations. LG may actually not intend to spy on customers—at least, not in the way people could think after watching the Gamers Nexus video. But functionally, smart TVs do just that. The collection of information happens silently, its scope broader than most people realize. More granular, too. For example, Automatic Content Recognition (ACR) samples video and audio from what you watch to figure out your viewing habits. You can be disconnected from a streaming service but still monitored anyway. Of course, you can take steps to reduce the surveillance. And many people will say they don’t care, as they have nothing to hide. But these Microsoft and LG examples show the problem with modern technology: the lack of transparency. The more our devices adapt to us, the more companies observe us. And yet, they wrap their efforts in soft-touch marketing language. No one wants to leave children defenseless against online predators. No one wants to think they’re constantly being studied by strangers. So no one stops to ask if sensitive data is being collected, much less the amount. Nor ask who gets to see the info. Companies end up with intimate details about you. They learn things that used to be reserved only for governments on one end of the spectrum, and those who lived with you on the other. Then they share those details. Without knowing exactly the how, what, and when of data collection, you can’t make an informed decision about how, what, and when you choose to share about your life. You won’t know much about a company’s partners, or even bother to consider when visiting friends what smart devices they own, much less which features they use. You’ll probably get caught in a data breach that happens to a company you’ve never heard of. In today’s world, we now must spend increasing time and energy—if not outright cash—toward preserving our privacy. I’m starting to think of it as a luxury feature that’s becoming rapidly harder to afford. In the news Hackers keep notching their belts with more leaks and exploits—all while AI agents crank up general chaos online. In particular, if you’re a driver in the U.S., watch out for scams and phishing attempts related to your license info. Mira Kireeva / Unsplash The bad: - Famed hacking group ShinyHunters says it breached Florida’s DMV database, stealing 200K records. This news comes on the heels of 153 million U.S. and Canadian driver’s licenses leaking to the dark web, making it the second hit to drivers this month. Again, lock down your credit, banking, and tax info asap. The ugly: - AI companies continue to share discoveries of their AI agents escaping and plotting on the open web. In particular, OpenAI recently shared how its AI agents took over an old German-language wiki to help each other escape their sandboxes. Just one more thing to watch for on the web—community spaces may become increasingly filled with bots. The fascinating: - Nightmare Eclipse is still beefing with Microsoft, this time disclosing another Defender zero-day exploit—one that bypasses the fix just issued for an earlier vulnerability also discovered by Nightmare Eclipse (“ShieldBreak”). This cat-and-mouse game ultimately benefits Windows users, with a bit of entertainment thrown in on the side. Tip of the week Thomas Joos Want to stay more anonymous while using your PC? If you’re up for trying a new operating system, Linux may be a worthwhile alternative to Windows (and Microsoft’s greater accommodation of age verification mandates). For now, this free, open-source software isn’t required to verify user identities. You can get started by trying a version of Linux (“distros”) that looks and feels more like Windows. Two that get most recommended are ZorinOS and Mint. Of the two, ZorinOS will feel more modern and familiar, but Mint shines in its rock-solid performance and stability.

item.title: Best SSDs: From SATA to PCIe 5.0, from budget to premium
item.description:
Source: PCWorld Score: 2.65
Solid state drives, or SSDs, are singularly responsible for vast improvements to PC performance over the last decade or so. Taking the place of mechanical hard drives, SSDs transformed once-ponderous boot times into being virtually instantaneous, programs and games are far more responsive, and the frustratingly long large-file loads are largely a thing of a past. If you’re not yet using an SSD, you are missing out. If you already have an older SSD, you might consider upgrading it for the even speedier performance offered by cutting-edge PCIe 4.0 and 5.0 designs — if your PC sports those technologies, of course. At a glance | | | | Check on Amazon | | Show Pros & Cons Pros Cons Hide Pros & Cons | | | | | | | | View Deal | | Show Pros & Cons Pros Cons Hide Pros & Cons | | | | | | | | View Deal | | Show Pros & Cons Pros Cons Hide Pros & Cons | | | | | | | | View Deal | | Show Pros & Cons Pros Cons Hide Pros & Cons | | | | | | | | View Deal | | Show Pros & Cons Pros Cons Hide Pros & Cons | | | | | | | | View Deal | | Show Pros & Cons Pros Cons Hide Pros & Cons | | | | | | | | View Deal | | Show Pros & Cons Pros Cons Hide Pros & Cons | | | | | | | | View Deal | | Show Pros & Cons Pros Cons Hide Pros & Cons | | | | | | | | View Deal | | Show Pros & Cons Pros Cons Hide Pros & Cons | | | | That said, a premium drive may not deliver any more real-world performance than a bargain drive. Mainstream software, including Windows Explorer has yet to implement the numerous performance tricks, such as multiple queues, that NVMe SSDs offer. PROMOTION EaseUS PDF Editor – Edit, Convert, Compress & Protect PDFs Integrate PDF maker, PDF editor, PDF converter, and PDF reader in one full pack with all the basics you need. The clean interface simplifies your PDF work to edit, convert, comment, annotate, merge, split, background, page, watermark, sign PDFs, or fill forms. Your PDF workloads are down by batch processing efficiently. Now 25% OFF Exclusive Code: PCWORLD25 Free Download One very large exception: FastCopy — a file copy and sync utility that allows your SSD to realize its full potential. We highly recommend it for transferring large amounts of data. It will save you tons of time, as will, oddly enough, the command-line utility Xcopy, if you want to exercise your inner geek. Our recommendations cover both internal SSDs (NVMe picks are listed first, SATA picks second) and external SSDs (listed last). See also PCWorld’s guide to the best external drives if you’re looking strictly for a portable storage solution. Note that due to the current global NAND storage (one of the many “benefits” of AI), SSD prices have skyrocketed, which renders some of the prices mentioned below and in the referenced review articles out of date. June 13, 2026: Phison E26-based SSDs have proven problematic in 80Gbps enclosures on Thunderbolt 5 Macs. Avoid them for that use. Why you should trust PCWorld for SSD reviews and buying advice: It’s in our name, PCWorld. Our reviewers have been testing PC hardware for decades. Our storage evaluations are thorough and rigorous, testing the limits of every product — from performance benchmarks to the practicalities of daily use. As PC users ourselves, we know what makes a product stand out. Only the best SSDs make this list. Which SSD should you buy? | If you need… | What to buy | Why | |---|---|---| | The best SSD for most PCs | PCIe 4.0 NVMe, 1TB or 2TB | Fast enough for nearly all everyday, gaming, and productivity workloads without the PCIe 5.0 price premium | | A gaming SSD | PCIe 4.0 NVMe, ideally 1TB+ | Modern games are large, and Gen 4 performance is already more than enough for most gaming PCs | | The fastest possible SSD | PCIe 5.0 NVMe | Best for heavy file transfers and demanding workloads, but more expensive and unnecessary for most users | | An upgrade for an older PC | 2.5-inch SATA SSD | Much faster than a hard drive and widely compatible with older desktops and laptops | | A laptop SSD | M.2 NVMe that matches your laptop’s supported size and PCIe generation | Compatibility matters more than buying the fastest drive available | | More storage on a budget | 2TB mainstream NVMe | 2TB is a good balance of capacity and value for games, photos, video, and everyday files | For most people, a 1TB or 2TB PCIe 4.0 NVMe SSD is the sweet spot. PCIe 5.0 drives are faster on paper, but most users won’t notice much difference in normal Windows use or gaming. SATA is mainly worth considering for older PCs that don’t support NVMe. WD Black SN7100 SSD – Best PCIe 4.0 SSD Pros - Top-notch HMB performance - Affordable - Sexy name Cons - Slower random performance than DRAM designs Who should buy the WD Black SN7100/Optimus GX 7100? Users who want the fastest 1TB to 4TB PCIe 4.0 SSD that won’t break the bank, will want the WD Black SN7100, which is still available under that name but will be sold as the SanDisk Optimux GX 7100 going forward. (SanDisk was acquired, then recently divested by WD.) We were wowed by the 2TB version’s first-place finish among host memory buffer (HMB/DRAM-less) SSDs in our benchmarks. It also beat out a number of DRAM designs. WD Black SN7100/SanDisk Optimus GX 7100: Further considerations The fact that it’s an HMB design, i.e. it uses your system’s memory for primary caching duties as opposed to featuring DRAM onboard, means the SN7100 is very competitively priced. We’re talking close to $50 less than our previous pick, the Solidigm P44 Pro, for both the 1TB and 2TB capacities. Combine that with an industry-standard five-year warranty / 600TBW rating (terabytes that can be written) per TB, and you’re looking at the best PCIe 4.0 SSD for average users and gamers. Read our full WD Black SN7100 review WD SN5100/SanDisk Optimus 5100 – Best budget PCIe 4.0 SSD Pros - Very good PCIe 4.0 performer for most workloads - Single-sided design fits in just about any 2280 slot - Reputable vendor Cons - QLC slows down during very long writes Who should buy the WD Blue SN5100/SanDisk Optimus 5100? Granted, given recent AI-induced price inflation, calling any SSD “budget” is relative, but you will currently spend quite a bit less with this DRAM-less (HMB/Host Memory Buffer) design. Once available at 2TB for $150, the drive is now $280. Thanks, OpenAI. Still, the SN5100, now renamed as the SanDisk Optimus 5100, is at least available to purchase, which can’t be said for a lot of the competition. The WD Blue SN5100 is the successor to our former bargain pick — the WD Blue SN5000. The newer drive exceeds its predecessor in most tests, particularly in sustained/sequential throughput. At the moment, the pricing of the two models is essentially the same, so we say go with the faster of the two. WD Blue SN5100/SanDisk Optimus 5100: Further considerations In our testing, the Blue SN5100 ranked third among all the HMB SSDs we’ve tested — and was first by a large margin writing our 450GB file. You lose nothing in sequential performance these days with HMB. The drive sports a five-year warranty limited by a TBW rating (terabytes that may be written) of 600TBW per 1TB of capacity. Read our full WD Blue SN5100 review Teamgroup Z540 – Best PCIe 5.0 SSD Pros - PCIe 5.0 - Up to 4TB in capacity - Second-fastest SSD we’ve tested overall Cons - Not particularly cheap Who should buy the Teamgroup Z540? Users looking for every last ounce of performance should be looking at this PCIe 5.0 SSD from Teamgroup. In all fairness, the Z540 traded benchmark wins and finished a hair behind our previous top pick the Crucial T705. But the Teamgroup Z540 beats that competitor when it comes to price, making it the new top pick for this category. Teamgroup Z540: Further considerations As with any PCIe 5.0 SSD, there are important caveats. For starters, you’re paying a hefty premium over extremely fast, and in some ways faster (real-world sequential performance) Host Memory Buffer NVMe PCIe 4.0 drives. Only if you use multi-threaded software and your system sports a late-gen Intel CPU (which the Phison PS5026-E26-52 controller inside this drive is optimized for), can you be assured of benchmarking-busting performance. Read our full Teamgroup Z540 PCIe 5 SSD review PNY CS2150 PCIe 5.0 SSD – Best budget PCIe 5.0 SSD Pros - Fast PCIe 5.0 HMB performer - Affordable for the speed - Maintains decent write rate after secondary cache is exhausted Cons - Not as fast as PCIe 5.0 DRAM designs Who should buy the PNY CS2150? Anyone who enjoys more for less will like this drive — serious coin can be saved on a PCIe 5.0 SSD by opting for a Host Memory Buffer (HNB) design such as PNY’s CS2150. Using the host system’s memory as the SSD’s primary cache instead of dedicated DRAM on the drive means significantly lower manufacturing costs. PNY CS2150: Further considerations HMB doesn’t stop the CS2150 from competing with more expensive SSDs. Indeed, the 2TB version that we tested placed 9th overall among all types of NVMe SSDs and it ran neck-in-neck with the Corsair MP700 — another HMB SSD whose performance impressed us. PNY’s CS2150 trumps its Corsair peer by costing from $10 to $40 less than the latter in the 1TB and 2TB versions, respectively. You still get the industry standard standard five-year warranty and 600TBW (terabytes that can be written) guarantee. If you have the PCIe 5.0 M.2 slot to support it, this SSD is an affordable way to performance future-proof your storage. Read our full PNY CS2150 review SanDisk Optimus GX 7100M – Best SSD for Steam Deck Pros - The fastest PCIe 4.0 SSD I’ve tested to date - Especially excellent 4K performance - 2230 form factor fits handheld gaming devices Cons - Really, really expensive Who should buy the Sandisk Optimus GX 7100M?
